# Tryll Engine

> On-device SLM inference for games and tools — C++, Python, Unity, Unreal.

Tryll runs small language models **on the player's own machine**. A C++ TCP server hosts
the models; game code drives it through a client library (Unity C#, Unreal C++, C++, or
Python) over a binary FlatBuffers protocol. There is no cloud API and no per-token cost.

A Tryll **agent** is not a prompt — it is a **workflow graph** of typed nodes that
communicate through named **slots** on a per-turn blackboard. Read
`concepts/workflows-graphs-nodes.md` and `concepts/slots-and-inter-node-value-passing.md`
before writing any graph.

Facts that are easy to get wrong, because they differ from cloud LLM SDKs:

- Models are **never** auto-downloaded. Acquire a model first (editor Model Manager, or
  `DownloadModel` over the wire); otherwise `CreateAgent` fails with
  `GraphCompilationFailed`.
- `CreateSession` is **mandatory and one-shot**. Every other request before it is
  rejected with `SessionNotReady`.
- Graph wiring lives on each node's own params as `<exit_name>_exit` string fields
  (`default_exit`, `then_exit`, …); an empty string means END. There is no `routes` array.
- Wire delivery is `send: SendAnswer {None, Whole, Streamed}` and cross-turn history
  replay is `history_role`. There is no `stream: bool`.
- Client node enums (`NodeType`, `TryllNodeType`) and the wire `NodeParams` union use
  **two different numbering schemes**. Never translate between them by hand.
- Some node params are **structural** and fixed for the agent's lifetime;
  `ChangeAgentParam` rejects them with `ParamNotMutable`.

# Getting Started

# Tryll

**On-device AI for games and tools.** Tryll runs small language models — and speech recognition, speech synthesis, and vector search — on the player's own machine. Instead of a single prompt call, you compose an **agent**: a workflow graph of typed nodes that retrieves from your own data, calls your game's functions, speaks and listens, and reads live game state. First-party clients for **Unity 6**, **Unreal Engine 5**, **C++**, and **Python** drive it over a binary protocol. No cloud API, no per-token cost, no network round-trip.

## Start here

New to Tryll? Read **[Tryll in Ten Minutes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tryll-in-ten-minutes.html)** first — the whole idea in one sitting. Then pick your engine:

- **Unity 6**

  Drop a `TryllAgentComponent` on a GameObject and chat with it.

  [First inference in Unity →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-unity.html)

- **Unreal Engine 5**

  Drop a `UTryllAgentComponent` on an actor and chat with it.

  [First inference in Unreal →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-unreal.html)

- **Python**

  Pip-install the client and see streaming tokens in 20 lines.

  [First inference in Python →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-python.html)

- **C++**

  Clone, configure, build, and run a tiny chat demo.

  [First inference in C++ →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-cpp.html)

## What Tryll gives you

- **A local model host.** One server process, many clients. It loads a model once and shares it across every session that needs it, and it ships *inside* the Unity package and Unreal plugin — there is no separate server to install or point at. [Model management →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html)
- **Agents are workflow graphs, not prompts.** An agent is a typed graph of [nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html) — generate, retrieve, classify, branch, call a tool, speak — wired by named exits and passing values to each other through a per-turn [slot](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/slots-and-inter-node-value-passing.html) blackboard. [Workflows, graphs, and nodes →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/workflows-graphs-nodes.html)
- **Your data, your rules.** Ground answers in your own lore with on-device [retrieval](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/rag.html) (dense, lexical, or hybrid), force machine-readable output with a [GBNF grammar](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/constrained-output.html), and short-circuit off-topic or out-of-character input before a model ever runs.
- **Voice both ways.** Streaming [text-to-speech](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tts-and-voice-output.html) with zero-shot voice cloning, and streaming [speech-to-text](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/stt-and-voice-input.html) with push-to-talk or hands-free turn taking — both on-device, alongside the language model.
- **Live game state in, real actions out.** [Agent variables](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) push the player's level, mood, or inventory straight into prompts and retrieval filters, and [tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html) lets the model invoke your functions and answer from the results.
- **Four first-party clients, and editor tooling.** Thin, idiomatic wrappers over the same wire protocol — [Unity](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unity/index.html) · [Unreal](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unreal/cpp/index.html) · [C++](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/cpp/index.html) · [Python](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/python/index.html) — plus a visual graph editor, model manager, chat window, and turn inspector inside both engines.

- **[Reference](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/index.html)** — every field, every enum, every error code.

## What you can build

- **An NPC that talks in character** — and keeps doing it over a long conversation, because history is projected and trimmed for you. [Design an NPC prompt →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-npc-prompt.html)
- **An NPC that knows your world** — quest logs, item descriptions, faction lore, indexed on-device and retrieved per line of dialogue. [Create a simple RAG assistant →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/create-simple-rag-assistant.html)
- **An NPC that acts** — the model calls your functions (open the door, set the price, start the quest), you run them, and it answers from the real result. [Define and handle tool calls →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html)
- **A conversation you can hold out loud** — the player speaks, the character answers in a cloned voice, all locally. [Add voice output →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html) · [Use voice input →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html)
- **Output your game code can trust** — a grammar makes a reply parse-safe by construction, and game code can own the numbers while the model owns the wording. [Constrain output with a grammar →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/constrain-output-with-a-grammar.html) · [Keep merchant prices deterministic →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/keep-merchant-prices-deterministic.html)
- **A character that stays in its world** — reject jailbreaks and out-of-character prompts with scripted replies, before spending a model call. [Build an immersion guard →](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/build-an-immersion-guard.html)

## Status and versioning

Tryll is in pre-release — expect breaking changes until the 1.0 API freeze. Every release documents what breaks and how to migrate; see the [release notes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/release-notes/index.html).

Docs are published per minor version (`/vX.Y/`). The header version switcher jumps between snapshots; an archived page shows a banner when you are not on the current release. To see which plugin you have installed, read `version` in Unity's `package.json`, `VersionName` in Unreal's `.uplugin`, or the `**Tryll plugin version:**` line in the package's `AGENTS.md`.

Tryll is currently in **closed beta**: the source repository is private and stays that way, and builds go to partners we have an agreement with. To report a problem or ask a question, email **[support@tryllengine.com](mailto:support@tryllengine.com)** — please include your Tryll version, engine and version, and the relevant server log.

# Getting Started

In about fifteen minutes you will install Tryll, download a model, and stream a reply from a language model running on your own machine. Pick the client that matches your project:

- **[First inference in Unity](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-unity.html)** Install the UPM package, add `TryllAgentComponent` to a GameObject, see streaming text in the Console. The server is bundled and launches itself.
- **[First inference in Unreal](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-unreal.html)** ★ Hero tutorial. Install the plugin, add `UTryllAgentComponent` to a sample actor, see streaming text in the Output Log. The server is bundled and launches itself.
- **[First inference in Python](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-python.html)** `pip install tryll-client`, a 20-line script, streamed tokens on stdout. You point it at a server yourself — see [Run the Tryll Server](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-the-tryll-server.html).
- **[First inference in C++](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-cpp.html)** Build the client library with CMake and run the `test-chat` console demo.

Each tutorial starts by downloading the distribution and ends with a working agent — including acquiring the model, which Tryll never does behind your back.

## What your machine needs

Tryll runs the model on the player's hardware, so the hardware is part of the design. Check this before you start.

**Operating system**

- **Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit.** Tryll ships as Windows x64 binaries — the server, the Unity package, the Unreal plugin, and the C++ client library. There is no Linux or macOS distribution.

**GPU**

- **8 GB of VRAM or more is the comfortable target.** That fits a quantised 7–8B model with a useful context window, and leaves room for speech synthesis and recognition running alongside it.
- **6 GB works** if you stay around **3B** models — a good fit for focused NPC dialogue, intent classification, and routing.
- **More VRAM is mostly about freedom to experiment**: larger models, longer contexts, and several agents resident at once. It is not required to ship something good.
- Speech recognition and the lighter Sherpa-ONNX voices (Supertonic, Pocket TTS) run on the **CPU** and cost no VRAM. The 3B voices, Orpheus and Maya1, are llama.cpp models: they follow the same GPU placement as a language model, and only their SNAC audio decoder stays on the CPU.

**Disk and RAM**

- **1.5–5 GB per language model**, plus a working internet connection the first time you download one.
- Budget **roughly the same again in system RAM**: a model file is memory-mapped *and* offloaded to the GPU, so it counts in both columns.

Work out the real numbers for a specific line-up with [Estimate the RAM and VRAM your setup needs](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html).

**Engine and language versions**

| Path   | Needs                                                                                    |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Unity  | Unity 6 (6000.x) or later                                                                |
| Unreal | Unreal Engine 5.7, a **C++** project (Blueprint-only projects cannot compile the plugin) |
| Python | Python 3.11 or newer                                                                     |
| C++    | Visual Studio 2022, CMake                                                                |

## What you will build

Each tutorial ends at the same milestone: the user sends one message, the server runs it through a minimal graph (just a `Generate` node), and the client prints the streamed reply. Everything else — retrieval, tool calls, voice, guardrails — builds on top of this pattern.

## After the tutorial

You have a one-node graph. These are the shortest paths to something that feels like a game feature:

- **Author the graph visually instead of in code.** [Edit workflows in the Unity graph editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/edit-workflows-in-graph-editor.html) or [in the Unreal graph editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/edit-workflows-in-unreal-graph-editor.html)
- **Iterate without entering Play mode.** [Test an agent in the editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-agent-in-editor.html)
- **Write a character worth talking to.** [Design an NPC prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-npc-prompt.html)
- **Ground answers in your own lore.** [Create a simple RAG assistant](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/create-simple-rag-assistant.html)
- **Give the character a voice.** [Add voice output to an agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html)
- **Feed it live game state.** [Drive prompts and retrieval from game state](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/drive-prompts-and-retrieval-from-game-state.html)

If you want the *why* before the *how*, start with [Tryll in Ten Minutes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tryll-in-ten-minutes.html).

# First Inference in Unity

Unpack a Tryll release, drop the package into your Unity project (the server is bundled inside it), configure one project setting, download a model through the Model Manager, and watch a single `Generate` node print its answer to the Console during Play Mode — no chat UI required.

Working with an AI coding agent?

The Unity package ships an **`AGENTS.md`** at its root. Attach it to your agent's context (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, …) before asking it to write Tryll code — it carries the graph/slot mental model and the ways Tryll differs from a cloud LLM SDK. Agents that fetch docs themselves can start from [`llms.txt`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/llms.txt).

## What you'll build

A scene with a `TryllAgentComponent` on a GameObject that, on `Start`, connects to a locally-spawned Tryll server and creates a one-node agent. You trigger the first inference by right-clicking the component in the Inspector (**Context Menu → Ask Tryll**), and the answer streams into the Unity Console.

## Before you start

- **Unity 6** (6000.x) or later, with a blank 3D project.
- **~5 GB free disk space** for the downloaded model and a working internet connection on first run.
- Familiarity with creating GameObjects, adding components, and writing a short C# MonoBehaviour.

You do **not** need to build anything from source — the distribution ships pre-generated FlatBuffers bindings.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1 — Get the distribution

1. Download `tryll-unity-<version>.7z` from the releases page and extract it somewhere temporary (e.g. `C:\Downloads\tryll\`).

1. Inside is the Unity package — **the server is bundled inside it**, so there is nothing else to install:

   ```
   UnityPlugin/                       <-- the UPM package (everything you need)
   ├── package.json
   ├── Runtime/
   ├── Editor/
   └── .Server/Default/               <-- bundled server (rides inside the package)
       ├── tryll_server.exe
       ├── llama.dll, ggml*.dll, ggml-vulkan.dll
       └── data/
           ├── server-config.json
           ├── models.json
           ├── default-canned-responses.txt
           └── default-guardrail-patterns.txt
   ```

The archive ships **no model weights** — you download the models your graph references up front through the Model Manager (Step 4). `CreateAgent` fails fast if a referenced model is not already on disk; the server does **not** download it for you at agent-creation time. In Client Dev, downloaded weights land under `<Project>/TryllStorage/models/`.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2 — Install the Unity package

Copy the `UnityPlugin/` folder into your project's `Packages/` directory and name it `com.tryll.client`. Unity auto-discovers embedded packages there, so there is **no `manifest.json` edit** to make:

```
<YourProject>/
├── Assets/
├── TryllStorage/                    <-- default storage root (outside Assets/)
├── Packages/
│   ├── manifest.json
│   └── com.tryll.client/        <-- copy UnityPlugin/* here
│       ├── package.json
│       ├── Runtime/
│       ├── Editor/
│       └── .Server/Default/     <-- server rides inside the package
└── <YourProject>.sln
```

Unity imports the package on focus; **Window → Package Manager → In Project** lists **Tryll Client**, and you should see no compile errors.

Keep the package **embedded** here (a writable folder) rather than in a read-only cache. Model downloads and authored storage files live under `<Project>/TryllStorage/`, not inside the package.

Add this to `.gitignore` if you do not want models in source control (committing them is optional):

```
/TryllStorage/models/
```

Nothing else to copy

The server binary and its `data/` ride **inside** the package's `.Server/Default/` folder, so installing the package installs the server too — one folder to drop in, one to update on a new release.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3 — Configure Tryll Client in Project Settings

Open **Edit → Project Settings → Tryll Client** and set:

| Setting                 | Value                    | Why                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Auto Launch Server**  | `true` (default)         | `TryllClient` spawns the bundled server automatically. Uncheck to run a server yourself.         |
| **Llama.cpp backend**   | `Vulkan` (default)       | Portable GPU API. Set `Auto` to prefer CUDA on NVIDIA (also ships CUDA DLLs in a player build).  |
| **Game Name**           | e.g. `my-game`           | Short slug for telemetry and the project-name fallback.                                          |
| **Storage Data Folder** | `TryllStorage` (default) | Project folder **outside** `Assets/`. The editor launches the server with `--storage-root` here. |

There is **no server-path setting** — the location is resolved from the package automatically, identically in the Editor and in packaged builds. Client Dev usage telemetry is always on in the editor; set `TRYLL_SERVER_MODE=tryll-dev` only for Tryll’s own CI. Player builds that still launch Client Dev are **unreleasable** until a Client Prod binary ships.

Settings are saved to `Assets/Resources/TryllRuntimeSettings.asset` (created on first access).

Models must be registered before use

`CreateAgent` fails fast if a referenced model is not already on disk — the server does not download it for you. Continue to Step 4 to download and register a model via the editor Model Manager before running the graph below.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4 — Download and register a model

Model name fields in the Inspector are **dropdown lists** populated from the models you have registered in this project. On a fresh installation those dropdowns are empty — you must open the Model Manager, download a model, and register it before it appears.

1. Open **Window → Tryll → Model Manager**.\
   The window launches the bundled server, connects, and lists every model the server knows about. Wait for the status indicator in the toolbar to show **● Ready**.

1. In the model list, find a language model to start with.\
   **Recommended:** `Gemma 3 4B Instruct (Q4_K_M)` (~3 GB download).\
   **Smaller / quicker:** `Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)` (~2 GB download).

1. Click the model row to select it. In the **Model properties** panel on the right:

   - Status shows **Absent** — the files are not on disk yet.
   - Click **Download**. A progress bar appears and the toolbar shows active download count.

1. Once the status changes to **Downloaded**, set the **Build registration** to **Experimental** (usable in the editor, excluded from packaged builds) or **Production** (shipped in builds).

   - For this tutorial, **Experimental** is fine.

1. Close the Model Manager.

The Model Manager writes a `TryllModelManifest` asset to `Assets/Resources/TryllModelManifest.asset`. Any `Model Name` dropdown in the Inspector now lists the models you registered here.

Registration controls build inclusion

**Experimental** models are available during development but stripped by the build post-processor when you build a player. **Production** models are staged into the `Server/` folder next to the player executable. A model that is downloaded but unregistered (status **None**) is invisible to the build system.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 5 — Create a workflow asset and set up the scene

1. In the Project window, right-click → **Create → Tryll → Workflow Asset**. Name it `DemoWorkflow`.
1. Select `DemoWorkflow`. In the Inspector, expand **Graph**:
   - Under **Nodes**, click **+** to add one entry.
   - Set **Name** = `answer`.
   - Click the **Params** type picker (shows `<null>` by default) and select **Generate** from the dropdown. The node's parameter fields expand below it — leave them all at their defaults; the **Default Exit** field stays empty, which routes the turn to END.
   - Set **Start Node** = `answer`.
   - Set **Default Model Name** using the dropdown — it now lists the models you registered in the Model Manager. Pick the one you downloaded in Step 4.
1. Create a new empty **GameObject** — call it `TryllDemo`.
1. Add a **Tryll Agent Component** (`Add Component → Tryll → Tryll Agent Component`).
1. Assign `DemoWorkflow` to the component's **Workflow Asset** field.
1. **Un-check Auto Create On Connect** — this tutorial wires the lifecycle explicitly so you control exactly when the agent is created.
1. Create a C# script `TryllDemo.cs` and attach it to the same GameObject:

```
using UnityEngine;
using Tryll.Client;

public class TryllDemo : MonoBehaviour
{
    private TryllAgentComponent _agent;

    void Start()
    {
        _agent = GetComponent<TryllAgentComponent>();

        _agent.OnAnswerText.AddListener((nodeName, text, isDelta, isFinal) =>
        {
            // Send = Streamed: every chunk is a delta, and the last one is an
            // empty terminator with isFinal = true.
            // Send = Whole: one chunk with isDelta = false and the full text.
            if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(text))
                Debug.Log($"[Tryll] {(isDelta ? "delta" : "reply")} from {nodeName}: {text}");
            if (isFinal)
                Debug.Log($"[Tryll] {nodeName} finished its answer");
        });

        _agent.OnTurnComplete.AddListener((status, debugInfo, tokens) =>
            Debug.Log($"[Tryll] turn complete — status={status} tokens={tokens}"));

        _agent.OnError.AddListener(error =>
            Debug.LogError($"[Tryll] error: {error}"));

        _agent.OnAgentCreated.AddListener(() =>
            Debug.Log("[Tryll] agent ready — right-click this component and choose 'Ask Tryll'"));

        var client = TryllClient.Instance;
        client.CreateSessionComplete += err =>
        {
            if (!err.IsOk) { Debug.LogError($"[Tryll] CreateSession failed: {err}"); return; }
            _agent.CreateAgent();
        };

        client.StartSession();
    }

    [ContextMenu("Ask Tryll")]
    void AskTryll()
    {
        if (!_agent.HasAgent)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning("[Tryll] agent not ready yet");
            return;
        }
        _agent.SendMessage("In one sentence: what is Tryll?");
    }
}
```

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 6 — Test without entering Play Mode

Before pressing **Play**, use the **Chat Window** to verify your setup is working:

1. Open **Window → Tryll → Chat**.
1. Confirm the **Tryll Settings** field shows your `TryllRuntimeSettings` asset (auto-found).
1. Drag the `TryllDemo` GameObject's **Tryll Agent Component** into the **Agent Component** slot.
1. Click **Start** — the window launches the server, connects, and creates the agent. The status label turns green: **Ready**.
1. Type a message and press **Enter**. You should see a streamed reply.
1. Click **Stop** when done.

See [Test an Agent in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-agent-in-editor.html) for the full walkthrough including troubleshooting.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 7 — Enter Play Mode

Press **Play**.

On the **first** run you'll see:

1. A brief pause while the server starts and the client connects.
1. The model loads from disk (a few seconds the first time it is used in a session) — this only works because you already downloaded and registered it in Step 4; `CreateAgent` fails fast otherwise.
1. The Console prints: `[Tryll] agent ready — right-click this component and choose 'Ask Tryll'`.

Once the agent is ready:

1. In the **Hierarchy**, select the `TryllDemo` GameObject.
1. In the **Inspector**, right-click the `TryllDemo` script component header and choose **Ask Tryll**.
1. Watch the Console — answer deltas stream in as `[Tryll] delta from answer: …` lines, then `[Tryll] answer finished its answer` and `[Tryll] turn complete`.

______________________________________________________________________

## Where to see what's happening

Open the **Console** window and filter by `[Tryll]`:

| Prefix          | Source                                               | Useful for                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `[TryllClient]` | `TryllClient` singleton                              | Connection attempts, session config, agent lifecycle.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `[TryllAgent]`  | `TryllAgentComponent`                                | Agent created/destroyed, `DownloadProgress`, errors.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `[TryllServer]` | `tryll_server.exe` stdout (re-emitted by the client) | `[Listener] Listening on 127.0.0.1:<port>` (in the editor, auto-launch binds loopback on the **Server Port** project setting, default 9100, and falls back to a free port only if that port is taken; player builds always pick a free port), model load lines, server errors. |

Client Dev writes one log file per run under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\` (project key from the sanitized game name plus a hash of the project directory).

______________________________________________________________________

## What you built

- A session connected to a Tryll server the client spawned for you.
- One agent with a one-node graph authored in the `DemoWorkflow` Workflow Asset (`Generate` node, driven by a model you downloaded and registered in the Model Manager).
- Model output surfaced as `OnAnswerText` events, which stream token-by-token by default (`Send = Streamed` on the `Generate` node); set `Send = Whole` for a single full-reply frame instead of delta chunks.
- A `[ContextMenu]` method as the simplest way to trigger a turn from the Inspector without any UI setup.

## Troubleshooting

- **Compile errors on import** — check that the package's `Runtime/Generated/` folder contains `.cs` files. If it's empty, the distribution was packaged without the FlatBuffers step; contact support or re-download.
- **`[TryllServer]` server not found** — the package's `.Server/Default/` folder is missing or empty. A release package ships it populated; if you cloned the repo instead, build the Tryll server so the committed `.Server/Default` symlink resolves to your build.
- **Model name dropdown is empty** — open the Model Manager (**Window → Tryll → Model Manager**), download a model, and set its build registration to **Experimental** or **Production**. Unregistered models do not appear in Inspector dropdowns.
- **Stuck at connecting** — the server crashed or didn't start in time. Check the Console for `[TryllServer]` lines and the Client Dev log under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\` as a fallback.
- **`CreateSession` fails** — usually a server-side error reading `models.json` or initialising the inference engine. Check `[TryllServer]` Console output.
- **`OnError` fires during `CreateAgent`** — read the error message. Common causes: **Default Model Name** is empty or doesn't match any entry in `models.json` (fails fast — download it via the Model Manager first), or a route targets a node that doesn't exist.
- **Right-clicking the script shows no `Ask Tryll` option** — you must be in Play Mode with the agent already created. Check the Console for the `agent ready` log line first.
- **Nothing appears in the Console** — confirm `OnAnswerText` is wired in `Start()` and that the script is attached to the same GameObject as `TryllAgentComponent`. With the default `Send = Streamed` on the `Generate` node, `OnAnswerText` fires once per chunk (`isDelta = true`), the last call is an empty terminator (`text` is empty, `isFinal = true`), and `OnTurnComplete` follows. Set `Send = Whole` to get a single full-reply frame (`isDelta = false`, `isFinal = true`).

# First Inference in Unreal

Unpack a Tryll release, drop the plugin into your Unreal project (the server is bundled inside it), set a few project settings, download a model through the Model Manager, and watch a single `Generate` node print its answer to the screen during PIE — no chat UI required.

Working with an AI coding agent?

The Unreal plugin ships an **`AGENTS.md`** at its root. Attach it to your agent's context (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, …) before asking it to write Tryll code — it carries the graph/slot mental model and the ways Tryll differs from a cloud LLM SDK. Agents that fetch docs themselves can start from [`llms.txt`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/llms.txt).

## What you'll build

A blank actor with a one-node workflow. You download a model up front in the Model Manager, then the plugin auto-launches a local Tryll server, connects, and creates the session for you; the agent component creates itself once the session is ready. The actor runs one inference turn with the prompt *"In one sentence: what is Tryll?"* and prints the answer to the viewport and the Output Log.

## Before you start

- **Unreal Engine 5.7** and a blank **C++** project (Blueprint-only projects can't compile the plugin source).
- **~5 GB free disk space** for the downloaded model and a working internet connection on first run.
- Familiarity with creating a Blueprint actor and binding events.

The Unreal plugin bundles the server and spawns it for you, so installing the plugin is the whole setup.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1 — Get the distribution

1. Download `tryll-unreal-<version>.7z` from the releases page and extract it somewhere temporary (e.g. `C:\Downloads\tryll\`).

1. Inside is the `UnrealPlugin/` folder — **the server is bundled inside it**, so this one folder is everything you install:

   ```
   UnrealPlugin/                     <-- everything you need for Unreal
   ├── TryllClient.uplugin
   ├── Generated/messages_generated.h
   ├── Source/
   └── Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/Default/  <-- bundled server
       ├── tryll_server.exe
       ├── llama.dll, ggml*.dll, ggml-vulkan.dll
       └── data/
           ├── server-config.json
           ├── models.json
           ├── default-canned-responses.txt
           └── default-guardrail-patterns.txt
   ```

The archive ships **no model weights** — you download the models your graph references up front through the Model Manager (Step 4). `CreateAgent` fails fast if a referenced model is not already on disk; the server does **not** download it for you at agent-creation time. In Client Dev, downloaded weights land under `<Project>/TryllStorage/models/`.

How the archive is built

`ci/scripts/release.py` builds the production server, then stages the Unreal plugin (FlatBuffers codegen + the server bundled into its `Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/Default/` folder) and zips it into a per-engine archive. The server's `data/server-config.json` is patched with production overrides and `models.json` is filtered to the shipping audience. The Unity package ships separately as `tryll-unity-<version>.7z`.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2 — Install the Unreal plugin

Copy the `UnrealPlugin/` folder into your project as `<YourProject>/Plugins/TryllClient/`:

```
<YourProject>/
├── TryllStorage/                    <-- default storage root (outside Content/)
├── Plugins/
│   └── TryllClient/
│       ├── TryllClient.uplugin
│       ├── Generated/messages_generated.h
│       ├── Source/TryllClient/{Public,Private}/
│       └── Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/Default/  <-- server rides along
└── <YourProject>.uproject
```

The bundled server ships inside the plugin, so installing the plugin places the server alongside it. The plugin resolves it at `<Plugin>/Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/<variant>/tryll_server.exe` via the plugin directory, so the path is identical in the editor and in packaged builds (a shipped plugin has just the `Default` variant). Auto-launch passes `--mode client-dev`, `--storage-root` (default `<Project>/TryllStorage/`), and related project flags. Models download into `TryllStorage/models/`.

Then:

1. Right-click `<YourProject>.uproject` → **Generate Visual Studio project files**.
1. Open the solution and build in **Development Editor**.
1. Launch the editor. **Edit → Plugins → Project** lists **Tryll Client** as enabled.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3 — Configure Tryll Client in Project Settings

Open **Edit → Project Settings → Plugins → Tryll Client** and set:

| Setting                                                    | Value                    | Why                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Auto Launch Server**                                     | `true` (default)         | Subsystem spawns the bundled server on `Initialize`. Uncheck to run a server yourself.                                                                |
| **Llama.cpp backend**                                      | `Vulkan` (default)       | Portable GPU API. Set `Auto` to prefer CUDA on NVIDIA (also ships CUDA DLLs in a packaged build).                                                     |
| **Auto Connect**                                           | `true` (default)         | Subsystem opens the session on `Initialize` (connect-retry covers server startup). Uncheck to call `Connect` yourself.                                |
| **Auto Create Session**                                    | `true` (default)         | On connect, the subsystem creates the session from the models you registered — no Blueprint wiring needed. Uncheck to call `Create Session` yourself. |
| **Connect Max Attempts** / **Connect Retry Delay Seconds** | defaults                 | Subsystem retries while the freshly-spawned server warms up.                                                                                          |
| **Game Name**                                              | e.g. `my-game`           | Short slug for telemetry and the project-name fallback. Please fill it.                                                                               |
| **Storage Data Folder**                                    | `TryllStorage` (default) | Project folder **outside** `Content/`. The plugin passes `--storage-root`.                                                                            |

Settings are persisted to `Config/DefaultGame.ini` under `[/Script/TryllClient.TryllRuntimeSettings]`.

Client Dev usage telemetry is always on in the editor; set `TRYLL_SERVER_MODE=tryll-dev` only for Tryll’s own CI. Player builds that still launch Client Dev are **unreleasable** until a Client Prod binary ships.

The Model Manager is the primary way to get models

You download and register your model up front in the next step, so it is already on disk before the first turn. `CreateAgent` fails fast if the model is not already there — it does not download it for you — so shipped builds rely on the Model Manager's registration tiers. See [Manage Models in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4 — Download and register a model

Before your agent can run, it needs a model on disk. Download one with the Model Manager and register it to your project, then you can select it on the workflow in the next step.

1. Open **Window → Tryll → Tryll Model Manager**. The window launches the bundled server, connects, and lists every model the server knows about. Wait for the toolbar status to read **Ready · *N* models** (green).
1. In the list, pick a language model to start with:
   - **Recommended:** `Gemma 3 4B Instruct (Q4_K_M)` (~3 GB download).
   - **Smaller / quicker:** `Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)` (~2 GB download).
1. Select the row. In the **Model Properties** panel on the right, the **Status** section shows **State: Not downloaded**. Click **Download** — a progress bar tracks the bytes and the toolbar shows the active download count.
1. When the state turns to **Downloaded**, set **Build registration (this project)** to **Experimental** — that makes it available in the editor, which is all this tutorial needs. (**Production** additionally ships the files inside packaged builds; choose that when you're ready to ship.)
1. Close the Model Manager.

Registrations live in your project, written to `Config/DefaultGame.ini` via the **Tryll Model Manifest** developer settings. Every model-name dropdown in the editor now lists what you registered here.

Registration controls where a model is available

The tier you pick decides a model's reach: **Experimental** keeps it in the editor for development; **Production** ships it inside packaged builds beside the server. Node dropdowns list your Experimental and Production models, each with a tier badge. See [Manage Models in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 5 — Create a workflow asset and add the demo actor

1. In the **Content Browser**, right-click → **Tryll → Workflow Asset**. Name it `DemoWorkflow`.
1. Open `DemoWorkflow`. In the Details panel configure the graph:
   - Under **Nodes**, add one entry and set **Name** = `answer`.
   - On that node's **Params**, pick **Generate** from the type picker — that makes it a Generate node and expands its parameter fields below. Leave them at their defaults; the **Default Exit** field stays empty, which routes the turn to END.
   - Set **Start Node** = `answer`.
   - Set **Default Model Name** to the model you registered in Step 4.
1. Create a blank Blueprint actor — call it `BP_TryllDemoActor`.
1. Add a **Tryll Agent Component** to it.
1. Assign `DemoWorkflow` to the **Workflow Asset** slot on the component.
1. **Leave Auto Create On Connect ticked** (the default). The component waits until the session is created before creating the agent, and queues itself if it spawns earlier — so it manages its own lifecycle.
1. Drop `BP_TryllDemoActor` into the level.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 6 — Wire the Blueprint

With **Auto Launch Server**, **Auto Connect**, and **Auto Create Session** on (Step 3), the subsystem launches the server, opens the connection, and creates the session from your settings — all by itself. The agent component then creates itself as soon as the session is ready. So the only thing left to wire is *what to do when the agent answers*.

Open `BP_TryllDemoActor`'s Event Graph:

```
flowchart LR
    OAR[OnAgentReady] --> SM["Send Message<br>In one sentence: what is Tryll?"]
    OAT[OnAnswerText] --> P1["Print String: Text"]
    OTC[OnTurnComplete] --> P2["Print String: Done."]
```

Select the **Tryll Agent Component** in the Components panel, then add each event from the **Events** section at the bottom of the Details panel:

1. **On Agent Ready** → **Send Message** with `"In one sentence: what is Tryll?"`.
1. **On Answer Text (Node Name, Text, bIsFinal)** → **Print String** — wire `Text` into **In String**, set `Print to Screen = true`, `Print to Log = true`, `Duration = 10`. The `Generate` node streams by default, so this fires once per chunk with `Text` holding only the new text. The last call is an empty terminator: `Text` is empty and `bIsFinal` is `true`. `Node Name` names the node that produced the chunk (`answer` here).
1. **On Turn Complete (Status, DebugInfo, TokensGenerated)** → another **Print String** that prints `"Done."` (or **Enum to String** on `Status`).

That's the whole graph — no `Connect`, no `Create Session`, no `Create Agent`. Those are the subsystem's job now.

Want the whole reply as one line?

Streaming (`Send = Streamed`) is the `Generate` node's default. To get a single frame with the complete reply instead of per-chunk deltas, either bind **On Answer Full** (fires once after `OnTurnComplete` with the full accumulated text) or set the node's **Send** to **Whole** in Step 5.

Driving the session yourself

For full control — a loading screen, or deciding yourself when the session opens — untick **Auto Connect** / **Auto Create Session** and call `Connect` then `Create Session` (or `Create Session From Settings`) yourself. Engines are not a reason to do this: each model's engine comes from the model catalog, and `Create Session` only takes an optional warm-up hint. `Create Agent` still waits for the session to be ready, so the old connect-vs-create race can't happen either way.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 7 — Test without entering PIE

Before pressing Play, use the **Chat Window** to verify the agent responds — no Blueprint wiring required:

1. Open **Window → Tryll → Tryll Chat**.
1. Select the actor that has your `UTryllAgentComponent` (with `DemoWorkflow` assigned on the component).
1. Click **Start** — the panel launches the server, connects, and creates an editor agent from that component. The status label turns green: **Ready**.
1. Type a message and press **Enter**. You should see a streamed reply.
1. Click **Stop** when done.

See [Test an Agent in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-agent-in-editor.html) for the full walkthrough including troubleshooting.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 8 — Play

Press **Play**. On the **first** run you'll see:

1. A few seconds while the server starts and the plugin connects.

1. The model you downloaded in Step 4 loads from disk into memory — a few seconds the first time it's used in a session.

1. The answer streams to the viewport and the Output Log, one chunk per `OnAnswerText` event, followed by your `OnTurnComplete` marker:

   ```
   LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor] Tryll is a local
   LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor]  small-language-model
   LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor]  inference server.
   LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor] Done.
   ```

The `Generate` node streams by default (`Send = Streamed`), so each `OnAnswerText` chunk carries a delta. The last call is an empty terminator with `bIsFinal = true` (it prints an empty line), then your `OnTurnComplete` handler prints `Done.`. For a single full-reply frame instead, bind **On Answer Full** or set the node's **Send** to **Whole** (see the tip in Step 6).

Subsequent runs skip the download and load steps — the model stays in the server process, and `TryllStorage/models/` survives across PIE sessions.

______________________________________________________________________

## Where to see what's happening

Open **Window → Output Log** and use the **Categories** filter:

| Category                   | Source                                                                        | Useful for                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LogTryllServer`           | `tryll_server.exe` stdout (drained by the subsystem and re-emitted in Unreal) | `[Listener] Listening on 127.0.0.1:<port>` (in the editor, auto-launch binds loopback on the **Server Port** project setting, default 9100, and falls back to a free port only if that port is taken; Standalone Game and packaged builds always pick a free port), `ConnectionReady`, model load lines, server-side errors. |
| `LogTryll`                 | Plugin (subsystem, agent component, connection thread)                        | Connect attempts, `CreateSession` outcome, agent lifecycle, `DownloadProgress`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `LogBlueprintUserMessages` | `Print String` calls                                                          | The answer text, your "Done." marker.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

The server's output funnels through the Unreal Output Log, so a single window shows everything.

Client Dev writes one log file per run under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\`.

______________________________________________________________________

## What you built

- A session connected to a Tryll server that the plugin spawned for you.
- One agent with a one-node graph.
- Model output surfaced to Blueprint as `OnAnswerText` events, which stream token-by-token by default (`Send = Streamed`); set the node's **Send** to **Whole**, or bind **On Answer Full**, for a single full-reply frame.

Everything the plugin exposes in Blueprint — connection, session, agents, models, string storages, tool calls — is listed in the [Blueprint Catalog](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unreal/blueprint-catalog.html).

- **[Concepts](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/index.html)** — the mental model behind the graph abstraction.
- **[Unreal C++ API](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unreal/cpp/index.html)** and the [Blueprint Catalog](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unreal/blueprint-catalog.html).

## Troubleshooting

- **`Tryll server exe not found at '...'` in `LogTryll/Error`** — no variant folder under `<Plugin>/Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/` resolves. From a release archive the `Default` variant ships populated; from a source build, run `cmake --build` of the server so the committed `Default` symlink resolves to your build.
- **`OnConnectionChanged(false)` fires repeatedly** — the server crashed or didn't start. Check `LogTryllServer` for the failure reason and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\` as a fallback.
- **`OnCreateSessionComplete(false)`** — usually a server-side error reading `models.json` or initialising the inference engine. Check `LogTryllServer`.
- **`Default Model Name` dropdown is empty** — register a model first. Open **Window → Tryll → Tryll Model Manager**, download one, and set its **Build registration** to **Experimental** or **Production**; it then appears in the dropdown.
- **`OnError` fires during `CreateAgent`** — read `ErrorMessage`. Common causes: `Default Model Name` is empty or names a model that isn't yet on disk (fails fast — download it via the Model Manager first), or a route targets a node name that doesn't exist.
- **`CreateAgent` takes several seconds even after the model is downloaded** — normal on the first agent using a given model in a session; the server is loading it from disk into RAM/VRAM. Subsequent agents on the same model are instant.
- **Nothing prints after `Send Message`** — bind both **On Answer Text** *and* **On Turn Complete**. With the default `Send = Streamed`, `OnAnswerText` fires once per chunk (each `Text` is a delta), the last call is an empty terminator with `bIsFinal = true`, and `OnTurnComplete` follows. Set the node's **Send** to **Whole** to get a single full-reply frame with the whole text and `bIsFinal = true`.

# First Inference in C++

Build the C++ client library from source, run the bundled `test-chat` demo, and see streamed tokens on stdout.

## Before you start

- Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ workload, CMake 3.24+, and Git.
- An internet connection the first time you run the demo. It downloads `Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)` from the server's `models.json` catalog if that model is not on disk yet.

No need to start the server manually

`tryll_test_chat` finds `tryll_server.exe` in the `tryll\build` tree and starts it automatically. If you prefer to manage the server yourself, launch the demo with `--profile external-text`.

## Step 1 — build the two projects

The server and the console demo are **two separate CMake projects**. Build the server first (its tree also produces the `tryll_client` static library), then build `test-chat`:

```
git clone <tryll-repo-url>

:: 1. Server + C++ client library — built from the tryll/ tree.
cd tryll
cmake --preset default
cmake --build --preset debug

:: 2. test-chat console demo — its own CMake project that links tryll/
::    with the server disabled.
cd ..\test-chat
cmake --preset default
cmake --build --preset debug
```

The `default` preset uses the Visual Studio 17 2022 generator with CUDA and Vulkan `PREBUILT` — no GPU SDK required. For a CPU-only build add `-DTRYLL_VULKAN=OFF -DTRYLL_CUDA=OFF`. The first build produces `tryll_server.exe` under `tryll\build\server\Debug\`; the second produces `tryll_test_chat.exe` under `test-chat\build\Debug\`.

One-shot build-and-run

`test-chat\build_and_run_dbg.bat` runs both builds in order and then launches the demo — handy while iterating.

## Step 2 — run the demo

```
test-chat\build\Debug\tryll_test_chat.exe --profile managed-text
```

Profiles live in `test-chat\data\test-chat-config.json`. The default profile, `managed-voice`, turns on speech output and push-to-talk voice input, so this tutorial picks `managed-text`: a typed chat on the `demo` workflow. Add `--workflow rag` or `--workflow tools` to start on a different workflow.

The demo looks for `tryll_server.exe` under `tryll\build\server\` (the `Debug`, `Release`, then `Production` folder), starts it, waits for it to be ready, and then connects. Set `TRYLL_SERVER_EXE` or pass `--server-exe <path>` to use a different binary.

If you want to connect to a server you started yourself on `127.0.0.1:9100`, use the `external-text` profile instead. Add `--server-host` and `--server-port` for another address:

```
test-chat\build\Debug\tryll_test_chat.exe --profile external-text
```

After the launch lines, the demo prints the session id and a table of the models the server lists, then the prompt:

```
[test-chat] Session <id> ready
[test-chat] Models returned by the server for this session's engine (…)
[test-chat] ListModels count: …
…
[test-chat] Workflow: demo. Type a message or /help. Press Ctrl+C or Ctrl+Z then Enter to quit.

You: hello
AI (generate): Hi! How can I help you today?
You:
```

Each token of the reply appears on stdout as it is produced, which is exactly what your own application will see through the `SetOnAnswerText` callback. The name in brackets is the node that produced the text. Type `/help` to list the demo's commands.

## Step 3 — write your own minimal client

For a smaller starting point than `test-chat`, use `RunAndConnect` to spawn the server and connect in a single call. The returned `ConnectedSession` owns both the child process and the TCP session; its destructor shuts them down in the correct order:

```
#include <filesystem>
#include <future>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

#include <tryll/TryllClient.h>

int main()
{
    namespace TC = Tryll::Client;

    // Spawn the server and connect. Throws Tryll::Client::TryllError on failure.
    // Leaving opts.port at its default (9100) picks a free port.
    TC::ManagedServerOptions opts;
    opts.exe = std::filesystem::path{"tryll/build/server/Debug/tryll_server.exe"};

    auto session = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::RunAndConnect(opts);
    session.GetClient().CreateSession({});

    // Build the simplest possible graph: one Generate node.
    // default_exit defaults to "" = END, so no wiring needed.
    TC::GraphDescription graph;
    graph.AddGenerate("answer", ::Tryll::NodeParams::GenerateParamsT{})
         .SetStartNode("answer")
         .SetDefaultModelName("Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)");   // downloaded by test-chat

    auto agent = session.GetClient().CreateAgent(graph);

    // SendText is fire-and-forget, so we must block until the turn finishes;
    // otherwise the session (and the process) would tear down before the
    // streamed tokens arrive. Signal completion from OnTurnComplete.
    std::promise<void> turnDone;
    agent.SetOnAnswerText([](std::string_view /*nodeName*/, std::string_view text,
                             bool /*isDelta*/, bool /*isFinal*/)
    {
        std::cout << text << std::flush;   // streams by default (SendAnswer::Streamed)
    });
    agent.SetOnTurnComplete([&turnDone](::Tryll::TurnStatus, std::string_view, std::int32_t)
    {
        std::cout << "\n";
        turnDone.set_value();
    });

    agent.SendText("In one sentence: what is Tryll?");
    turnDone.get_future().wait();   // block until OnTurnComplete fires

    agent.Destroy();
    // session destructor: shuts down the client, then stops the server
}
```

`ManagedServerOptions::port` defaults to 9100, and that default means "pick a free port": the launcher allocates an unused port and starts the server on it. Only a different value is bound exactly as given. To connect a second client to the same server, use the port it really bound, `session.GetServer().Port()`.

Already running a server?

If your server is managed separately (remote host, Docker, etc.) use `Connect` directly — no `ManagedServerOptions` needed. A server you start yourself listens on the `port` in its `server-config.json` (9100 in the shipped file):

```
auto client = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::Connect("127.0.0.1", 9100);
client.CreateSession({});
// …
client.Shutdown();
```

Link it against `tryll_client` and `tryll_common` (both already built by the preset):

```
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE tryll_client tryll_common)
```

## What you built

- A C++ client that connects, creates the session, creates a one-node agent, and streams a reply to stdout.
- The same surface as the bundled `test-chat` demo, which is a good reference when you are ready to add RAG, tool calls, or guardrails.

## Where to go next

- **[How-to Guides](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/index.html)** — task recipes for RAG, tool calls, streaming to UI, model setup.
- **[Concepts](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/index.html)** — the mental model. Start with [Tryll in Ten Minutes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tryll-in-ten-minutes.html).
- **[C++ Client API](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/cpp/index.html)** — the header / class surface.

## Troubleshooting

- **`FindServerExe: could not locate tryll_server`** — the server exe was not found under `tryll\build\server\Debug`, `Release`, or `Production` in the repository the demo was built from. Build the server with `cmake --build --preset debug` in `tryll\`, set `TRYLL_SERVER_EXE`, or pass `--server-exe <path>` to point directly at the server binary. Use `--profile external-text` to skip auto-launch entirely and start the server yourself: see [Run the Tryll Server](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-the-tryll-server.html).
- **`connection refused` with `--profile external-text`** — the server is not running or is on a different port. Check the server log, and pass `--server-port` if it does not listen on 9100.
- **Linker errors about `FlatBuffers`** — make sure you are linking the generated target that was built alongside `tryll_client`; the CMake preset handles this automatically.
- **Build picks Ninja accidentally** — pass `--preset default` explicitly or add `-G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64` to the configure command.

# First Inference in Python

Install the Python client, connect to a running Tryll server, and stream a reply from a local language model — all in about twenty lines of code.

## Before you start

- The Tryll server is running on `127.0.0.1:9100`. If not, see [Run the Tryll Server](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-the-tryll-server.html).
- At least one language model from the server's `data/models.json` is on disk, with status `Downloaded`, `Local`, or `Loaded`. You can check with any client, or bring your own — see [Use Your Own Local Model](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-your-own-local-model.html).
- Python 3.11 or newer.

## Step 1 — install the client

```
pip install tryll-client
```

That installs the `tryll_client` package and its one dependency, the `flatbuffers` runtime.

## Step 2 — write the script

Save this as `first-inference.py`:

```
from tryll_client import TryllClient
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription, GenerateParams

# Connect and create the session.
client = TryllClient.connect("127.0.0.1", 9100)
client.create_session()

# Pick a model — use the actual name from your server's models.json.
MODEL = "My Local Model"

# Build the simplest possible graph: one Generate node.
# default_exit defaults to "" = END, so no wiring needed.
graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
    .set_start_node("answer")
    .set_default_model_name(MODEL)
)

agent = client.create_agent(graph)

# Ask a question and print the full reply.
reply = agent.send_message("In one sentence: what is Tryll?")
print(reply)

agent.destroy()
client.shutdown()
```

## Step 3 — run it

```
python first-inference.py
```

Want the client to start the server for you?

Use `TryllClient.run_and_connect` — it spawns the server, waits for it to be ready, and returns a `ConnectedSession` that shuts everything down automatically:

```
from pathlib import Path
from tryll_client import TryllClient
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription, GenerateParams

with TryllClient.run_and_connect(
    exe=Path("path/to/tryll_server.exe"),
) as session:
    session.client.create_session()

    graph = (
        GraphDescription()
        .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
        .set_start_node("answer")
        .set_default_model_name("My Local Model")
    )
    agent = session.client.create_agent(graph)

    reply = agent.send_message("In one sentence: what is Tryll?")
    print(reply)
# server is stopped automatically when the `with` block exits
```

`run_and_connect` takes a `port` argument, and its default of 9100 means "pick a free port": the launcher allocates an unused port for the server. Only a different value is bound exactly as given. A second client must use the port the launcher really bound, `session.server.port`. The fixed 9100 in Step 2 is the port a server you start yourself takes from its `server-config.json`.

For lower-level control, or if you need to manage the server lifetime independently, see [Auto-launch the Server](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/auto-launch-server.html).

Expected output (your model's wording will vary):

```
Tryll is a local small-language-model inference server with C++, Python, and Unreal clients for building on-device AI agents.
```

`send_message` blocks until the server's `TurnComplete` arrives and returns the full reply as a single string — the simplest thing for a script. The server streams tokens as they're generated, and **Python receives them too**: register `agent.set_on_answer_text(cb)` — callback `(node_name, text, is_delta, is_final)` — before sending, or use the non-blocking `agent.send_message_async(...)`. Every client (Python, C++, Unity, Unreal) exposes the same per-token streaming callback; see [Stream Answers to a UI](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/stream-answers-to-ui.html).

## What you built

- A minimal session with one agent.
- A one-node graph: `Generate → END`.
- A blocking `send_message` call that returns the full reply.

The graph is deliberately minimal; everything else in Tryll (retrieval, tool calls, guardrails) plugs into exactly this shape by inserting extra nodes before `Generate`.

## Where to go next

- **[How-to Guides](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/index.html)** — ready-made recipes: RAG, tool calls, streaming to UI, guardrails.
- **[Concepts](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/index.html)** — the mental model. Start with [Tryll in Ten Minutes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tryll-in-ten-minutes.html).
- **[Python Client API](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/python/index.html)** — surface map of `tryll_client`.

## Troubleshooting

- **`ConnectionRefusedError`** — the server is not running on the expected host/port, or a firewall blocked it. Re-check [Run the Tryll Server](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-the-tryll-server.html).
- **`TryllError` `[3003]` from `create_agent`** — the graph does not compile, most often because the model name in your script does not match any entry in `models.json` (`GraphCompilationFailed`). List models with `client.list_models()`.
- **Script hangs after `send_message`** — the model is loading for the first time. Watch the server log; the next turn will be fast.
# Use Cases

# Use Cases

What can you build with Tryll, and which pieces do you need for it? Each page in this section starts from something a player experiences and walks through the building blocks that produce it. The pages link to the [How-to Guides](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/index.html) for the exact steps, so read a use case first to choose your design, then follow the links to build it.

All of these run on the player's own PC, inside your Unity or Unreal game.

## The building blocks

Every use case combines the same few blocks:

| Block                          | What it does for your game                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Speech-to-text (STT)**       | Turns the player's voice into text.                                                                            |
| **Small language model (SLM)** | Reads the conversation and writes the reply.                                                                   |
| **Text-to-speech (TTS)**       | Speaks the reply in a character's voice.                                                                       |
| **Retrieval (RAG)**            | Looks up lore, history or game facts and hands the relevant ones to the model.                                 |
| **Classification**             | Reads the player's line and turns it into a value your game can use, such as "accusing", "flirting" or "rude". |
| **Tool calls**                 | Lets the model ask your game to do something, such as open a door or attack. Your code decides and runs it.    |
| **Graph**                      | Connects the blocks. An agent is a graph of nodes, edited visually in Unity or Unreal.                         |

## The use cases

| Use case                                                                                    | The player experiences                                                                                                                                                            | Main blocks                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| **[Talking NPC](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/talking-npc.html)**             | A character you speak with, who knows the world, plays a mechanic, shows emotion and acts. Built up one step at a time.                                                           | STT, SLM, TTS, then retrieval, classification, tool calls |
| **[Ambient world](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/ambient-world.html)**         | Background characters who chat among themselves, and a narrator, radio or newspaper that reports what happened in the game.                                                       | SLM, TTS, game events, background priority                |
| **[Voice control](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/voice-control.html)**         | Commanding the game or your squad by voice. Characters may answer with prewritten lines.                                                                                          | STT, SLM, tool calls                                      |
| **[In-game assistant](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/in-game-assistant.html)** | A helper that knows the game, remembers what you did, looks things up and acts for you.                                                                                           | STT, SLM, TTS, retrieval, tool calls                      |
| **[AI director](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/ai-director.html)** *(idea)*    | A model that plans quests or directs the story, while your game systems carry out the plan. We have not built this yet; the page shows the research and the blocks you would use. | SLM, grammar-constrained output, tool calls               |

# AI Director (Idea)

This is an idea, not a feature

We have not built an AI director, and we have not measured how well small on-device models do this job. This page describes the idea, what published research says about it, and which Tryll building blocks you would use to try it. Every block it needs exists today.

So far, every use case has the model *talking*. An AI director has the model *deciding*: which quest to offer next, how a rival faction responds to the player, what a village does tomorrow, when to raise the tension. Think of a dungeon master who watches the game and plans what happens next.

______________________________________________________________________

## The model plans, the game executes

A language model is good at reading a messy situation and proposing a sensible next move. It is bad at keeping exact rules, counts and world state consistent over a long game. Research on LLM game masters finds exactly this split: models write engaging stories but struggle to run consistent, verifiable game mechanics ([RPGBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00595)), and they cannot reliably check their own plans ([Kambhampati et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01817)).

So divide the work:

- **High level, the model:** pick goals and write a plan. "The bandits raid the mill at dawn, because the player killed their scout and the guard is away."
- **Low level, your game:** carry out the plan with the systems you already have: pathfinding, combat AI, crafting recipes, schedules. These are exact and tested.

The best-known example of this loop is [Voyager](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291): in Minecraft, the model proposes the next task and writes the steps, the game's own API executes them, and the results go back to the model for the next round. [Generative Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442) uses the same split for characters: the model writes each character's plan for the day, and the game moves them around.

```
flowchart LR
    State["Game state<br/>snapshot"] --> Plan["Model writes<br/>a plan (JSON)"]
    Plan --> Check["Game validates<br/>the plan"]
    Check -->|invalid| Plan
    Check -->|valid| Run["Game systems<br/>execute it"]
    Run --> Events["Outcomes<br/>become events"]
    Events --> State
```

______________________________________________________________________

## How you would build it with Tryll

1. **Give it the current state, every time.** Your game sends a short, up-to-date summary of the world with each planning request: who is where, what the player did, what the factions want. Do not rely on the model to remember the world across many turns. Run the director **stateless**, or with a [summary](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/summarize.html) at most.
1. **Give it your design.** Put your designers' material in a [knowledge base](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/rag.html): quest templates, faction goals, story beats that are allowed to happen. The model then chooses and adapts authored content instead of inventing the world. [Drama Llama](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09099) works this way: authors write story fragments with conditions, and the model decides when they fire.
1. **Force a plan your game can read.** Add a grammar to the generation node, so the output is always a JSON plan in your schema. Grammar-constrained decoding produces reliable structured output without fine-tuning ([Geng et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13971)). See [Constrained output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/constrained-output.html). Alternatively, let the director call [tools](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html) such as `spawn_patrol(...)` or `offer_quest(...)`; giving an LLM game master game-specific functions improved both its storytelling and its consistency with the game state ([Song et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.06949)).
1. **Validate before you run.** The grammar guarantees the plan's *shape*, never that it makes sense. Your game checks every plan: does this character exist, is this recipe real, can this patrol reach the mill? If not, send the errors back and ask for a new plan, or fall back to a scripted choice. This "the model proposes, something exact checks" structure is the core recommendation of [Kambhampati et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01817), and [LLM+P](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11477) takes it further by letting a classical planner do the planning.
1. **Plan in stages.** Ask for the big picture first (this act's three main beats), then the details of each beat in separate calls. A recent world-to-quest pipeline found that each stage conditioned on the structured output of the previous one reduced drift and invented facts ([Borawski et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25482)).
1. **Keep it off the player's path.** A director thinks between moments, not during them. Create it with the `Background` workload so its work yields to the characters the player is talking to. See [Ambient world](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/ambient-world.html#keeping-the-world-from-slowing-the-player-down).

An illustrative plan schema, the kind of output a grammar would enforce:

```
{
  "goal": "raid_mill",
  "faction": "red_bandits",
  "reason": "scout killed by player; mill guard reassigned",
  "steps": [
    {"action": "gather", "units": 6, "at": "bandit_camp", "time": "night"},
    {"action": "move",   "to": "old_mill", "time": "dawn"},
    {"action": "attack", "target": "old_mill"}
  ]
}
```

______________________________________________________________________

## Risks to plan for

- **Invalid plans.** Models name places, items and characters that do not exist. Validation in step 4 is not optional.
- **Drift over a long game.** In a benchmark of long interactive stories, the best model tested kept its narrative commitments in only 42% of runs after 20 turns ([NCP-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08160)). Your game, not the model, must hold the canonical state, and send it fresh every time.
- **Latency.** Plan, check and retry loops take several model calls. That is fine for a director that plans the next hour of play, and wrong for anything that must react within a second.
- **Small models are untested here.** The research above uses large cloud models. Whether a 4B to 14B model on the player's GPU plans well enough is an open question. Start small to find out.

## A small first experiment

Do not start with a full story director. Pick one narrow decision with a clear fallback:

- **Choose the next side quest** from ten authored templates and fill in its parameters (giver, target, reward) from the current game state.
- **Plan a villager's day** as a list of activities and places that your schedule system then runs.
- **Pick a faction's response** to the player's last major action from a short menu of authored responses.

Each is one grammar-constrained call, easy to validate and easy to replace with a scripted choice when the plan is rejected.
