# Ambient World

Not every character waits for the player to speak. Townsfolk gossip at the market, two guards argue at the gate, a radio host reports last night's raid, a newspaper prints the player's latest scandal. This page covers the agents that **talk on their own**: the player hears or reads them but does not converse with them.

There are two kinds:

- **Background characters**: short lines and overheard conversations that make a place feel alive.
- **Narrators**: a radio, a newspaper, a chronicler or an in-world announcer that turns what happened in the game into a story.

Both follow the same pattern as the [Talking NPC](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/talking-npc.html): **your game owns the events, the agent owns the words.** Your game decides what happened and when it is worth mentioning. The agent decides how to say it.

```
flowchart LR
    Ev["Game events<br/>(raid, trade, rumour)"] --> Game["Your game picks<br/>what to report"]
    Game -->|SendMessage| Agent["Ambient agent"]
    Agent --> Out["Spoken line, radio segment,<br/>newspaper text"]
```

______________________________________________________________________

## Getting game events into the model

The model only knows what you send it. Three ways to pass events, usually combined:

- **Describe the event in the message.** Send a short factual line as the agent's input, such as `The player stole bread from the baker. Two guards saw it.` The agent's prompt tells it to react to the event in character.
- **Put standing facts in variables.** Facts that change slowly, such as the town's mood, the season or the player's reputation, go in [agent variables](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) and are rendered into the prompt template with `{{var.reputation}}`. Your game updates them; it does not have to repeat them in every message.
- **Seed recent history.** To give an agent a few recent events as context without asking it to answer each one, append them to its history while it is idle. See [Seed and edit dialog history](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/seed-and-edit-dialog-history.html).

Decide whether the agent should remember. A gossiping villager who reacts to one event at a time works best **stateless**: every call starts fresh, so old events never leak into new lines. A radio host running a whole evening's show should keep its history, so it can say "as I told you earlier", with a [`Summarize`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/summarize.html) node to keep that history short.

______________________________________________________________________

## Background characters

**Barks.** Short reactive lines ("Hey, watch it!", "Lovely weather today"). Three options, from most to least controlled:

- **Prewritten lines.** A [`CannedResponse`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/canned-response.html) node picks a line from a list, and a [`Speak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/speak.html) node voices it. No language model is involved.
- **Generated, but from a fixed set.** A grammar on the generation node limits the output to an allowed list, so the model chooses the fitting bark but cannot invent new ones. See [Constrain output with a grammar](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/constrain-output-with-a-grammar.html).
- **Free generation.** The model writes a fresh line for the situation. Best for ambient chatter, where variety matters more than control.

**Overheard conversations.** Two background characters talking to each other are two agents, and your game passes the lines between them: A's reply becomes B's input, and so on. Your game controls the whole exchange: who starts, what the topic is (a recent event works well) and when it stops. Cap it at a few lines; long AI-to-AI conversations drift.

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant Game
    participant A as Guard A
    participant B as Guard B
    Game->>A: "Topic: the player was seen near the vault."
    A-->>Game: line 1 (spoken)
    Game->>B: line 1
    B-->>Game: line 2 (spoken)
    Game->>A: line 2
    A-->>Game: line 3 (spoken), game ends the exchange
```

Each speaking character has its own [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html), so the guards do not sound alike.

______________________________________________________________________

## Narrators: radio, newspaper, chronicler

A narrator is one agent with a strong style and a stream of events.

1. **Collect events.** Your game logs what happens: quests finished, fights won, prices rising, the player's notable choices.
1. **Pick and batch.** At the right moment (the radio's next segment, the morning edition, the end of a chapter) your game selects the events worth reporting and sends them to the narrator in one message.
1. **Write in style.** The narrator's prompt sets the voice: a tabloid headline writer, a breathless sports commentator, a dry royal chronicler. One example paragraph in that style steers a small model better than any description.
1. **Deliver.** For a newspaper or a journal, display the text. For a radio or an announcer, use [`GenerateAndSpeak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate-and-speak.html) with a narrator voice.

Keep the facts in your game's hands. If the newspaper must state the exact bounty or the score, pass it as a variable and let Tryll insert it into the text, as described in [Substitute agent variables in output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/substitute-agent-variables-in-output.html). The model then cannot get the number wrong.

A narrator can also sit inside a conversation. One turn can produce a narrator line and a character line, each tagged with the node that wrote it, so your UI can show them differently. See [Send multiple answers in one turn](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/send-multiple-answers-in-a-turn.html).

______________________________________________________________________

## Keeping the world from slowing the player down

Ambient agents compete with the conversation the player is actually having, and with your game's rendering, for the same GPU. Tryll has two controls for this.

- **Background priority.** Create ambient agents with the `Background` workload. Nobody is waiting on their output, so the server paces them and gives way to the agent the player is talking to. The workload is a scheduling hint only: it changes when the work runs, never what is generated.
- **Inference throttle.** When your game needs the GPU back, for example during a heavy fight or a level load, it can tell the server to yield. Background work slows first; visible streaming text slows last. See [Inference throttle and agent workload](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/wire-protocol.html#inference-throttle-and-agent-workload).

```
// Set before the agent is created; it is fixed for the agent's lifetime.
agentComponent.Workload = TryllWorkload.Background;
```

```
from tryll_client import AgentWorkload

narrator = client.create_agent(graph, workload=AgentWorkload.Background)
```

Ambient agents are also cheap in memory when they share a model. A model loads once and every agent that uses it shares the weights; each agent adds only its own working cache. Give ambient agents small context sizes, since their prompts are short. See [Run many agents on a small GPU](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-many-agents-on-a-small-gpu.html).

______________________________________________________________________

## Ideas

| Idea           | Kind       | Input from the game                     | Output                                |
| -------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Market gossip  | Background | Recent player actions, town mood        | Overheard lines between two villagers |
| Guard barks    | Background | Player is sneaking, running, armed      | One spoken line from a fixed set      |
| War radio      | Narrator   | Battles won and lost, territory changes | Spoken news segment                   |
| Town newspaper | Narrator   | The player's notable deeds and scandals | Headline and short article            |
| Captain's log  | Narrator   | Mission events                          | Written journal entry                 |
| Case notes     | Narrator   | Each finished interrogation             | Running investigation summary         |

**In the demo:** the *Death on Set* murder mystery has a note-taker: after every interview, the game sends a summary of the exchange and the note-taker updates the detective's case notes. The other ideas have no demo yet.

# In-Game Assistant

A helper that lives in the game: a ship's computer, a familiar on your shoulder, a guild clerk, a tutorial companion. The player asks it things ("what does this rune do?", "where did I leave the cart?", "what did the mayor promise me?") and it answers from what it knows about the game and about this playthrough. It can also do things for the player.

**Building blocks:** speech-to-text, a small language model, text-to-speech, retrieval and tool calls. It is a [Talking NPC](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/talking-npc.html) whose main job is knowledge instead of drama.

______________________________________________________________________

## Two kinds of knowledge

An assistant answers from two very different sources, and each needs its own tool.

|               | Game knowledge                                            | Playthrough history                                              |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Examples**  | Item stats, crafting recipes, lore, quest hints, controls | Where the player went, what they bought, who they promised what  |
| **Changes**   | Only when you patch the game                              | Every minute of play                                             |
| **Lives in**  | A knowledge base you ship with the game                   | Your game's own records, or a knowledge base written during play |
| **Read with** | Retrieval                                                 | Tool calls, or retrieval from a writable knowledge base          |

### Game knowledge: retrieval

Ship your game's reference material as a [knowledge base](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/rag.html) and put a [`Retrieve`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve.html) node in front of the answer. Each question pulls the few matching entries into the prompt. If nothing matches, the assistant says it does not know, instead of guessing.

Two things matter for an assistant in particular:

- **No spoilers.** Tag entries with the chapter or quest they belong to, and filter on the player's progress, kept in an [agent variable](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html). The assistant cannot reveal what it cannot retrieve.
- **Vague questions.** Players ask "how do I beat him?". A [query-rewriting step](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/query-rewriting-for-rag.html) turns the question, together with the recent conversation, into a proper search.

### Playthrough history: two options

**Option A: query your game's records with tool calls.** Your game already tracks what happened: inventory, quest log, visited places, combat log. Give the assistant a tool such as `query_log(event_type, place, character)`. When the player asks "where did I last see the orc?", the model calls the tool, the turn pauses, your game runs the query and returns the result, and the assistant answers from it.

```
flowchart LR
    Q["'Where did I last<br/>see the orc?'"] --> TC["ToolCall:<br/>query_log(...)"]
    TC -->|turn pauses| Game["Your game<br/>runs the query"]
    Game -->|result| G["GenerateAndSpeak:<br/>'In the north mine,<br/>an hour ago.'"]
```

This keeps the facts exact, because they come straight from game state. Choose the model with care: this is the hardest of our tool-call suites. On our [game-log suite](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html) (two tools, four filters, and players who never name every detail), NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B, Ministral 3 14B and Qwen 3.5 4B pass 19 of 20 cases, while Llama 3.1 8B passes 12.

**Option B: a memory the assistant writes and reads.** Tryll can keep a *writable* knowledge base for the session. Your game, or the agent itself, writes notes into it during play ("The mayor promised 200 gold for the wolf pelts"), and a `Retrieve` node finds the relevant ones when the player asks. The [`WriteToMemory`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/write-to-memory.html) node lets the agent record facts from the conversation without any game code. The whole memory is saved and loaded with the player's save game.

Option B suits loose, conversational facts that your game does not track in a table. Option A suits anything your game already stores precisely. Many assistants use both.

______________________________________________________________________

## Acting for the player

The same tool-call mechanism lets the assistant act: mark a location on the map, sort the inventory, set a waypoint, pause the game and open the right menu. As always, the model only *asks*; your game checks and performs the action. For anything the player might regret, such as selling an item, have your game ask for confirmation first.

______________________________________________________________________

## Putting it together

```
flowchart LR
    In["Player question"] --> TC["ToolCall<br/>(query_log, set_waypoint, ...)"]
    TC -->|tool_called| Game["Your game:<br/>query or act"]
    Game --> R["Retrieve game knowledge<br/>(filtered by progress)"]
    TC -->|no_tool_called| R
    R --> C["Transform:<br/>facts + question"]
    C --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]
```

Keep the assistant inside the fiction where your game has one. A ship's computer that answers "as an AI language model..." breaks it. The [immersion guard](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/build-an-immersion-guard.html) from the Talking NPC page applies here too.

**In the demo:** *AquariumExpert* (an assistant that answers from a knowledge base, with query rewriting and an "I don't know" path), *Mother* (an experimental ship computer that reports status and reads and writes the ship's log through tools and a writable knowledge base) and *Nessa* (an experimental character who records what the player tells her with `WriteToMemory`).

## Related

- [Use Cases](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/index.html)
- [Create a simple RAG assistant](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/create-simple-rag-assistant.html)
- [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html)
- [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html)
- [Save and load agent state](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/save-and-load-agent-state.html)
- [Drive prompts and retrieval from game state](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/drive-prompts-and-retrieval-from-game-state.html)

# Talking NPC

A character the player can speak with: it listens, answers in its own voice, knows its world, takes part in your game's mechanics, shows emotion and acts.

You do not build all of that at once. This page is a ladder. Each step adds one building block to the step before it, and each step is a complete NPC you could ship. Stop at the step your game needs.

```
flowchart LR
    S1["1 · Talks"] --> S2["2 · Knows the world"]
    S2 --> S3["3 · Plays a mechanic"]
    S3 --> S4["4 · Shows emotion"]
    S4 --> S5["5 · Acts in the game"]
```

One principle runs through every step: **your game owns the rules, the agent owns the words.** The model never decides a price, a relationship score or whether a door opens. It reads the player, and it speaks. Your game code holds the state and makes the decisions.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1 · An NPC you can talk to

**The player experiences:** a character who answers out loud, in character, for as long as they keep talking.

**Building blocks:** speech-to-text, a small language model, text-to-speech.

The smallest working graph is one node, [`GenerateAndSpeak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate-and-speak.html). It writes the reply and starts speaking the first sentence while later sentences are still being generated, so the character starts talking almost at once. The voice belongs to the agent, set through its [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html).

Voice input sits outside the graph. Your game streams microphone audio to Tryll, gets the transcript back, and sends the final phrase to the agent as if the player had typed it. You choose push-to-talk or hands-free.

```
flowchart LR
    Mic["Player's voice"] -->|STT| Text["Transcript"]
    Text --> GAS["GenerateAndSpeak"]
    GAS -->|TTS| Audio["NPC speaks"]
```

What makes the character feel right is mostly the prompt. Our [NPC prompt study](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-npc-prompt.html) found two rules that matter most: include at least one line of the character's own dialogue, and never put a speaker label such as `Kira:` in front of it, because models copy the label into the reply.

For long conversations, add a [`Summarize`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/summarize.html) node. It folds older turns into a rolling summary, so the conversation can go on at a fixed token cost.

**In the demo:** *VoiceCharacter* (the full voice loop) and *TavernBartender* (a text NPC with long-conversation memory).

**Build it:** [Design an NPC prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-npc-prompt.html) · [Add voice output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html) · [Use voice input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html) · [Clone a voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html) · [Add lip sync](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-lip-sync-to-a-character.html) · [Keep long conversations coherent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/keep-long-conversations-coherent.html)

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2 · An NPC who knows your world

**The player experiences:** the character knows the world's history, the town's gossip and its own past, and stays consistent about them.

**Building block:** retrieval (RAG).

You could paste all your lore into the prompt, but a long prompt is slow, and small models lose track of facts buried in it. Instead, keep the lore in a knowledge base and add a [`Retrieve`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve.html) node in front of the answer. Each turn, it finds the few passages that match what the player said and hands only those to the model.

```
flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> R["Retrieve"]
    R -->|found| C["Transform: lore + question"]
    R -->|not_found| D["CannedResponse: 'I don't know about that'"]
    C --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]
```

Three things make retrieval work in a game:

- **Separate world lore from character history.** Use one shared knowledge base for the world and one per character, so a blacksmith does not know the queen's secrets.
- **Gate what the character is allowed to say.** Each passage can carry metadata, and a filter can compare it with a game variable. For example, a filter that keeps passages whose `secret_level` is at most the player's `trust` variable reveals more as trust grows, without changing the graph.
- **Handle the miss.** When nothing matches, route to a short in-character answer instead of letting the model invent lore.

If players ask vague follow-ups ("what about him?"), a [query-rewriting step](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/query-rewriting-for-rag.html) turns the line into a proper search before retrieval.

**In the demo:** *AquariumExpert* (retrieval, the miss path and query rewriting) and *Death on Set* in the murder-mystery project (world lore plus per-suspect history, with secrets unlocked as the investigation progresses).

**Build it:** [Retrieval-augmented generation](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/rag.html) · [Create a simple RAG assistant](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/create-simple-rag-assistant.html) · [Query rewriting for RAG](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/query-rewriting-for-rag.html) · [Drive prompts and retrieval from game state](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/drive-prompts-and-retrieval-from-game-state.html)

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3 · An NPC who plays a mechanic

**The player experiences:** talking *is* the gameplay. Flattery works on one character and annoys another; an accusation backed by evidence breaks a suspect; a good argument lowers a price.

**Building blocks:** classification, branching, game state.

A mechanic needs numbers and decisions, and those belong in your game code. The agent's job is to turn the player's free-form line into values your mechanic can read, and then to voice whatever your mechanic decided. That makes a loop:

1. **Classify.** Judge the player's line along the dimensions your mechanic cares about. [`ClassifyAttributesLLM`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-attributes-llm.html) scores up to 16 dimensions in one batched call, each as a choice, a yes/no or a 0–1 score.
1. **Let the game decide.** Your game receives the results as an event, updates its own state (affection, suspicion, the current price) and decides what happens.
1. **Pass the decision back.** Put a [`Pause`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/pause.html) node after the classifier. While the turn is paused, your game can set [agent variables](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) and node parameters, and the rest of the same turn sees the new values. Then it resumes, either along the graph or straight to a node it names.
1. **Branch.** If the character has distinct modes (friendly, suspicious, hostile), a [`Branch`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/branch.html) node or the resume target picks the path.
1. **Speak.** The answering node reads the state through its template, such as `{{var.affection}}` or `{{var.mood}}`, and phrases the reply to fit.

```
flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> CL["ClassifyAttributesLLM"]
    CL --> P["Pause"]
    P -. "game updates state,<br/>picks the path" .-> P
    P --> B["Branch on mode"]
    B -->|friendly| T1["Transform: friendly tone"]
    B -->|hostile| T2["Transform: hostile tone"]
    T1 --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]
    T2 --> G
```

What to classify and what the game owns depends on the mechanic:

| Mechanic          | Classify the player's line                         | Your game owns                                                  |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Dating**        | charm, respect, humour, pushiness                  | affection, relationship stage, what the character will agree to |
| **Interrogation** | accusation, evidence presented, pressure, sympathy | suspicion, which secrets are unlocked                           |
| **Trading**       | which item, offer, insult to the goods             | prices, stock, whether the deal closes                          |
| **Negotiation**   | concession, threat, appeal, counteroffer           | each side's limits, the current offer                           |

When a number must be exact, such as a price, do not ask the model to say it. Let the model write a placeholder, and Tryll replaces it with your game's value before the player hears it. See [Keep merchant prices deterministic](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/keep-merchant-prices-deterministic.html).

Simpler options

If you only need one label per turn, such as the player's intent, [`ClassifyIntentLLM`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-intent-llm.html) picks it from a short menu, and [`IntentToInstruction`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/intent-to-instruction.html) turns the label into a tone instruction for the reply without any game code.

**In the demo:** *Death on Set* (interrogation: intents shape the suspect's answers, and the game unlocks per-suspect secrets as the case progresses), *QuestGiver* (the same character behaves differently for a newcomer and a hero, driven only by game variables), *IntentGuard* (intent becomes a tone directive) and *StationMerchantHaggle* (an experimental price-haggling loop).

**Build it:** [Build an intent-driven NPC](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/build-intent-driven-npc.html) · [Classify intent without a knowledge base](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/classify-intent-without-a-knowledge-base.html) · [Pause and resume a turn](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/pause-and-resume-turns.html) · [Branch on a slot](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/branch-on-a-slot.html) · [Agent variables](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) · [Keep merchant prices deterministic](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/keep-merchant-prices-deterministic.html)

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4 · An NPC who shows emotion

**The player experiences:** the character's mood changes with what happens, and you can hear it in both what they say and how they say it.

**Building blocks:** your game's emotion system, instructions in the prompt, voice delivery modes.

The emotional state is another piece of game state, so your game owns it, just like the mechanic in step 3. It can change because of the classifier's results or because of anything else in the game: the player broke a promise, the character was hurt, night fell. Tryll then carries the mood into two places.

**What the character says.** Pass the mood into the reply prompt:

- as an agent variable in a [`Transform`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/transform.html) template, for example `The innkeeper is {{var.mood}} right now.`;
- or as an instruction, set by your game through an [`Instruction`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/instruction.html) node, or chosen from a table by [`IntentToInstruction`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/intent-to-instruction.html).

An adjective alone is a weak signal for a small model. A single example line spoken in that mood works much better, because models imitate an example far more reliably than they follow a description. Keep one short example line per mood and inject the one that matches.

**How the character sounds.** A voice profile can define [delivery modes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html#delivery-modes), one per mood. For voices cloned from a recording, each mode has its own reference clip, such as `mack_calm.wav` and `mack_angry.wav`, and the mood of the clip carries into the speech. Your game switches mode through the client API, for example `SetDeliveryModeAsync("angry", 0.8f)` in Unity. The change applies from the next sentence, even in the middle of a reply. Only your game code switches modes; the model cannot.

| Voice                             | Emotion control                                                                       |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Pocket TTS, Qwen3-TTS, Chatterbox | A reference clip per mood                                                             |
| Maya1                             | A spoken-style instruction per mood, such as "whisper" or "sarcastic", with intensity |
| Supertonic 3, Orpheus             | No emotion control; a mode can only change speed                                      |

On Unreal, the MetaHuman lip-sync plugin can also take the mood, so the face matches the voice.

**In the demo:** *EmotionalVoiceCharacter* (one voice with eight moods, each from its own clip; the mood is switched from the editor rather than by game logic).

**Build it:** [Add voice output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html) · [Add emotions to a voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-emotions-to-a-voice.html) · [Design a voice clip with Qwen3-TTS](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-voice-with-qwen3-tts.html) · [Voice profile reference](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html) · [Use Mustache templates](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-mustache-templates.html) · [Add lip sync to a MetaHuman](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-lip-sync-to-metahuman.html)

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 5 · An NPC who acts in the game

**The player experiences:** the conversation has consequences. The guard opens the gate, the merchant hands over the item, the bandit draws a sword, the healer heals.

**Building block:** tool calls.

You give the agent a list of actions, each with a name, a description and optional arguments, through a [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html) node. When the conversation calls for an action, the model picks one. Tryll sends the action's name and arguments to your game, and **your game decides whether to do it and does it.** The server never runs anything itself.

Two patterns cover most cases:

- **Fire and forget.** The NPC attacks, follows or leaves. Your game plays the action and the conversation moves on.
- **Wait for the result.** The NPC asks the game something before answering, such as the price of an item or whether a door is locked. The turn pauses, your game returns the result, and the reply uses it.

```
flowchart LR
    In["Player: 'Open the gate!'"] --> TC["ToolCall"]
    TC -->|tool_called| Game["Game: open_gate()"]
    Game --> G["GenerateAndSpeak: 'Fine, go through.'"]
    TC -->|no_tool_called| G
```

Choose the model by the job. In our [tool-call comparison](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html), on an NPC reaction suite (attack, trade, follow, leave, stay quiet), Nemotron Orchestrator 8B scored 20 of 20 and Qwen 3.5 4B scored 16, while Llama 3.2 1B scored 2. Keep the action list short and the descriptions clear: the descriptions are the prompt the model actually reads.

**In the demo:** *StationMerchant* (the merchant asks the game for a price and waits for it) and *Mother* (an experimental ship computer that reads and writes the ship's log through tools).

**Build it:** [Tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html) · [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html) · [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html) · [Compare tool-call models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html) · [Test tool calls in the editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-tool-calls-in-editor.html)

______________________________________________________________________

## At every step · Keep the NPC in its world

Players will test your character: "ignore your instructions", "what model are you?", "tell me about smartphones" in a medieval village. An immersion guard in front of the NPC catches these lines and answers in character instead.

The recommended guard has three stages, cheapest first: a pattern check that costs almost nothing, then a classifier for lines aimed at the software, then a classifier for lines that do not belong in your world. A caught line gets a prewritten, in-character deflection and never reaches the reply model. Your game can also remove it from the conversation history, so it does not echo in later turns.

**Build it:** [Build an immersion guard](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/build-an-immersion-guard.html) · [Use canned responses and guardrails](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-canned-responses-and-guardrails.html)

______________________________________________________________________

## All five steps together

The *Death on Set* murder mystery in the Unity demos combines almost the whole ladder in one graph per suspect:

```
flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> Guard["Immersion guard<br/>(regex + 2 classifiers)"]
    Guard -->|caught| Deflect["CannedResponse → Speak"]
    Guard -->|ok| CI["ClassifyIntentLLM"]
    CI -->|intent| I2I["IntentToInstruction"]
    CI -->|none| RW["Retrieve world lore"]
    RW --> RC["Retrieve suspect history<br/>(gated by game state)"]
    I2I --> Comp["Transform"]
    RC --> Comp
    Comp --> GAS["GenerateAndSpeak<br/>(per-suspect voice)"]
    GAS --> Sum["Summarize"]
```

Four suspects share one loaded model, each with its own voice. The game tracks what the player has discovered and widens each suspect's retrieval filter as secrets unlock. A fifth agent, the note-taker, quietly writes up each interview; see [Ambient world](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/ambient-world.html) for agents the player does not talk to.

# Voice Control

The player speaks, and the game does it. Order a squad to flank, cast a spell by saying its name, tell a companion to wait by the door, steer a ship, open a menu. Unlike a [Talking NPC](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/talking-npc.html), the point here is not conversation. It is turning free-form speech into a command your game can run.

**Building blocks:** speech-to-text, a small language model, and either tool calls or a grammar. Text-to-speech is optional.

```
flowchart LR
    Mic["'Bravo, get behind<br/>the red truck'"] -->|STT| Text["Transcript"]
    Text --> SLM["SLM: understand"]
    SLM --> Cmd["move(unit=bravo,<br/>target=red_truck)"]
    Cmd --> Game["Your game checks<br/>and runs it"]
    Game --> Ack["'Moving!'<br/>(prewritten line)"]
```

The model's only job is understanding. Players do not say commands the same way twice ("Bravo, cover behind that truck", "get Bravo to the red truck", "Bravo, truck, now"), and a small model maps all of them to the same command. Your game does everything else: it checks the command makes sense, runs it, and plays the reply.

The characters' replies do not need a language model at all. A soldier answering "Moving!" can use your game's usual recorded lines, or a [`CannedResponse`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/canned-response.html) node picking from a list. Add [text-to-speech](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html) only if you want generated replies.

______________________________________________________________________

## Two ways to get a command

|                           | Tool calls                                                                                                 | Grammar                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **What the model writes** | A call to one of your tools, with typed arguments, such as `move(unit, target)`                            | One line that must match a pattern, such as `<action> <object>`                                                  |
| **Best for**              | Commands with different shapes and arguments                                                               | One flat vocabulary of actions and objects                                                                       |
| **How it fails**          | The model can call no tool when it should; that path is routed, not an error                               | The output always fits the pattern, but can be the wrong command                                                 |
| **Node**                  | [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html)                             | [`Generate`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate.html) with a `grammar`                   |
| **Read**                  | [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html) | [Constrain output with a grammar](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/constrain-output-with-a-grammar.html) |

**Tool calls** fit most games. Each command is a tool with a clear description and only the arguments it really needs. When the player says "get Bravo behind the red truck", your game receives the tool name and its arguments as JSON.

**A grammar** fits a fixed vocabulary, such as `open door`, `take key`, `go north`. The grammar only allows lines in that form, so the output is always machine-readable. The grammar can be changed at runtime, so your game can rebuild it from what is on screen right now: only the units that exist, only the doors in this room.

Either way, the model guarantees the *form* of the command, never that it is the right one. Your game must still check it: is there a red truck, is Bravo alive, can Bravo reach it? When the answer is no, have the character say so ("Can't see a red truck, sir"), the same way a human squadmate would.

______________________________________________________________________

## Make it hear your words

Voice control fails first in speech recognition, not in the model. Game words are hard for it: unit call signs, invented place names, spell names.

- **Hotwords.** Give the speech recognizer a list of your game's words, and it will prefer them: "Aeltharion" instead of "Al Therion", "frostbolt" instead of "frost bolt". See [Bias voice input with hotwords](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input-hotwords.html). Not every speech model supports this: Parakeet and Zipformer do; Whisper, SenseVoice and Paraformer do not.
- **Push-to-talk.** For commands, a key to hold while speaking is more reliable than always listening. The player decides what is a command and what is chatter with friends.
- **Short words.** One-word commands such as "Fire!" are easy to clip. Keep a little silence padding around each recorded phrase. See [Use voice input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html).

______________________________________________________________________

## Keep each command independent

A command agent usually should not remember earlier commands. Make it **stateless**: every phrase is understood on its own, and an old order can never leak into a new one. If a command depends on what the player sees, such as "attack *that* one", pass the current situation with each phrase, for example the selected target, as an [agent variable](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) rendered into the prompt.

______________________________________________________________________

## Choosing a model

Command parsing is one of the easier jobs for a small model. In our [tool-call comparison](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html), on a suite that maps player speech to heist-game commands:

| Model                  | Commands passed |
| ---------------------- | --------------- |
| NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B | 20 / 20         |
| Ministral 3 14B        | 20 / 20         |
| Bonsai 8B (1-bit)      | 20 / 20         |
| Qwen 3.5 4B            | 18 / 20         |
| Llama 3.1 8B           | 17 / 20         |
| Llama 3.2 1B           | 14 / 20         |

Bonsai 8B in its 1-bit form scores 20 of 20 while needing about 1.9 GB of video memory, which leaves the rest of the GPU to your game.

**In the demo:** *CommandParser* (a stateless agent that turns any phrase into one of 16 `<action> <object>` commands with a grammar, on Llama 3.2 3B).

# Concepts

# Concepts

These pages explain *how Tryll thinks* — the mental models behind the server, the client libraries, and the workflows you build on top of them. Read one when you want to understand *why* something works the way it does; reach for a [how-to guide](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/index.html) or the [reference](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/index.html) when you want to do a specific thing or look up a specific field.

## Start with these

- **[Tryll in Ten Minutes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tryll-in-ten-minutes.html)** — read this first. What Tryll is, why it runs on the player's machine, why an agent is a workflow rather than a prompt, and the building blocks every other page is made of.
- **[Architecture at a Glance](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/architecture-at-a-glance.html)** — the engineer's view. Server → session → agent → graph → node → model, and the hot path of one turn.
- **[Workflows, Graphs, and Nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/workflows-graphs-nodes.html)** — the building block that turns a model into an application.
- **[Agents and Sessions](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agents-and-sessions.html)** — who owns what, and how a conversation comes into and goes out of existence.
- **[Lifetime and Ownership](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/lifetime-and-ownership.html)** — how string storages, embedded string storages, and models stay alive across agents, turns, and sessions.

## Dive into the pieces

- **[Models and Inference Engines](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/models-and-inference-engines.html)** — the catalog's model types (language, embedding, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice activity), the one engine each catalog model runs on, and what the KV cache does.
- **[TTS and Voice Output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tts-and-voice-output.html)** — how streaming speech synthesis works: `GenerateAndSpeak` vs. `Speak`, PCM audio frames, voices, and the Supertonic, Pocket TTS, Orpheus, and Maya1 families.
- **[STT and Voice Input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/stt-and-voice-input.html)** — how spoken audio becomes text: the utterance lifecycle, push-to-talk vs. hands-free, and offline vs. streaming recognisers.
- **[Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/rag.html)** — how Tryll grounds answers in your data: chunking, embeddings, dense, lexical, and hybrid search, and where retrieved text lands in the prompt.
- **[Tool Calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html)** — making small local models invoke tools: chat-template-driven prompting, limits, and what the detection-based design means for your game or app. To pick a catalog model or shape the schema, see [Compare tool-call models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html) and [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html).
- **[Agent Variables](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html)** — a typed, per-agent key→value store the game writes over the wire and the server reads from Mustache templates (`{{var.<name>}}`), the Retrieve filter, and (opt-in) `__NAME__` markers in Generate / GenerateAndSpeak output.
- **[Slots and Inter-node Value Passing](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/slots-and-inter-node-value-passing.html)** — the per-turn blackboard nodes read and write: `input` selection, `{{slot.<name>}}` templates, and `send` / `history_role` delivery.
- **[Constrained Output (GBNF)](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/constrained-output.html)** — forcing a model to emit exactly a fixed shape (a command, a choice, a tiny JSON object) with a grammar: what it guarantees (syntax) and what it never does (meaning).
- **[Projection and Token Budgets](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/projection-and-token-budgets.html)** — how a growing dialog is turned into a bounded prompt, how the token budget trims it, and how a rolling summary keeps the thread.

# Tryll in Ten Minutes

This page is the whole idea of Tryll in one sitting: what it is, why it runs where it runs, and the handful of building blocks everything else is made of. Read it before anything else in these docs — every tutorial, how-to guide, and concept page assumes the picture drawn here. Each section ends with a link to the page that goes deeper.

## What Tryll is

Tryll runs **small language models** — together with speech recognition, speech synthesis, and vector search — **on the player's own PC**, inside your Unity or Unreal game. It ships inside the Unity package and the Unreal plugin and starts itself; there is no service to host and nothing to call over the internet.

Running a model is the easy part. The hard part is getting a small model to behave like *your* character, in *your* world, following *your* rules. So Tryll is mostly a **harness** around the model: the scaffolding that decides what the model sees, what it is allowed to say, and what happens with its output. If you know how a coding agent wraps a large model in tools and loops, or what a LangGraph-style workflow is, this is the same idea — built for small local models inside a game.

## Why on the player's machine

It is a trade-off, and it is worth being clear about both sides.

**What you gain:**

- **No bill that grows with your success.** A cloud model charges per token, so every extra player and every extra hour of play costs you money. On-device, the player's hardware does the work.
- **No credits to abuse.** When a player talks your NPC into writing them a Java program, that is their GPU's time, not your invoice.
- **Privacy and reliability.** Nothing the player says leaves the machine. It works offline, with no network round-trip and no outage that is not on the player's desk.

**What it costs you:**

- **You share the machine with your game.** The model needs GPU memory and RAM that your renderer would also like to have.
- **Small models need structure.** A 3–4 billion parameter model will not hold a huge lore dump in its head or improvise reliably from a vague prompt. It does well when each step it takes is small and well defined — which is exactly what the rest of this page is about.

→ [What your machine needs](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/index.html#what-your-machine-needs) · [Estimate memory footprint](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html)

## The model is the small part: agents are workflows

An **agent** is one character, or one conversation. Its behaviour is not a prompt; it is a **workflow graph** of small steps called **nodes**, which the agent walks once every time the player says something. Some nodes call a model. Most do not.

Here is the simplest useful agent, the *Safe Receptionist* from the demo project. It has two jobs: answer the player, and refuse what it should not answer.

```
flowchart LR
    P([Player line]) --> G{guard<br>Regex Guardrail}
    G -- triggered --> D[deflect<br>Canned Response]
    G -- not triggered --> A[answer<br>Generate]
    D --> E([Reply])
    A --> E
```

The guard checks the line against a list of patterns. If one matches, a scripted reply goes back and **no model runs at all**. Only a clean line reaches `answer`, the one node that calls the language model. Real agents add more steps — retrieve some lore, classify the request, call a game function — but they are all built the same way.

This is the key design choice: **the rules and the decisions stay in your game.** The model supplies words and choices, inside boundaries you set. Whether the door opens, how much the sword costs, and when the killer's name may be revealed are for your game code to decide.

→ [Workflows, graphs, and nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/workflows-graphs-nodes.html) · [All node types](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html)

## The building blocks

Every Tryll feature is one of the following, placed as a node in the graph or as data the graph reads.

**The character and the conversation.** The system prompt defines the character: who they are, what world they live in, how they talk, plus a few example lines. It is always kept. As a conversation grows, the oldest turns are trimmed so the prompt stays within budget — the character never forgets who it is, but it does eventually forget what you said an hour ago. → [Design an NPC prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-npc-prompt.html) · [Projection and token budgets](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/projection-and-token-budgets.html)

**Knowledge.** Do not paste all your lore into the prompt. Keep it as a knowledge base of short facts, and let a Retrieve node pick the few that are relevant to each line of dialogue (this is *retrieval-augmented generation*, or RAG). It can search by meaning, by exact keywords — useful for the made-up words in your setting — or both. Facts can carry metadata, so you can gate them: the detective only learns what the player has already uncovered. → [Retrieval-augmented generation](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/rag.html) · [Create a simple RAG assistant](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/create-simple-rag-assistant.html)

**Game state in.** Agent variables let your game push live values — the player's level, the NPC's mood, the current quest stage — straight into prompts and knowledge filters, so the character reacts to what is actually happening. → [Agent variables](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) · [Drive prompts and retrieval from game state](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/drive-prompts-and-retrieval-from-game-state.html)

**Decisions.** A classifier node works out what the player *means* — a threat, a bribe, a question about the quest — and the graph branches on the answer. The same technique can sort a line by tone, which is how you move an NPC's attitude towards the player. → [Build an intent-driven NPC](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/build-intent-driven-npc.html) · [Classify intent without a knowledge base](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/classify-intent-without-a-knowledge-base.html) · [Branch on a slot](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/branch-on-a-slot.html)

**Actions out.** With a tool call, the model picks an action and its arguments — *open the gate*, *follow the player*, *sell item 12*. Your code runs it and hands back the result, and the model answers from what really happened. Tryll never runs game code itself. When you need output in an exact shape, a grammar makes anything else impossible to generate; when numbers matter, your code owns the number and the model only owns the wording. → [Tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html) · [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html) · [Keep merchant prices deterministic](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/keep-merchant-prices-deterministic.html)

**Staying in character.** Pattern and intent guards, paired with scripted replies, catch jailbreaks and out-of-world questions ("what model are you?") before a model ever sees them — and can keep them out of the conversation history, so they never become context. → [Use canned responses and guardrails](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-canned-responses-and-guardrails.html) · [Build an immersion guard](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/build-an-immersion-guard.html)

**Voice.** The player can speak, push-to-talk or hands-free. The character can answer out loud: speech is synthesized sentence by sentence while the reply is still being written, so it starts talking almost at once. Voices can be cloned from a short sample or described in words, and lip sync drives your character's face from the same audio. → [Voice output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tts-and-voice-output.html) · [Voice input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/stt-and-voice-input.html) · [Add lip sync to a character](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-lip-sync-to-a-character.html)

**More than one agent.** Agents are cheap next to models, so do not force one agent to do everything. Next to the character you can run a narrator, a note-taker that summarises what happened, or a judge that scores the player's argument. An agent can also be *stateless* — no memory between calls — which suits classification and other utility jobs. → [Agents and sessions](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agents-and-sessions.html) · [Run many agents on a small GPU](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-many-agents-on-a-small-gpu.html)

## Models and memory

Models are files. You pick them from Tryll's catalog — or bring your own GGUF file — and download them in the editor's **Model Manager**. The models you register for production are packaged with your build, so a shipped game never downloads anything behind the player's back.

A model is loaded once and shared by every agent that uses it, so ten NPCs on the same model cost one model, plus a small working cache for each node that generates. A few numbers to calibrate against:

- **8 GB of VRAM** is the comfortable target for a game with a language model in it; 6 GB works if you stay around 3B models.
- A **3–4B model** takes roughly 2–3 GB. The tutorials use Gemma 3 4B, with Llama 3.2 3B as the smaller, quicker choice.
- **Speech recognition and the lighter voices run on the CPU** and cost no VRAM. The most expressive voices are themselves 3B models and are budgeted like one.

Each model can be placed in VRAM or in system RAM, so you can keep the GPU for rendering when the game needs it.

→ [Models and inference engines](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/models-and-inference-engines.html) · [Manage models in the editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html) · [Choose where models run](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/choose-where-models-run.html)

## How you work with it

On a team, the work splits naturally. **Programmers** wire agents into the game: which tools exist, which variables the game pushes, what happens when the model asks to act. **Designers** shape the character: the prompt, the lore, the graph — and they can do most of that without a programmer, because Tryll lives inside the editor:

- a **graph editor** to build workflows visually,
- a **Chat** window to talk to an agent without entering Play mode,
- the **Dialog Lab** to run the same dialog across many prompt, model, and parameter variants and compare the spread — so you test changes, or a model swap, on hundreds of runs instead of a few typed lines,
- the **Agent Log** to see what each agent received and produced, and the **Memory** window to see what it all costs.

AI coding agents can help too: both plugins ship an `AGENTS.md` that briefs them on Tryll, and on Unreal they can author workflows directly through the editor's MCP server.

→ [Test an agent in the editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-agent-in-editor.html) · [Compare dialog variants](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-dialog-variants.html) · [Agentic coding with Tryll](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/agentic-coding-with-tryll.html)

## What Tryll is not

- **Not a cloud API.** Everything runs locally; there is no hosted fallback.
- **Not a model.** Tryll runs open models you choose; it does not train or fine-tune them.
- **Not an image, 3D, or animation generator.** Tryll covers text, speech, and retrieval — the workloads that run well on today's player hardware.
- **Not a code runner.** The model can *ask* for an action; only your code performs it.
- **Windows only, for now.** Tryll ships as Windows 10/11 x64 binaries.

# Architecture at a Glance

Tryll is a C++ TCP server that runs small language models on the user's own machine and exposes them to games and apps through a binary protocol. This page is the engineer's view: what runs where, what owns what, and what the hot path looks like when a user hits "send".

New to Tryll? Read [Tryll in Ten Minutes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tryll-in-ten-minutes.html) first — it explains the ideas this page assumes. The other concept pages each zoom into one layer of the picture below.

## The five layers

```
flowchart TB
    subgraph Client["Client process (your game / app / script)"]
        CL["tryll-client<br>(Unity / Unreal / C++ / Python)"]
    end
    subgraph Server["tryll-server process"]
        S[Session<br>one per TCP connection]
        A[Agent<br>one per CreateAgent]
        G[Graph<br>nodes + exit fields]
        M[Model pool<br>shared models &amp; KV caches]
    end
    subgraph Hardware["Local hardware"]
        HW[CPU / GPU<br>llama.cpp · ONNX Runtime]
    end
    CL -- "TCP (localhost)<br>FlatBuffers framing" --> S
    S --> A
    A --> G
    G --> M
    M --> HW
```

- **The server** is a single C++ process. One instance, many clients. It runs small language models on-device through [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp), runs speech models through Sherpa-ONNX and ONNX Runtime, and uses [USearch](https://github.com/unum-cloud/usearch) for vector search; everything else — the workflow engine, the wire protocol, logging — is built inside the server.
- **A [session](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#session)** is one TCP connection. It owns the client's [agents](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#agent), [string storages](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/string-storage.html), and [embedded string storages](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html). When the socket closes, everything in the session goes with it.
- **An [agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#agent)** is one conversation. It carries its own [workflow graph](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#graph), its own dialog history, and its own default model. A single session can own several agents in parallel.
- **The [graph](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#graph)** is a set of [nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html), each owning its own exit fields that wire it to the next node. The agent walks it once per user turn — see [Workflows, Graphs, and Nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/workflows-graphs-nodes.html).
- **Models** are loaded once per process by the server and shared across every agent that needs them. The KV cache, by contrast, is per-node, because each node sees a different slice of the dialog.

## One turn end to end

The hot path when a user sends a message:

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant A as Agent
    participant N as Node (e.g. Generate)
    participant M as Model

    C->>S: SendMessageRequest(text)
    S->>A: dispatch to the agent
    A->>N: execute current node
    N->>M: generate / stream tokens
    M-->>N: tokens
    N-->>S: AnswerText(delta, is_delta=true, is_final=false)
    S-->>C: AnswerText frame
    Note over N,M: repeats until stop
    N-->>S: AnswerText(text="", is_delta=true, is_final=true)
    S-->>C: AnswerText terminator
    N-->>A: exit route (default / found / …)
    A->>A: follow route to next node or END
    A-->>S: TurnComplete(status)
    S-->>C: TurnComplete frame
```

This is the streamed case (`send=Streamed`, the Generate default): every chunk is a delta, and the node's last chunk is an empty terminator. With `send=Whole` the node sends one `AnswerText` with `is_delta=false`, `is_final=true`, and the full text.

A turn is always atomic at the agent level. A second `SendMessage` for the same agent while a turn is live is rejected with [3004 `AgentBusy`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent); in-flight work keeps running.

## Concurrency, in one line

Turns on one session run serially — if agent A is mid-turn, agent B on the same session waits; separate sessions run concurrently. Inference is serialised per model: every agent that shares a loaded model queues on that model's scheduler, which hands out work in bounded chunks, while two different models can run at the same time.

## The wire protocol

Clients speak to the server over local TCP using length-prefixed FlatBuffers messages. A server auto-launched by the Unity or Unreal plugin in a player build listens on a free port the OS assigns; the editor and a standalone server use port 9100 by default. The shape every message takes — and the end-to-end session flow — is documented in [Wire Protocol](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/wire-protocol.html).

The session lifecycle, in one line:

```
ConnectionReady → CreateSession → (CreateStringStorage…)* → CreateAgent → SendMessage …
```

All four client libraries (Unity, Unreal, C++, Python) are thin wrappers over this protocol. Nothing else special happens on the client side — the intelligence lives in the server.

## Why it is shaped this way

Three product constraints drove the split:

- **On-device.** A game or tool that wants a local model cannot afford a Python runtime or a separate inference microservice per platform. A single C++ server binary plus tiny clients keeps every integration small.
- **Workflow over prompt.** Turning a raw model into useful behaviour (RAG, guardrails, tool calls, canned refusals, …) needs composition. Tryll makes the composition first-class by giving you a graph instead of a prompt template.
- **Shared, not duplicated, compute.** Models are big, KV caches are bigger. The server loads each model once and lets every agent share it; evict rules are explicit ([model management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html)).

## Edges and pitfalls

- A session is owned by its socket. If the TCP connection drops, the server destroys every agent and storage created through it. Client libraries surface this as a connection-changed event — reconnect and re-create what you need.
- A [KV cache](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#context-kv) is per node, not per agent. Two nodes in the same graph that use the same model still have separate caches; that is intentional, because they see different prompt prefixes. See [Projection and Token Budgets](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/projection-and-token-budgets.html).
- The server never runs user-supplied code. Tool calls are *detection-only* — see [Tool Calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html).

# Workflows, Graphs, and Nodes

A Tryll [agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#agent) is not a prompt. It is a *graph* of small, single-purpose steps that you wire together. Each user turn re-walks the graph; each step decides where to go next. This page explains why Tryll is built this way and how the pieces fit.

## The building blocks

A [graph](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#graph) has two things:

- A set of **[nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html)**, each with a name, a [node type](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#node), and a set of **typed params** that include the node's configuration *and* its exit wiring. Each exit is a string field on the params object (e.g. `default_exit`, `triggered_exit`); an empty value means *route to END*. The full set of sixteen node types is: [`Generate`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate.html), [`GenerateAndSpeak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate-and-speak.html), [`Speak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/speak.html), [`Retrieve`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve.html), [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html), [`CannedResponse`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/canned-response.html), [`RegexGuardrail`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/regex-guardrail.html), [`Instruction`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/instruction.html), [`IntentToInstruction`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/intent-to-instruction.html), [`ClassifyIntent`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-intent.html), [`ClassifyIntentLLM`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-intent-llm.html), [`Transform`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/transform.html), [`Pause`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/pause.html), [`Branch`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/branch.html), [`WriteToMemory`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/write-to-memory.html), and [`Summarize`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/summarize.html). See [Workflow Nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html) for the full catalog.
- A **start node** — the first node to run on every user turn.

Graphs are authored once, sent to the server with [`CreateAgentRequest`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/agent-parameters.html), frozen at agent creation, and then re-walked for every turn the agent lives.

Here is the simplest useful graph — a guardrail in front of a generator, with a scripted refusal on the rejected path:

```
flowchart LR
    guard["RegexGuardrail<br>guard"]
    refuse["CannedResponse<br>refuse"]
    gen["Generate<br>answer"]
    guard -- "triggered" --> refuse
    guard -- "not_triggered" --> gen
    refuse -- "default" --> END
    gen -- "default" --> END
```

The same graph, in each client:

```
var graph = new TryllGraphBuilder()
    .AddRegexGuardrail("guard", new TryllRegexGuardrailParams
    {
        StringStorage    = "jailbreak_patterns",
        TriggeredExit    = "refuse",  // → refuse node
        NotTriggeredExit = "answer",  // → answer node
    })
    .AddCannedResponse("refuse", new TryllCannedResponseParams
    {
        StringStorage = "refusal_lines",
        // DefaultExit is "" (END) by default
    })
    .AddGenerate("answer", new TryllGenerateParams())
    .SetStartNode("guard")
    .SetDefaultModelName("My Local Model")
    .Build();
```

```
auto* GuardParams  = NewObject<UTryllRegexGuardrailParams>();
GuardParams->StringStorage    = TEXT("jailbreak_patterns");
GuardParams->TriggeredExit    = TEXT("refuse");
GuardParams->NotTriggeredExit = TEXT("answer");

auto* RefuseParams = NewObject<UTryllCannedResponseParams>();
RefuseParams->StringStorage = TEXT("refusal_lines");
// RefuseParams->DefaultExit defaults to "" (END)

FTryllGraphDescription Graph = FTryllGraphBuilder()
    .AddNode(TEXT("guard"),  GuardParams)
    .AddNode(TEXT("refuse"), RefuseParams)
    .AddNode(TEXT("answer"), NewObject<UTryllGenerateParams>())
    .SetStartNode(TEXT("guard"))
    .SetDefaultModelName(TEXT("My Local Model"))
    .Build();
```

```
namespace TC = Tryll::Client;

namespace NP = ::Tryll::NodeParams;

NP::RegexGuardrailParamsT guardParams;
guardParams.string_storage     = "jailbreak_patterns";
guardParams.triggered_exit     = "refuse";
guardParams.not_triggered_exit = "answer";

NP::CannedResponseParamsT refuseParams;
refuseParams.string_storage = "refusal_lines";
// refuseParams.default_exit defaults to "" (END)

TC::GraphDescription graph;
graph.AddRegexGuardrail("guard",  std::move(guardParams))
     .AddCannedResponse("refuse", std::move(refuseParams))
     .AddGenerate("answer", NP::GenerateParamsT{})
     .SetStartNode("guard")
     .SetDefaultModelName("My Local Model");
```

```
from tryll_client import GraphDescription
from tryll_client.graph import (
    RegexGuardrailParams, CannedResponseParams, GenerateParams,
)

guard_params = RegexGuardrailParams(
    string_storage     = "jailbreak_patterns",
    triggered_exit     = "refuse",
    not_triggered_exit = "answer",
)
refuse_params = CannedResponseParams(
    string_storage = "refusal_lines",
    # default_exit defaults to "" (END)
)

graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("guard",  guard_params)
    .add_node("refuse", refuse_params)
    .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
    .set_start_node("guard")
    .set_default_model_name("My Local Model")
)
```

## Exit fields: how nodes "talk" to each other

Nodes do not call each other. They return a named **exit**, and the agent follows the matching edge. Every node type declares its possible exits as **typed string fields** on its params object — see the table in [Workflow Nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html).

For example:

| Node type        | Exit fields on params                     |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `Generate`       | `default_exit`                            |
| `Retrieve`       | `found_exit`, `not_found_exit`            |
| `ToolCall`       | `tool_called_exit`, `no_tool_called_exit` |
| `CannedResponse` | `default_exit`                            |
| `RegexGuardrail` | `triggered_exit`, `not_triggered_exit`    |

An **empty string** means *route to END*; this is the field's default value. A **non-empty string** must name another node in the same graph — the server rejects graphs where an exit field names a node that doesn't exist ([`3003 GraphCompilationFailed`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent)).

Because exits are fields on the params object, exits that terminate the turn (route to END) can simply be left at their default — you only need to set the fields that route somewhere other than END.

## The per-turn loop

When a `SendMessage` arrives, the agent:

1. Appends a new [interaction](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#interaction) to its dialog, starting with the user's message.
1. Walks the graph from `start_node`, one node at a time. Each node:
1. reads from the current interaction (and anything earlier nodes attached to it),
1. does its work (retrieve from an index, run the model, match a pattern, pick a canned line, …),
1. optionally attaches new components to the interaction, and
1. returns its chosen exit.
1. Follows the route for that exit to the next node.
1. Stops when the route target is `"END"`, when the step budget is exceeded, or when the turn is cancelled.

What each node attaches along the way is what makes the dialog *itself* useful state. A `Retrieve` node attaches retrieved knowledge to the current turn, and a downstream `Generate` node's [projection](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/projection-and-token-budgets.html) picks that knowledge up and folds it into the prompt.

## Passing values between nodes: slots

Producing nodes (`Generate`, `GenerateAndSpeak`, `CannedResponse`, `Transform`, `Instruction`/`IntentToInstruction`) don't just route — they each write their text into a named **slot** on the turn's shared blackboard (the slot name is the node's `output_name`, or its own name if unset). Downstream nodes select which slot they consume with an `input` param (empty = the reserved `user_message` slot), and Mustache templates reference slots as `{{slot.<name>}}`. Two more per-node knobs control delivery: `send` (a `SendAnswer` of `None` / `Whole` / `Streamed`) decides whether/how the slot is emitted to the client this turn, and `history_role` decides whether it replays as history on later turns. This is how you build things like a hidden query-rewrite step (`send=None`) or a multi-sender turn. See [Slots and inter-node value passing](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/slots-and-inter-node-value-passing.html).

## Why a graph instead of a prompt template

Three reasons:

**1. Composition.** "Retrieve, then generate" is different from "check for jailbreak first, then retrieve, then generate". Prompt templates push this branching into strings; a graph makes it executable and inspectable. Every node is typed and [diagnostics-friendly](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html).

**2. Cost control.** The graph lets you short-circuit expensive work. A [guardrail](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/regex-guardrail.html) that routes to a [canned response](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/canned-response.html) never touches the model. A [tool-call node](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html) with `mode=DetectOnly` does zero extra generation on a miss (the default, `CallOrAnswer`, instead emits the model's plain-text reply).

**3. Reuse.** Graphs are data. You can build them at runtime from C++, Python, or Unreal, ship them in a [`UTryllWorkflowAsset`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unreal/cpp/index.html), or construct them dynamically from user configuration. The server does not know or care where the graph came from.

## Turns are serial; graphs are stateless between turns

An agent runs one turn at a time. If a second `SendMessage` arrives while the previous turn is still running, it is rejected with [`3004 AgentBusy`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent); the in-flight turn keeps running. Cancellation is explicit (`CancelRequest`, `DestroyAgent`, socket close), not pre-emption.

The graph itself carries no per-turn state. All state lives on the agent's dialog (the accumulated interactions) and in the per-node KV caches. This is why the same graph description can be replayed cleanly every turn — the work of "what has been said" is separate from the work of "what to do next".

## Edges and pitfalls

- **Routing loops.** Nothing stops you from routing node A → node A; every agent stops after 64 node steps in one turn, which breaks infinite loops by aborting the turn with an error. The budget is fixed; it is not a `CreateAgent` setting.
- **Exits you "know" will never fire still need a value.** Leave them at the default empty string (routes to END). The server validates that no exit field names a missing node, but it does not enforce that every exit field is reachable.
- **Model sharing is *cross-graph*, not cross-node.** Two `Generate` nodes in one graph that use the same model share the underlying weights (good) but have independent KV caches (necessary — they see different prompts). Budget token-count accordingly; see [Projection and Token Budgets](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/projection-and-token-budgets.html).
- **The start node runs every turn.** If your start node is `Generate`, it will generate every turn, even if a later node would have short-circuited. Put guardrails and retrieval *before* the model, not after, if you want them to actually gate work.

- [Concept: Tool Calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html)
