# Agents and Sessions

Everything a client does with Tryll happens inside a *session*, and every conversation inside that session is an *agent*. Understanding how these two objects come into being, what they own, and what happens when they go away is the single most useful piece of mechanical knowledge for integrating the server.

## Session: one TCP connection, one world

The TCP **connection** and the logical **session** are distinct. The connection is created when the server accepts your socket; the [session](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#session) is created only when you send `CreateSession`. From the client's side, the steps are:

1. `Connect(host, port)` opens the socket.
1. The server sends an unsolicited `ConnectionReady` frame — a connection-level hello (it carries the protocol version and codegen fingerprint, but **no** `session_id`). The client compares `protocol_version` (currently 25) with its own and fails the connection locally with `5004 ProtocolVersionMismatch` if they differ; the server never sends 5004.
1. You send `CreateSessionRequest` to create the session. This is **mandatory and one-shot**: it must precede every other request. It sets session-wide options such as the game name and locale (the locale can be changed later with `SetSessionLocale`). It does not choose an inference engine — each catalog model names its own engine. Its `model_config` may carry an optional list of `(role, engine)` hints that only warm those engines early. The server replies with `CreateSessionResponse`, which carries the server-allocated `session_id`.
1. Only now can you create per-session helpers ([string storages](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/string-storage.html), [embedded string storages](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html)), manage models, and create agents. Any of these before `CreateSession` is rejected with `SessionNotReady`; a second `CreateSession` with `SessionAlreadyExists`.

Everything in steps 3 and 4 belongs to the session. When the socket closes, the server:

- cancels every active agent turn,
- destroys every agent in the session,
- drops every string storage and embedded storage the session owned.

Models are not unloaded at that moment. An on-demand model that no other session holds stays cached until the next session's pre-load sweep drops it; pinned models stay loaded (see [Model Management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html)).

A process can hold many sessions; a session holds many agents; and a single server process is shared across all of them. If the socket drops, the client re-connects and re-creates what it needs — there is no server-side persistence for session state.

### The implicit session state machine

Sessions do not have an explicit state enum, but they behave like a tiny state machine:

```
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*]            --> Connected:        TCP accept + ConnectionReady
    Connected      --> Connected:        any non-CreateSession request → SessionNotReady
    Connected      --> SessionActive:    CreateSessionRequest (mandatory, one-shot)
    SessionActive  --> SessionActive:    second CreateSession → SessionAlreadyExists
    SessionActive  --> AgentActive:      CreateAgentRequest
    AgentActive    --> AgentActive:      SendMessage / DownloadModel / Load / …
    AgentActive    --> SessionActive:    last agent destroyed
    Connected      --> Closing:          socket EOF / server shutdown
    SessionActive  --> Closing:          socket EOF / server shutdown
    AgentActive    --> Closing:          socket EOF / server shutdown
    Closing        --> [*]:              reader + writer exit
```

`CreateSession` is valid exactly once, and only on a bare connection. Model management, storage, voice, and agent requests are valid only **after** `CreateSession` — you can warm up a model before creating any agents, but not before creating the session.

## Agent: one conversation, one graph

An [agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#agent) is a single ongoing conversation. You create one by sending `CreateAgentRequest` with:

- a [workflow graph](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/workflows-graphs-nodes.html) (required),
- a default model name for nodes that do not override it,
- optional `template` and `placement` params on `Generate` nodes (see [Use Mustache Templates](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-mustache-templates.html)) if the graph contains any `Retrieve` or `Instruction` node,
- an optional [`variables`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agent-variables.html) declaration (the agent's complete typed key→value store) and a `kv_cache_initialization` choice (`AllocateOnly` / `Prefill` / `DeferAllocation`) — see [Agent Parameters](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/agent-parameters.html) and [Manage an Agent's KV Cache](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-agent-kv-cache.html),
- a [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html) (`voice`), required when the graph has a `Speak` or `GenerateAndSpeak` node — the agent's one voice, shared by every speaking node,
- optional per-agent flags like `enable_diagnostics` and `maintain_dialogue_history`.

The server responds with `CreateAgentResponse` once the graph compiles and the default model resolves — after that you can send messages. Models referenced by the graph must already be on disk; `CreateAgent` fails fast with `GraphCompilationFailed` if one is missing, rather than downloading it on the spot. Acquire models beforehand via the editor Model Manager or `DownloadModelRequest`.

A session can own as many agents as you want. Each has its own dialog (the growing list of [interactions](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#interaction)), its own per-node KV caches, and its own sampling parameters. Turns on a single session run one at a time — agent A's turn finishes before agent B's turn starts. The dialog is not a save file: to persist it across sessions, export a snapshot into **your** game save. See [Save and load agent state](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/save-and-load-agent-state.html).

### The implicit agent state machine

```
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*]     --> Idle:    CreateAgent compiled the graph
    Idle    --> Running: SendMessage → turn starts
    Running --> Running: nodes execute; inference runs on the shared model
    Running --> Paused:  Pause node / pausing ToolCall disposition
    Paused  --> Running: Resume (continue exit route, or jump to a node)
    Running --> Idle:    graph reaches END → TurnComplete(Success)
    Running --> Idle:    Cancel / teardown → TurnComplete(Cancelled)
    Running --> Idle:    64-step budget exceeded / error → TurnComplete(Error)
    Paused  --> Idle:    Cancel → TurnComplete(Cancelled)
    Paused  --> Idle:    pause timeout, no timeout exit → TurnComplete(PauseTimedOut)
    Idle    --> [*]:     DestroyAgent or session close
    Running --> [*]:     session close (turn is cancelled first)
```

Four facts about this machine matter in practice:

1. **Turns are atomic per agent.** A second `SendMessage` while the previous turn is running is rejected with [error 3004 `AgentBusy`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent). The in-flight turn is *not* pre-empted; it runs to completion.
1. **A turn can pause between nodes.** A [`Pause`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/pause.html) node, or a [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html) with a pausing `disposition` (`Pause`, `PauseAndAcknowledge`, `AwaitResult`), suspends the turn mid-flight. While **Paused** the turn is still open (`SendMessage` still returns `AgentBusy`), but [`ChangeAgentParam`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/change-agent-parameters.html) — normally forbidden while a turn runs — is allowed. `Resume` continues it. A pause can also time out: `Pause.pause_timeout_ms` of `0` waits forever, and with a timeout the turn follows `timeout_exit`, or ends with `TurnComplete(PauseTimedOut)` when that exit is empty. A `ToolCall` with `pause_timeout_ms` `0` inherits the server's `workflow.tool_call_pause_timeout_ms` (2000 ms in the shipped `server-config.json`) and has no timeout exit. See [Pause and Resume a Turn](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/pause-and-resume-turns.html).
1. **Cancellation is cooperative.** A [`Cancel`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/cancel-a-turn.html), destroying the agent, or closing the session signals the turn to stop; it unwinds at the next convenient point and produces `TurnComplete(Cancelled)`.
1. **Step budget, not time budget.** Every agent stops a turn after 64 node steps. The budget is fixed, not a `CreateAgent` setting. This is the escape valve for routing loops, not a generation timeout.

## What an agent owns

```
flowchart TB
    A[Agent] --> D[Dialog<br>list of Interactions]
    A --> G[Graph<br>frozen at CreateAgent]
    A --> V[Voice<br>one per agent, optional]
    A --> N1[Node 1<br>KV cache / params]
    A --> N2[Node 2<br>KV cache / params]
    A --> N3[Node N<br>...]
    G --> ExitFields[exit fields on params]
    G --> Start[start id]
```

- The **dialog** is the source of truth for the conversation. Every turn appends one interaction: the user's message, the model's reply, and anything the graph attached along the way (retrieved knowledge, recorded tool calls).
- The **graph** is frozen for the life of the agent. You cannot swap nodes or exit wiring after `CreateAgent` — destroy and re-create the agent if you need a different shape.
- **Per-node state** — KV caches, sampling defaults, and any node-local caches — belongs to the agent, not the session. Two agents using the same model still have independent KV state.
- The **voice** belongs to the agent, not to its graph. Every speaking node uses it, so one graph can serve characters with different voices. Replace it with `SetAgentVoice` while the agent is idle, and switch its [delivery mode](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html#delivery-modes) with `SetAgentDeliveryMode` at any time. Agents that use the same TTS model share the loaded model.

## Lifecycle in one picture

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Session
    participant A as Agent

    C->>S: connect
    S-->>C: ConnectionReady
    C->>S: CreateSessionRequest
    S-->>C: CreateSessionResponse
    C->>S: CreateAgentRequest(graph, model, …)
    S->>A: compile graph, resolve model
    S-->>C: CreateAgentResponse(agent_id)
    loop one per user turn
        C->>S: SendMessageRequest(agent_id, text)
        S->>A: dispatch
        A-->>S: AnswerText (stream)
        S-->>C: AnswerText
        A-->>S: TurnComplete(status)
        S-->>C: TurnComplete
    end
    C->>S: DestroyAgentRequest(agent_id)
    S->>A: cancel + destroy
    S-->>C: Ack
    C->>S: disconnect
```

## Edges and pitfalls

- **Agent ids are session-scoped.** An `agent_id` is only meaningful inside the session that created it. If you reconnect, all previous agent ids become invalid.
- **`CreateSession` is one-shot.** A second `CreateSession` is rejected with `SessionAlreadyExists`; to start over with different settings, open a new connection and create a new session. Engines are not a session setting: each model runs on the engine its catalog entry names, whatever engine hints the session sent.
- **Shared string storages need the storage alive at `CreateAgent` time.** Destroying a [string storage](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/string-storage.html) after creating an agent that references it is safe — the agent keeps using the data until the agent itself is destroyed. But the reverse is not: you cannot reference a storage that does not yet exist. See [Lifetime and Ownership](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/lifetime-and-ownership.html) for the full picture of who holds what reference and when each goes away.
- **Multiple agents on one session run serially.** The server multiplexes their turns fairly, but on a given session only one turn runs at a time. Open more sessions if you need parallelism.

# Lifetime and Ownership

Three kinds of resources in Tryll outlive any single wire request: [string storages](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/string-storage.html), [embedded string storages](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html), and [language / embedding models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html). Agents reference them by name, often for the whole conversation. This page explains *who owns each one*, *how long it stays alive*, and *what actually happens when you destroy it* — so you can reason about the edge cases without reading the server source.

## The dual-ownership pattern

Every resource of the three kinds follows the same shape:

- A **manager** owns a shared reference plus a **retention mode** (`Pinned` or `OnDemand`). The manager is the surface you see on the wire — it answers `Create…` / `Destroy…` requests.
- Each **node** that needs the resource is given its own shared reference at [`CreateAgent`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/agent-parameters.html) time.
- The resource lives as long as **any** reference still exists — manager or node, whichever is last.

Consequence: destroying a storage from the client never yanks data out from under a live agent. `Destroy…Request` drops only the manager's reference (or demotes it to OnDemand). Any agent whose nodes still hold the resource finishes cleanly; the bytes are freed once the *last* reference drops.

The only difference between the three resource kinds is *where* the manager lives:

| Resource              | Manager scope                        | Lives until                                                                                                             |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| StringStorage         | **Session**                          | Session closes, or `DestroyStringStorageRequest` (Unpin / unregister) + the last agent holding it is destroyed.         |
| EmbeddedStringStorage | **Session**                          | Session closes, or `DestroyEmbeddedStringStorageRequest` (Unpin / unregister) + the last agent holding it is destroyed. |
| Model                 | **Process** (shared across sessions) | The server unloads it (`UnloadModelRequest` for Pinned, or automatically for OnDemand once unused).                     |

The rest of this page walks through each case.

## StringStorage

The preferred way to supply a string storage to a node is to set the node's `string_storage` param to a **relative file path** under the process storage root, which is set when the server starts (`--storage-root`, `storage_root` in `server-config.json`, or the mode default); there is no per-session root, and a path that resolves outside the root is rejected with `StorageOutsideRoot`. The server loads the file on demand at `CreateAgent` time — no explicit `Create…` / `Destroy…` wire round-trip is needed.

When you need to share the same inline data across multiple agents, use an explicit [`CreateStringStorageRequest`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/string-storage.html), which Pins the storage in the session manager.

```
flowchart LR
    subgraph Session
        Mgr["StringStorageManager\n(Pinned | OnDemand)"]
    end
    subgraph Agent
        N1[CannedResponse node]
        N2[RegexGuardrail node]
    end
    Mgr -- "shared ref" --> S[(StringStorage)]
    N1  -- "shared ref" --> S
    N2  -- "shared ref" --> S
```

**Retention modes:**

- **Pinned** — set by `CreateStringStorageRequest` (explicit Pin) or when `NodeFactory` loads a file-backed storage at `CreateAgent` time. The manager holds a reference of its own; `EvictUnusedOnDemand()` will not evict it.
- **OnDemand** — the default for lazy file-backed loads that are then Unpinned (e.g. after `DestroyStringStorageRequest`). The manager releases its reference; once the last node drops its reference the storage is freed.

**What each operation actually does:**

- `CreateStringStorageRequest` — loads or registers the storage and Pins it. Server responds with `CreateStringStorageResponse`.
- `DestroyStringStorageRequest` — for file-backed storages: demotes from Pinned to OnDemand (eligible for eviction once no node holds it). For virtual / inline storages: removes the named entry. The node references are unaffected in either case.
- `CreateAgentRequest` (with a relative-path `string_storage` param) — the session's `NodeFactory` resolves the path, loads-or-gets the storage from the manager, Pins it while the agent is alive, and gives the node a shared reference.
- `DestroyAgentRequest` — each node's shared reference drops. If the storage was loaded as part of this agent and has since been Unpinned (or was never explicitly Pinned), the manager demotes to OnDemand and the entry is evicted on the next `EvictUnusedOnDemand` call.
- Session close — every remaining agent is cancelled and released first, then the session drops its storage managers. The last reference goes with whichever of them is released last.

Updating a storage in place is not supported — create a new one under a different name (and, if needed, rebind via [`change_param`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/change-agent-parameters.html)) instead of mutating one that agents already hold.

## EmbeddedStringStorage

The preferred way to supply a knowledge base is to set the node's `embedded_string_storage` param to a **relative path** pointing at the KB config JSON under the process storage root. The server loads the config and builds (or reuses a cached) HNSW index at `CreateAgent` time — no explicit `Create…` is needed.

```
flowchart LR
    subgraph Session
        Mgr["EmbeddedStringStorageManager\n(Pinned | OnDemand)"]
    end
    subgraph Agent
        R[Retrieve node]
    end
    Mgr -- "shared ref" --> E[(EmbeddedStringStorage<br>records + HNSW index)]
    R   -- "shared ref" --> E
```

The in-memory object — records, embeddings, HNSW index — follows the same dual-ownership rules as `StringStorage`, including Pinned vs OnDemand retention.

**Create = Pin; Destroy = Unpin:**

- `CreateEmbeddedStringStorageRequest (config_path)` — resolves the relative path against the process storage root, loads via `FindOrLoad` (reusing a cached entry if available), and Pins the entry.
- `CreateEmbeddedStringStorageRequest (strings)` — builds an in-memory index and registers it as a **virtual** entry under `name`. Always Pinned while registered; evicted when destroyed.
- `DestroyEmbeddedStringStorageRequest` — for file-backed (Path A) entries: demotes from Pinned to OnDemand. For virtual (Path B) entries: removes the entry. Node references are unaffected.

**On-disk artifacts are separate.** A Path-A storage reads from a records file and optionally a pre-built `.usearch` index on the server's disk. Those files are *not* owned by the session; they remain on disk after the session ends and are reused on the next request that points at the same config. What is rebuilt per session is the in-memory index object, not the cached bytes on disk.

## Models

Models follow the same manager + node pattern, but the manager lives on the **server process**, not on a single session. That is why pinning a model in one session keeps it loaded for every other session on the same server.

```
flowchart LR
    subgraph Server process
        MM[ModelManager]
    end
    subgraph Session A
        GA[Generate / ToolCall node]
    end
    subgraph Session B
        GB[Generate / ToolCall node]
    end
    MM -- "shared ref<br>(only while Pinned)" --> M[(Model)]
    GA -- "shared ref" --> M
    GB -- "shared ref" --> M
```

Two things decide how long the model stays resident. The same rules apply to **language, embedding, STT, and TTS** (each kind has its own cache; VAD is catalog/download-only and follows the STT model that loads it):

- **Retention mode.** `LoadModelRequest` installs the model as **Pinned** — the `ModelManager` holds a reference of its own. A model loaded implicitly (because an agent's graph, voice input, TTS, or embedding use referenced it without a prior `LoadModelRequest`) is **OnDemand** — only the live users hold references beyond the cache entry.
- **Active users.** Each `Generate` / `ToolCall` context (and STT / TTS / embedding holder) keeps a reference for the life of its agent or voice-input session.

The model is unloaded when the last reference goes away *and* the manager decides to drop the cache entry:

- **Pinned** → released by `UnloadModelRequest`, but only after every user has been torn down. If agents are still active the request is acknowledged immediately and the actual unload is deferred until the last context drops.
- **OnDemand** → the server runs `EvictUnusedOnDemand` after every `DestroyAgentRequest`, and again immediately before the next validated load into any of the four caches (cross-cache sweep). No explicit unload call is needed.

## Session end

When the TCP connection closes (or the server shuts down), a single cleanup sequence runs for the session:

1. Every active turn is cancelled.
1. Every agent in the session is released. The session object stays alive until they are gone.
1. The session then drops its `StringStorageManager` and `EmbeddedStringStorageManager`, releasing their references. No storage eviction sweep runs during shutdown.
1. Models are left in place. An OnDemand model that no other session holds stays cached until the next session's pre-load sweep drops it.

Pinned models survive — that is the whole point of pinning. A fresh session can reuse them without paying the load cost again.

## Common questions

**Do I need to call `CreateStringStorageRequest` before `CreateAgentRequest`?** No. Set the node's `string_storage` to a relative file path and the server loads it automatically at `CreateAgentRequest` time. Explicit `Create…` is only needed for shared inline data or to pre-warm a Pinned entry.

**Can I `destroy_string_storage` while an agent is running?** Yes. The call is safe at any time. Live nodes keep the data alive for the rest of the agent's life; the storage name just becomes available for reuse in the same session.

**Can I use any name for an inline storage?** The name must not resolve to an existing real file under the process storage root. If it does, the registration is rejected with `7004 StorageNameInUse` to prevent the virtual entry from silently shadowing a file with the same name.

**Do I need to re-pin my model after each agent?** No. Pinned stays loaded across agent create / destroy cycles — and even across sessions on the same server process. Only `UnloadModelRequest` demotes it.

**Is the Path-A `.usearch` index rebuilt every session?** No. The cached index on disk is reused; only the in-memory index object follows the normal shared-reference rules.

**What if two agents reference the same storage?** Each holds its own reference. Destroying one agent drops that agent's reference; the other keeps using the storage normally.

**Can I mutate a string storage in place?** No — there is no wire request to edit one. Create a new storage and, if a live agent needs the new content, use [`change_param`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/change-agent-parameters.html) to rebind the node's `string_storage` param.

- [Reference: Embedded String Storage](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html)
- [Reference: Model Management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html)
- [Concept: Agents and Sessions](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/agents-and-sessions.html)

# Models and Inference Engines

Tryll is a model host first and a workflow engine second. This page is about the host side: what counts as a "model", how the server talks to the hardware, what the KV cache is doing under your agents, and how to think about context size and quantisation when you pick one.

## Four kinds of models

Tryll treats four kinds of models as first-class citizens:

- **Language models** — generate text. These are what [`Generate`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate.html) and [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html) nodes use.
- **Embedding models** — turn text into fixed-length float vectors. [`Retrieve`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve.html) uses one to embed the current user message before searching an [embedded string storage](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html).
- **STT models** (speech-to-text) — transcribe audio to text for voice input. Exposed in every client via the voice-input API (C++ `CreateVoiceInput`, Unity `CreateVoiceInputAsync` / `TryllVoiceInput`, Unreal `UTryllVoiceInputComponent`).
- **TTS models** (text-to-speech) — synthesise speech from text. Exposed via the [`Speak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/speak.html) and [`GenerateAndSpeak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate-and-speak.html) nodes, with ready-made playback components (`TryllSpeaker` in Unity, `UTryllSpeakerComponent` in Unreal). See [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html).

Every entry in the catalog (`models.json`) declares which kind it is. Asking for a model of the wrong kind fails fast with a clear error. See [Model Management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html) for the full catalog schema.

You do not pick an engine per kind. Each catalog entry names the engine that runs it, so downloading or registering a model is all a session needs. `CreateSession`'s `model_config` may carry an optional `engines` list of (role, engine) pairs, but only as a warm-up hint: the server starts those engines at session creation instead of at first use. It never gates a session or a load, and leaving it empty is normal. (Before protocol v13, `CreateSession` had four engine fields that defaulted to `Mock`; they are gone.)

## Inference engines: how the model actually runs

An **inference engine** is the runtime that executes the model against your CPU or GPU. Tryll currently ships these engines:

| Engine                                              | Backend                                              | Status                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Mock`                                              | In-process stub                                      | Used for tests; no real inference.                                                                                                            |
| `LlamaCpp`                                          | [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp)  | Default for language + embedding. Also hosts SNAC TTS (Orpheus, Maya1) via a shared ONNX decoder. GGUF files; CPU + Vulkan / CUDA / ROCm GPU. |
| `SherpaOnnx`                                        | [sherpa-onnx](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx) | STT, TTS, and VAD. TTS families: Supertonic and Pocket TTS — see [TTS Models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/tts-models.html).   |
| `OnnxRuntime`                                       | ONNX Runtime                                         | TTS for the Chatterbox family — internal only, not in the public catalog.                                                                     |
| `OnnxGenAI`, `WindowsML`, `OpenVino`, `TensorRtLlm` | Reserved                                             | Enum slots exist; implementations land in future releases.                                                                                    |

The engine comes from the model's catalog entry, not from the session (see the [C++ API](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/cpp/index.html#tryllclientcreatesession) or [wire protocol](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/wire-protocol.html#session-lifecycle) for the optional warm-up hint).

A catalog entry lists one or more **variants**. Variants describe different files, not different engines: every variant of one model must name the same engine, and the catalog is rejected otherwise.

```
{
  "name": "Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
  "variants": [
    { "engine": "llama-cpp",
      "huggingface_repo": "bartowski/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-GGUF",
      "files": ["Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf"],
      "kv_cache_type": "q8_0",
      "tool_call_support": "supported" }
  ]
}
```

(The JSON keys are `engine`, `huggingface_repo`, and `files` — an array. Use `local_path` + `files` for a model already on disk. Every language-model variant must declare `tool_call_support` as `"supported"` or `"unsupported"`.)

The server loads a model on the engine its catalog entry names. If this server build does not include that engine, the load fails with [`6008 EngineNotAvailable`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#6xxx-model-download).

## The KV cache: why generation is fast *after* the first token

A language model's prompt can be thousands of tokens long. Naively re-running the full prompt through the model on every new token would be unworkable. Instead, transformer models keep an intermediate per-token state — the **key/value cache**, or [KV cache](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/glossary.html#context-kv) — that encodes "everything the model has seen so far". Adding one more token costs one more forward pass, not N.

Tryll keeps one KV cache per node, per agent. Each turn, the node compares the new prompt against the cached token sequence:

- **Unchanged prefix** is kept.
- **Stale tail** (tokens that differ) is evicted.
- **New suffix** is processed in batches.

So the cost of "remembering the conversation" is the cost of appending the new user turn's tokens — not the whole history — as long as you are not rewriting the past.

### KV cache dtype

Each llama.cpp variant can declare a `kv_cache_type`:

| Value  | Bytes/element | Notes                                                                                                |
| ------ | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `f16`  | 2             | Highest quality.                                                                                     |
| `q8_0` | ~1            | Default when `kv_cache_type` is absent, on every build. Indistinguishable quality for most chat use. |
| `q4_0` | ~0.5          | Halves memory vs. q8_0; small quality hit. Useful on memory-constrained GPUs.                        |

The cache size dominates VRAM / RAM for long conversations. Moving from `f16` to `q8_0` roughly halves it; from `q8_0` to `q4_0` halves it again. Catalog `kv_cache_type` is the model-load default. A node's structural `context` table can override it per context (`Inherit` keeps the catalog value). At a right-sized window (Classify / ToolCall 2048) a `q4_0` override is usually not a measurable VRAM win; the dtype delta shows up at large `n_ctx` (around 8192).

## Context size and why 4k is not 4k

Every language model has a maximum **context size** — the total number of tokens the model can attend to at once (prompt + generation buffer). Tryll reserves a slice at the end for the generation itself (`generation_reserve`), and uses the rest as the **high water mark** for projection. Tokens beyond the high water mark get trimmed by [token-budget projection](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/projection-and-token-budgets.html) before the model ever sees them.

So a model nominally advertised as "4k context" will, in practice, give you something like 3.5k of usable history — more than enough for most dialog, but worth knowing about when you design a RAG prompt.

## Embedding models

Embedding models are much smaller and simpler: a stateless encoder that turns text into fixed-dimension vectors, with mean pooling to produce one vector per input. The server calls the model once per query and once per chunk at index-build time; that is the whole story.

An embedding model is **required** whenever you create an [embedded string storage](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html) — either sent on the wire (Path B) or declared in the `*.kb.json` config (Path A). The two sides must match.

## The loaded-model pool

Language, embedding, STT, and TTS models are loaded once per process into separate caches and reference-counted with the same retention rules:

- **Pinned** retention — set by `LoadModelRequest` for any of the four kinds. The model stays in memory until you explicitly unload it *and* no active contexts / sessions reference it.
- **OnDemand** retention (default) — set by the lazy load path when an agent, voice input, TTS, or embedding use first needs the model. The server frees unused OnDemand models after `DestroyAgentRequest` and again immediately before the next validated load into any cache (cross-cache sweep). Pinned models and models still held by agents are left alone.

VAD models appear in the catalog for download/config, but they are **not** part of this pin/unload pool — offline STT loads VAD as a dependency of the STT model.

This pair lets you either nail a model in place ("this is the chat model, always keep it warm") or let the pool breathe when sessions cycle through models. See [Lifetime and Ownership → Models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/lifetime-and-ownership.html#models) for the full reference-counting story, including what happens when `UnloadModelRequest` arrives while agents are still using the model.

## Downloading and the "Downloaded" status

Models you did not bundle with the server can be pulled from Hugging Face via `DownloadModelRequest`. The server streams `DownloadProgress` frames and finishes with a `DownloadComplete(success=true)`. After that the model has status `Downloaded` and can be loaded. `Local` is reserved for a model whose catalog `local_path` resolved to a file on disk. See [Model Management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html#model-status) for the full lifecycle and the distinction between on-disk statuses and `Loaded` (memory).

## Edges and pitfalls

- **No model swap mid-turn.** The model a context points to is resolved at agent-creation time. Pinning or unloading any model while an agent is running is safe: unloading *the* model a running agent depends on only drops the pin, and the model stays resident until that agent's contexts are destroyed.
- **KV cache is *per node, per agent*.** Two `Generate` nodes using the same model in the same graph still each pay their own KV cost. Budget memory accordingly.
- **Embedding and language models are not interchangeable.** Trying to point a `Retrieve` node at a language model (or a `Generate` node at an embedding model) fails validation with a clear error.
- **Context-window claims are rough.** Official context sizes assume no generation buffer; the high-water mark is what actually governs your prompt budget.
- **One base model, several behaviours.** An LLM node can run its model with [LoRA adapters](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-a-lora-adapter.html): small GGUF files trained for that base model. The base weights stay loaded once; only the nodes that name an adapter use it.

# TTS and Voice Output

Tryll supports server-side text-to-speech synthesis. Sherpa-ONNX hosts Supertonic 3 and Pocket TTS. llama.cpp runs Orpheus and Maya1, whose audio codes a shared SNAC 24 kHz ONNX decoder turns into sound on the CPU. See [TTS Models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/tts-models.html) for which catalog names are public and which controls each family accepts. Two graph nodes produce speech:

- [GenerateAndSpeak](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate-and-speak.html) fuses LLM inference with TTS synthesis, streaming PCM audio frames alongside the text reply — lowest latency for a *generated* spoken answer.
- [Speak](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/speak.html) is TTS-only: it voices the slot named by its `input` param with no LLM pass. The default is `user_message`, the player's own words, so set `input` to an upstream node's output (e.g. a [CannedResponse](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/canned-response.html)).

Both stream the same PCM audio frames to the client and use the same playback components. Neither node holds a voice: both speak with the agent's one [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html). They differ only in whether generation is involved.

## The streaming pipeline

When a `GenerateAndSpeak` node runs:

1. **Format announcement** — the first speaking node of the turn sends one `TtsAudioFormatFrame`: sample rate, channels (1) and bits per sample (16). It is sent once per turn: a later speaking node in the same turn reuses it, because the agent has one voice.
1. **Token generation** — the language model produces tokens, forwarded to the client as `AnswerText` deltas (identical to `Generate`).
1. **Sentence segmentation** — tokens accumulate until a sentence ends and the text since the last cut is at least `min_sentence_chars` wide (a CJK or other 3–4-byte character counts as 2):
   - `.` `!` `?` or `…` followed by a space or by the end of the text so far. A `.` right after a digit waits for the next character, so "3.14" stays whole.
   - At once: CJK `。！？｡`, Devanagari `। ॥`, Arabic `؟`, Urdu `۔`, Ethiopic `።` and `‼`. Closing quotes and brackets right after them (`」』）”`…) stay with the sentence.
   - With `first_chunk_max_chars` set, the *first* chunk may also end at `,` `;` `:` followed by a space or at an em dash, or at the next space once it is that wide — never before 5 words or `min_sentence_chars`. This has no effect on text without spaces, such as CJK.
   - Text that runs 16 KiB with no sentence end is cut at the last space, so the buffer stays bounded; the server logs a warning.
1. **TTS synthesis** — each chunk is synthesized to mono int16 PCM at the model's native sample rate and streamed as `TtsAudioFrame` messages. At most one chunk is synthesizing at a time: the next finished chunk waits for it, and the text stream pauses briefly while it waits.

This keeps time-to-first-audio low: the NPC starts speaking as soon as the first chunk is ready, while the language model is still generating the rest of the answer.

```
Client                          Server
  │                                │
  ├─ SendMessageRequest ──────────►│
  │◄── TtsAudioFormatFrame ────────┤  (node starts)
  │◄── AnswerText … ───────────────┤  (LLM tokens)
  │◄── TtsAudioFrame … ────────────┤  (first sentence)
  │◄── AnswerText … ───────────────┤  (LLM still running)
  │◄── TtsAudioFrame … ────────────┤  (next sentences)
  │◄── TurnComplete ───────────────┤  (after the last audio)
```

## Audio format

All TTS audio is **mono signed-16-bit PCM** at the sample rate reported in the `TtsAudioFormatFrame` frame. The sample rate is model-specific: for example 44 100 Hz for Supertonic 3 and 24 000 Hz for Orpheus and Maya1. Always read it from the format frame. The Unity speaker converts the int16 samples to float32; the Unreal speaker queues the int16 PCM directly.

## End of stream

`TtsAudioFrame` carries no `is_final` flag. The last frame arrives before `TurnComplete`. The audio queue on the client drains naturally — the playback component fills the audio buffer with silence on underrun until the queue is empty.

## Session configuration

There is no TTS engine to declare. Download a voice (a TTS model) in the Model Manager and name it in the agent's voice profile (`tts_model_name`). The catalog chooses the engine for each voice — Sherpa-ONNX for Supertonic / Pocket, llama.cpp for Orpheus / Maya1. A session warm-up hint is optional; see [Choose where models run](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/choose-where-models-run.html).

## Voice configuration

An agent has **one voice**, a [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html), passed when the agent is created. Every speaking node of the agent uses it, so one workflow can serve many characters with different voices. A graph that speaks must be given a voice: without one, agent creation fails with `3025 AgentVoiceRequired`. An agent whose graph never speaks loads no TTS model, even if it has a voice.

The profile holds:

| Field               | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tts_model_name`    | Catalog voice name. **Required**; there is no default model.                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `speaker_id`        | Built-in voice index, `0` to the model's speaker count − 1. Supertonic 3: `0`–`9`. Orpheus: `0`–`7` (Tara … Zoe). Maya1: `0`–`1` (or override with `voice_description`). Single-speaker models (Pocket TTS) must stay `0`.             |
| `reference_voice`   | Reference clip (storage-root-relative) for voice-cloning models (Pocket TTS, Qwen3-TTS Base). Empty = model default voice (Qwen3-TTS Base has none). See [Clone a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html). |
| `voice_description` | Maya1 only: natural-language identity (age, accent, pitch, timbre).                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `speed`             | Speech-rate multiplier, `0.1`–`3.0`. Orpheus, Maya1 and Qwen3-TTS: only `1.0`.                                                                                                                                                         |
| `lang`              | Synthesis language on models that choose it per call (Supertonic 3: 31 languages). Empty = the session locale, then the catalog default. Rejected on fixed-language models.                                                            |
| `emit_visemes`      | Send a lip-sync viseme track for every sentence the agent speaks.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `delivery_modes`    | Named deliveries (`angry`, `calm`, …). See below.                                                                                                                                                                                      |

The profile is validated once, when it is set. A field the loaded model cannot use fails with `3023 InvalidVoiceProfile` rather than being ignored.

The nodes keep only their chunking settings, because chunking acts differently on streamed LLM text than on ready text:

| Node parameter          | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `min_sentence_chars`    | Minimum width of a chunk before a sentence end closes it (a CJK or other 3–4-byte character counts as 2). Default `12`, two or three English words. Lower = shorter first-audio latency.                                                                                                                           |
| `first_chunk_max_chars` | First chunk only: also end it at a clause mark, and at the next space once it is this wide (never under 5 words or `min_sentence_chars`). `0` = off. `48` cut the model-side wait before the first audio by about 40% in our measurements. Listen to it with your voice first: a clause can end on a falling tone. |

Both are mutable with `ChangeAgentParam` (see [Change Agent Parameters at Runtime](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/change-agent-parameters.html)). The voice itself is not: replace it with `SetAgentVoice`, which is accepted only while the agent is idle.

## Delivery modes

A **delivery mode** is a named way of speaking that a voice defines, such as `angry` or `whisper`. Game code switches it with `SetAgentDeliveryMode(mode, intensity)` at any time, even mid-turn; the change applies from the next sentence. The built-in mode `neutral` is the plain voice.

What a mode can change depends on the model. Clone models switch to a different recording of the same character. Maya1 adds a delivery clause such as "angry tone at high intensity". Supertonic 3 and Orpheus have no emotion control, so a mode can only change speed (Supertonic) or must be empty. A profile can still define the same mode names on every voice, so game code that says `angry` works for every character. See [Voice Profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html#delivery-modes) for the per-model table and what `intensity` does.

Do not encode identity or delivery as a spoken `[emotion]` prefix — that syntax is not supported. Model-native `<tag>` tokens (for example Maya `<laugh>`) may appear in the text the synthesizer hears; unknown tags are stripped from the audio copy only and do not rewrite history.

If synthesis fails during a turn, the client gets an `ErrorResponse` with `4001` ("TTS synthesis failed") and the turn still completes; the text reply is not affected.

## Lip sync (visemes)

An agent whose voice has `emit_visemes` on also sends a **viseme track** from every speaking node, `Speak` and `GenerateAndSpeak` alike: the mouth shapes that go with the speech, and when each one starts. It uses the 15 standard Oculus visemes (`sil` for rest, `PP` for p/b/m, `aa` for an open vowel, …), which map onto a face rig's blendshapes.

The server builds the track for each sentence as soon as that sentence is synthesized, from two inputs:

- **the text** — the words are turned into speech sounds with an English pronunciation dictionary, and each sound into a mouth shape;
- **the synthesized audio** — silences become rests (anchored to the sentence's punctuation where possible), the shapes are spread over the spoken stretches in proportion to typical sound lengths, and louder speech opens the mouth further.

The track also keeps lip closures on screen long enough to read, merges shapes too short to see, and starts each shape slightly before its sound, as real lips do. It arrives as one `TtsVisemeFrame` per sentence, after that sentence's audio once its synthesis is done, so under normal buffering it reaches the client before that audio plays. A sentence that produced no audio sends no frame. Offsets are in samples from the start of the turn's audio (its one format announcement), and keep counting across every speaking node of the turn.

No extra model runs. What to expect:

- **Timing is estimated, not measured per sound.** Pauses, starts and ends follow the real audio closely; the shapes inside a stretch of speech are placed by proportion.
- **English pronunciation.** Text in other Latin-script languages gets approximate shapes from English spelling rules. Text in other scripts (Cyrillic, CJK, …) gets no shapes: the mouth stays at rest.
- **Voice-agnostic.** The track works with every TTS voice, since it only needs the text and the audio.

See [Add Lip Sync to a Character](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-lip-sync-to-a-character.html) for setup.

## Client-side playback components

The Tryll Unity and Unreal packages ship a ready-made playback component that wires the TTS audio stream to the platform audio engine:

| Platform | Component                                    | Audio backend                                     |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Unity    | `TryllSpeaker` (`MonoBehaviour`)             | Streaming `AudioClip` with `pcmReaderCallback`    |
| Unreal   | `UTryllSpeakerComponent` (`UActorComponent`) | `USoundWaveProcedural` + hidden `UAudioComponent` |

The Unreal speaker is always non-spatialized (2D). The Unity speaker plays through its `AudioSource` and leaves that source's spatial settings alone. For custom audio, such as your own spatializer, subscribe to the raw PCM: `TryllSpeaker.OnTtsPcm` (Unity) or `UTryllSpeakerComponent::OnTtsPcm` (Unreal). You can also replace the speaker entirely with `TryllAgent.SetOnTtsAudioFormat` / `SetOnTtsAudio`; each holds one callback, so setting it replaces the speaker's.

# STT and Voice Input

Voice input lets a player **speak** to an agent instead of typing. The client streams raw microphone audio to the server, a **speech-to-text (STT)** model transcribes it, and the transcript comes back as a stream of updates. The client can then send the final text to an agent as if the player had typed it.

This page explains the mental model: the utterance lifecycle, the two choices that shape how a turn ends, and the kinds of transcript update you receive. For the step-by-step API, see [Use Voice Input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html); to bias recognition toward game-specific words, see [Bias Voice Input with Hotwords](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input-hotwords.html).

## The pipeline

```
flowchart LR
    mic["Microphone<br>(client)"] -->|PCM frames| handle["VoiceInput handle"]
    handle -->|AudioBuffer| server["Server STT session<br>(Sherpa-ONNX)"]
    server -->|TranscriptUpdate| handle
    handle -.->|UtteranceFinal, then SendMessage| agent["Agent (optional)"]
```

You create a **VoiceInput handle** (bound to an STT model), open an **utterance**, stream 16-bit PCM audio as it's captured, and receive **transcript updates**. The server resamples your audio to the model's rate, runs it through the STT engine, and pushes updates back. A non-empty final transcript is text the client can send to an agent; the server does not start that turn.

Voice input needs an **STT model** on disk — download one in the Model Manager. Its catalog entry names its engine (Sherpa-ONNX), so the session needs no engine setting. STT runs on the **CPU**, so it costs system RAM but **no VRAM**; see [Models and Inference Engines](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/models-and-inference-engines.html).

## The utterance lifecycle

An **utterance** is one `Begin … End` cycle on a handle — a single thing the player says.

1. **Begin** — opens a recording window and starts mic capture. The server only transcribes. On a non-empty final, send the text to an agent yourself (the Unity and Unreal voice components do this when a target agent is set, and drop it when that agent already has a turn in flight).
1. **Stream audio** — push PCM chunks as they arrive. Sending is fire-and-forget; chunks that arrive with no open utterance are dropped.
1. **Updates arrive** — the server streams [transcript updates](#transcript-updates) as it recognises speech.
1. **End** — the utterance closes (see [who ends it](#the-two-choices)), producing exactly one `UtteranceFinal` with the complete text. An utterance also closes automatically after `max_utterance_ms` (default 60 s).

`Cancel` discards an open utterance without producing a final transcript.

## Transcript updates

Every update carries a **kind** and the text so far. Treat a `Partial` as overwrite-in-place — it is always superseded by a later update.

| Kind             | Meaning                                                                                                            |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SpeechStart`    | The recogniser detected the start of speech (empty text). Offline models only.                                     |
| `Partial`        | A revisable in-progress hypothesis (`"cast"` → `"cast fire"` → `"cast fireball"`). Streaming (online) models only. |
| `SegmentFinal`   | A committed chunk while the utterance stays open.                                                                  |
| `UtteranceFinal` | The last update for the cycle; carries the complete concatenated text. Exactly one per utterance.                  |

## The two choices

How a turn behaves comes down to two **independent** choices that combine into four cases.

### 1. Who ends the utterance — push-to-talk vs hands-free

- **Push-to-talk (PTT)** — *you* decide when the utterance ends by calling `End` (e.g. on key release). Set `autoFinishOnSilence = false`. Best when the player holds a button to talk.
- **Hands-free** — the *server* closes the utterance when the player stops talking. Set `autoFinishOnSilence = true` (the default). Best for always-listening NPCs.

### 2. Which recogniser — offline vs online

The STT model's family decides how speech is segmented and whether you get partials. You don't set this directly — it comes from the model you pick.

|               | Offline (e.g. Whisper, SenseVoice, Parakeet)                         | Online / streaming (e.g. streaming Zipformer, Paraformer, T-One) |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Partials      | none                                                                 | yes (revisable, low latency)                                     |
| `SpeechStart` | yes                                                                  | no                                                               |
| Segmentation  | **Silero VAD** (voice-activity detection) slices speech from silence | the recogniser's **built-in endpointer**                         |
| Feel          | segment-lagged (decodes a chunk once it's complete)                  | streaming (updates as you speak)                                 |

**Offline** models attend over a whole window at once, so Tryll wraps them with **Silero VAD** to cut the stream into speech segments. **Online** models decode incrementally and have their own endpointer — Tryll does not layer VAD on top of them.

### How the two combine

| PTT/hands-free × recogniser | What closes the turn                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **PTT + offline**           | your `End` call (or the timeout)                                                                                                            |
| **PTT + online**            | your `End` call (partials stream meanwhile)                                                                                                 |
| **Hands-free + offline**    | the first VAD speech segment                                                                                                                |
| **Hands-free + online**     | the first non-empty endpointer result; brief pauses emit empty "heartbeat" segments that keep the turn armed so the player can keep talking |

## Sending the transcript to an agent

The server never starts a turn from speech. When a Unity or Unreal voice component has a target agent, the component sends the non-empty `UtteranceFinal` text to that agent with `SendMessage`, and drops it if the agent already has a turn in flight. Without a voice component, call `SendMessage` with the final text yourself. Either way the spoken words drive a normal turn (streamed `AnswerText`, and TTS if the graph has a [`Speak`/`GenerateAndSpeak`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tts-and-voice-output.html) node). Open the next utterance *after* the reply and any TTS playback finish, so the mic doesn't transcribe the agent's own voice.

## Choosing a model

STT models are declared in the catalog like any other, with `model_type: "stt"` and `engine: "sherpa-onnx"`; you reference one by name when creating the handle. Rough guidance:

- **Latency-sensitive / always-listening** → a streaming model (partials give immediate feedback).
- **Best accuracy, short commands** → an offline model (Whisper family, Parakeet).
- **Hotword biasing** (NPC/spell names) is supported by transducer/CTC families (Parakeet, streaming Zipformer/Paraformer, T-One) — **not** by Whisper or SenseVoice.

Every offline model also loads a **VAD** model (default `Silero VAD`) as a dependency; VAD entries are download/config only and are not separately pinnable. See [Model Management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html) and, for on-disk sizes, [Estimate Memory Footprint](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html).

## Related

- [How-to: Use Voice Input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html) — the full API walkthrough.
- [How-to: Bias Voice Input with Hotwords](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input-hotwords.html)
- [Concept: TTS and Voice Output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tts-and-voice-output.html) — the other half of a voiced NPC.
- [Concept: Models and Inference Engines](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/models-and-inference-engines.html)
- [Reference: Error Codes — 4100–4107](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#4xxx-inference-workflow) — voice-input errors.

# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Small local models know general English. They do not know your game's lore, your product's changelog, or the contents of a customer's ticket history. RAG is the standard trick for fixing that: before the model answers, find the handful of most-relevant chunks of your data, and paste them into the prompt. This page explains how Tryll's RAG works end to end and when to use it.

## The moving parts

```
flowchart LR
    subgraph Session["Session"]
        ESS["Embedded string storage<br>(per-session, named)"]
    end
    subgraph Agent["Agent turn"]
        U["User message"] --> R["Retrieve node<br>embed + search"]
        R -- "chunks" --> KC["Knowledge on the turn"]
        KC --> P["Projection<br>weaves chunks into prompt"]
        P --> G["Generate node"]
    end
    R -. "reads" .-> ESS
```

Tryll splits RAG into two phases:

1. **Index once.** Your data is embedded and stored in an [embedded string storage](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html) — a named, per-session HNSW index over the embeddings.
1. **Retrieve every turn.** The [`Retrieve` node](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve.html) searches with the current user message (by embedding, keywords, or both), finds the top-K best-matching chunks, and attaches them to the current turn. The downstream `Generate` node's projection picks them up and rewrites the user turn to include them.

Nothing else changes. There is no special "RAG model", no separate server. A RAG agent is an agent with a `Retrieve` node in front of a `Generate` node.

## What an embedded string storage actually stores

Two things:

- a **records file** (`*.kb.json`) — an array of `{ id, text, metadata? }` entries, each a chunk you want retrievable;
- optionally an **on-disk index file** (`*.usearch`) — the HNSW graph for fast top-K lookup.

The index is rebuilt from scratch when it is missing, older than the records file, or for a different embedding model. When it is present and fresh, storage creation is near-instant.

You can create a storage two ways:

- **Path A — config on disk.** Ship a tiny `*.json` with pointers to a records file and an optional index file. Use this when the data lives alongside the server. See [Embedded String Storage](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html).
- **Path B — inline strings.** Pass a `strings[]` array and an `embedding_model` on the wire. Use this when the data is produced at runtime. Fine for hundreds or low thousands of chunks; for bigger corpora, go with Path A and avoid re-embedding every reconnect.

## Search modes, top-K, and the threshold

The `Retrieve` node's `retrieval_mode` picks how candidates are ranked:

| Mode              | Ranking                                                                                         |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Dense` (default) | HNSW vector search by **cosine distance** to the query embedding.                               |
| `Lexical`         | BM25 keyword scoring only. No embedding distance.                                               |
| `Hybrid`          | Runs both, then fuses the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, constant `rrf_k`). |

In dense search, for two unit vectors the distance is `1 − cosine_similarity`, so:

| Distance | Similarity             |
| -------- | ---------------------- |
| 0.0      | identical direction    |
| 0.2      | quite close            |
| 0.5      | loosely related        |
| 1.0      | orthogonal (unrelated) |
| 2.0      | opposite direction     |

The `Retrieve` node returns the `top_k` best-ranked chunks. Setting a `threshold` drops dense results with distance *above* it — i.e., the threshold is an upper bound on distance (lower bound on similarity). In `Hybrid` mode it gates only the dense candidates before fusion, and in `Lexical` mode it is ignored.

If *no* chunks survive, the node exits via `not_found` instead of `found`. Your graph decides what to do in that case — the most common pattern is to still route to `Generate` and let the template render gracefully with no chunks (empty `{{#knowledge}}` sections collapse to nothing, leaving only `system_prompt` and `user_message`).

## Metadata filtering

Beyond cosine similarity and the distance threshold, records can be **gated by typed metadata** declared in the knowledge base config's `fields` array. The Retrieve node's `filter` parameter accepts a JSON predicate that is compiled against that schema and evaluated per-candidate during vector search — records that do not match are excluded before `top_k` and `threshold` are applied.

This lets you answer questions like:

- "Only return lore the player's character class can access."
- "Only return quests the player's level is high enough to receive."
- "Only return lore entries the player has already unlocked."

The client embeds its own state as JSON literals when building the filter, and calls `change_param` to push an updated filter whenever the relevant state changes:

```
agent.change_param("retrieve", "filter", json.dumps({
    "op": "and", "args": [
        {"op": "ge",
         "lhs": {"value": player.level},
         "rhs": {"knowledge": "min_level"}},
        {"op": "in",
         "needle":   {"value": player.character_class},
         "haystack": {"knowledge": "character_classes"}},
    ]
}))
```

For the full grammar and all operator shapes, see [Retrieve filter grammar](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve-filter-grammar.html). For how to declare the schema, see [Embedded String Storage — Metadata schema](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/embedded-string-storage.html#metadata-schema).

## Where the chunks land in the prompt

Tryll does *not* fuse retrieved text into the system prompt and hope. You write a [Mustache](https://mustache.github.io/) template on the downstream `Generate` node's `template` param and pick a `placement`.

The projection stage builds a context from the current turn's data:

| Variable                                          | Contents                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `{{#knowledge}}…{{/knowledge}}`                   | Iterates over every retriever's result block. Inside: `{{name}}` (source label) and `{{#chunks}}…{{/chunks}}` (each chunk's `{{id}}`, `{{text}}`, `{{distance}}`). |
| `{{#knowledge_<source>}}…{{/knowledge_<source>}}` | Direct per-retriever iteration — e.g. `{{#knowledge_rag}}`.                                                                                                        |
| `{{user_message}}`                                | The raw user message.                                                                                                                                              |

The `placement` param on `GenerateNode` controls where the rendered text appears relative to the resolved input — it is always inserted as a separate turn *around* the input, never in place of it:

| Value                                         | Effect                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `before_user_as_system`                       | Rendered text becomes a system turn before the user message. **(recommended default)** |
| `before_user_as_user`                         | Rendered text becomes a user turn before the user message.                             |
| `after_user_as_system` / `after_user_as_user` | Appended after the user message.                                                       |

To fully replace what the model sees instead of framing it, compose the rendered text with a [`Transform`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/transform.html) node and have `Generate` consume it via `input` — see [Use Mustache Templates](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-mustache-templates.html#placement-values) for the pattern.

Why this is worth caring about: the single biggest lever on RAG quality is *how clearly the model can tell the difference between "here is context" and "here is the question"*. The template gives you full control over that framing, per-model, without touching any node code.

For step-by-step examples see the [Use Mustache Templates how-to](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-mustache-templates.html).

## Chunking is your problem (mostly)

Tryll does not chunk your source data. A record in the records file is a chunk — one thing the index can return. How you split your source text into records is up to you, and it is the part of RAG with the biggest quality impact. Rough guidelines:

- Keep chunks small enough that the top-K you intend to retrieve fits well inside the model's context window, with room for the conversation history and the answer.
- Prefer chunks with natural semantic boundaries: a paragraph, a Markdown heading section, one FAQ entry, one lore snippet. Chunks that straddle topics confuse the retriever.
- Include stable context inside the chunk itself — a section title, an entity name — so the chunk is meaningful in isolation. The retriever cannot see the surrounding document.

## When RAG helps, and when it hurts

RAG helps when:

- the answer depends on facts the base model cannot know (private data, recent events, internal documents),
- the corpus is large enough that you cannot paste it whole into the prompt, but small enough that the right few chunks will usually be among the top K,
- you want to give the user a feeling of "the assistant has read the docs".

RAG hurts when:

- the question is general reasoning and the retrieved chunks are unrelated noise — the model will often try to use them anyway and produce a worse answer than it would have without them,
- your corpus is tiny (a few hundred lines total). It is cheaper to paste the whole thing into the system prompt than to embed and retrieve.
- you expect the model to synthesise across many chunks — with top-K=3 and a small model, synthesis quality will be limited.

A sensible default for a first RAG agent: `k=3`, `threshold` in the 0.3–0.6 range (tune by watching the retriever log), `placement` = `before_user_as_system`, a template like `{{#knowledge}}{{name}}:\n{{#chunks}}- {{text}}\n{{/chunks}}{{/knowledge}}`, and a `system_prompt` that says "Use the context above to answer the user's question. If the context does not contain the answer, say so."

## Edges and pitfalls

- **Wire / config embedding-model mismatch** fails the index build with [error 8003 `EmbeddedStorageBuildFailed`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#8xxx-embedded-string-storage). Match the two, or leave one of them unset. (`8002` is a different error — a storage of that name already exists.)
- **Stale indexes** are rebuilt. If you bump your records file, the next storage creation detects the mtime and re-embeds. No cache poisoning.
- **Per-session ownership.** Storages die with the session. For a stable corpus across reconnects, re-create from the same config on connect; the on-disk `.usearch` makes that cheap.
- **Knowledge does not persist across turns.** Each turn, only the most recently retrieved chunks are projected. Anything retrieved on earlier turns is not re-surfaced to the model.

- [Reference: Retrieve node](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve.html)
- [Reference: Retrieve filter grammar](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/retrieve-filter-grammar.html)
- [Reference: Generate node](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate.html)
