# Inspect Server Memory

The editor **Memory** window (Unity and Unreal) shows how much RAM and VRAM the Tryll server process is using right now — models, per-agent KV caches, and the remainder we cannot attribute. It is the live check for the recipe in [Estimate Memory Footprint](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html).

It answers questions a download-size spreadsheet cannot: *is that model actually resident?*, *how much KV is sitting on background agents?*, *is "other" on the GPU the editor, or us?*

Scope: the whole server process

The snapshot is **server-wide**. Every session on that process is in the numbers — Chat, Model Manager, Play-in-Editor, a Python client, the QA harness. That is the opposite of the [Agent Log](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-agent-log.html), which sees only this editor connection. A row you do not recognise is not a bug in the window.

Prerequisites

- The Tryll Unity or Unreal plugin installed.
- A Ready editor session — Chat, Model Manager, PIE, or this window's own auto-launch. You do **not** need an agent, and this window does **not** wait for registered models to download.

## Open the window

| Editor | Menu                              |
| ------ | --------------------------------- |
| Unity  | **Window → Tryll → Memory**       |
| Unreal | **Window → Tryll → Tryll Memory** |

The window reuses the shared editor session. If Chat or Model Manager is already Ready, **Refresh** is enabled immediately. If not, it auto-launches the bundled server and calls `CreateSession` the same way Model Manager does — turn on **Auto Launch Server** in Tryll runtime settings if you usually rely on that.

Closing the window releases the connection lease. It does **not** kill the server.

Disconnected state still shows this editor process's RAM. The label is **Unity reserved** in Unity (allocator reserved) and **Unreal process RAM, not editor VRAM** in Unreal (`FPlatformMemory` used physical). Those are different metrics — do not compare them to each other. The server tables stay on screen if you already have a snapshot; they are not wiped.

## Take a snapshot

There is no poll and no graph. Click **Refresh**.

Refresh is disabled until the session is Ready, and while a fetch is in flight. A late reply cannot overwrite a newer one. If a fetch fails after you already have numbers, a stale-snapshot banner keeps the last good table and shows the error.

## How to read the numbers

### Confidence tiers

Every component row has a visible **Confidence** column. That is the feature: an estimate must never look like a measurement.

| Tier          | Meaning                                                                          | How it renders                                                                                      |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Measured**  | The engine or OS told us this number                                             | Plain bytes                                                                                         |
| **Derived**   | Computed from measured inputs (for example device `other` = total − free − ours) | Plain bytes                                                                                         |
| **Estimated** | A calibrated band, not a reading                                                 | Leading `~`, and a high band when the collector supplied one. Hover the row for the estimate basis. |

### System — working set, private, unattributed

The system table is four rows: this editor process's RAM, **Working set**, **Private**, **Unattributed**.

| Field                                       | What it is                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Unity reserved** / **Unreal process RAM** | This editor process — RAM, not editor VRAM. Unity reports allocator reserved; Unreal reports `UsedPhysical`. |
| **Working set**                             | Pages the OS currently has resident for `tryll_server`                                                       |
| **Private**                                 | Commit that is not shareable — closer to "what we allocated"                                                 |
| **Unattributed**                            | Working set minus the RAM we assigned to components                                                          |

Memory-mapped model files count as resident pages but are not allocations we make. A VRAM-placed model therefore often shows up in **unattributed** rather than under its own RAM column. The window calls that out when unattributed is more than half the working set and a model is resident.

### Devices — ours / other / free

One table row per device: **Device**, **Kind**, **Ours** (model weights + KV + compute), **Other** (everything on the device that is not Tryll), **Free**, **Total**.

`other` is where the editor, the compositor, and other processes live. Do not treat it as a Tryll leak. The editor's own VRAM cannot be split out of that number.

If the backend is not initialised yet, devices register on the first model load. That is not an error.

### KV by agent — reserved vs context used

The KV table is sorted **background → buffered → visible**, then by reserved bytes descending. Background KV is the reclaim signal: nobody is waiting on that memory.

| Column           | How to read it                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Class**        | Scheduler class of the last turn (`visible` / `buffered` / `background`), plus `evicted` when the context is not resident. Describes the work, not the agent.                                                 |
| **When**         | Relative time, or **never run** if the context has never completed a turn. Idle class and "never run" are different: a context can be allocated and unused.                                                   |
| **Context used** | A bar plus `used / capacity (pct)`. Headroom to the limit, **not memory growth**. The KV buffer is allocated for the full `context_size` when the context is created and does not grow with the conversation. |
| **Reserved**     | Bytes actually held for that context (RAM + VRAM)                                                                                                                                                             |

### Components

Kind, name, confidence, RAM (a `~` band when estimated), VRAM. KV rows are listed in the agent table above, not repeated here.

## What changes these numbers

| Knob                                               | Where                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Load / unload / pin                                | [Manage Models in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html)           |
| `MemoryPlacement` (RAM vs VRAM)                    | [Choose where models run](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/choose-where-models-run.html)               |
| Per-node `context_size` / `context`                | [Run many agents on a small GPU](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/run-many-agents-on-a-small-gpu.html) |
| Prefill / Evict / `DeferAllocation`                | [Manage an agent's KV cache](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-agent-kv-cache.html)              |
| Server `engines.llama_cpp.inference.default_n_ctx` | [Server configuration](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/server-configuration.html)                  |
| Catalog `kv_cache_type`                            | [Model management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html)                          |

## Relationship to the server monitor

|           | Memory window                            | Server monitor Memory panel      |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Scope     | Whole server process                     | Whole server process             |
| Collector | The same `CollectMemorySnapshot`         | The same `CollectMemorySnapshot` |
| Surface   | Unity / Unreal editor, over the TCP wire | Browser, `GET /api/memory`       |
| Refresh   | Button only                              | SSE / poll, plus a sparkline     |

The numbers should match. The monitor still has the sparkline and stacked bars; this window does not.

C++ (`TryllClient::GetMemoryConsumption`), Python (`client.get_memory_consumption()`), Unity (`RequestGetMemoryConsumptionAsync`), and Unreal (`UTryllSubsystem::RequestGetMemoryConsumption`) return the same snapshot.

## Related

- [Estimate Memory Footprint](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html) — the pre-ship recipe this window checks live
- [Use the Agent Log](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-agent-log.html) — per-connection traffic, not process memory
- [Wire Protocol](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/wire-protocol.html) — `GetMemoryConsumptionRequest` / `Response`

# Compare Dialog Variants in the Lab

A single chat turn tells you what one sample looked like — not whether your workflow is reliable. On-device SLMs are prone to *unreliability*: the same prefix can produce a great answer and a persona break on different seeds. **Tryll Dialog Lab** runs a scripted dialog several times across parameter variants and seeds, then shows every result side by side so you can see the spread at a glance. It ships in both editors — `Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Dialog Lab` in Unity, `Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Tryll Dialog Lab` in Unreal.

The Lab makes **no quality claims** — no judge, no score. It shows raw output, deterministic pass/fail checks, and timings; you decide what "good" means.

Prerequisites

- A `TryllRuntimeSettings` asset (Unity) or the Tryll Project Settings (Unreal).
- At least one `TryllAgentComponent` in the scene (Unity) or level (Unreal) with a workflow asset assigned. Add more if you want to compare models or whole workflows against each other.
- A `TryllDialogScriptAsset` (Unity: `Assets ▸ Create ▸ Tryll ▸ Dialog Script`; Unreal: Content Browser **Add ▸ Tryll ▸ Dialog Script**) — an ordered list of steps, each with a user line and (for seeded steps) an assistant line. At least one step after the seeded history must be a generated turn (user line only).

______________________________________________________________________

## Run against a workflow

1. Assign **Tryll Settings**, an **Agent (default)**, and a **Dialog Script**. The default agent is only needed by variants that don't set one of their own, so you can leave it empty if every variant brings its own agent.

1. Set **Repeats** (how many seeds per variant — default 4; a single sample per variant tells you almost nothing about reliability) and a **base seed** (the field clamps values below 1 up to 1 — `0` means *random seed* on the wire, which would defeat reproducibility).

1. Optionally add variants. Switch the toolbar to the **Variants** tab — its label carries the current count, e.g. `Variants (3)` — and add as many as you need. Each variant is one configuration to compare, and can differ in either of two ways:

   - **Parameter overrides** — system prompt, template, sampling, grammar, … picked from the workflow's own nodes. Leave the variant's **Agent** empty and it runs on the default agent. Values are validated (type, range, and whether the field still exists on the workflow); Run stays disabled until every override is valid. Stale rows stay visible so you can fix them rather than disappearing silently.
   - **A different model** — pick one in the variant's **Model** dropdown to run the *same* workflow on another language model. It lists the registered language models from your model manifest; `(workflow default)` means no override. This changes only what this run asks for — the workflow asset is never modified — and it applies to nodes that leave their own model empty, which is the usual setup. If a node pins its own model, the tab warns you that the override won't reach it.
   - **A different agent** — set the variant's **Agent** to another `TryllAgentComponent` to compare a different context size or a whole different workflow. These are *structural* and cannot be changed as parameters (the server rejects that with `3006`), which is why the override editor doesn't list them and why swapping the agent is the way to do it.

   Switch back to **Dialog** to see results.

Mixing the two

A variant with both an agent *and* overrides applies the overrides to that agent's workflow. If an override names a node the new agent doesn't have, the tab flags it before you run — it won't be applied, and it won't be silently discarded either.

1. Press **Run** — the button shows the planned cell count. A progress bar tracks turns as they complete; results are withheld until the whole run finishes — no partial rows appear mid-run, so you never draw a conclusion from a biased subset. **Reset** stops a run and clears results without publishing a half-finished grid.

Each variant gets its own fresh agent (clean, unmutated state); each repeat within a variant reuses that agent, changing only the seed and rewinding the dialog — the system prompt stays warm across repeats. The configuration used for a run is snapshotted when you press Run, so editing the script or variants while a run is in flight does not change that run's results or export.

Stateless agents

The Lab uses each variant's own **Maintain Dialogue History** setting, so an agent with it switched off is tested as the stateless agent it actually is: every step runs with no memory of the previous ones, and no rewind is needed between repeats. Such a variant is tagged `stateless` in the Grid and recorded that way in the export.

A stateless agent's dialog is cleared by the server after every turn, so seeded history cannot survive past the first generated turn. Run is blocked if a script with `SeedTurnCount > 0` is pointed at one — set it to `0`, or use a stateful agent.

## Add deterministic checks

A step can carry checks that are evaluated in the editor with no model involved — **Must Contain**, **Must Not Contain**, **Regex Forbid**, **Max Words**, and two intent checks:

- **Intent is** — at least one addressed classifier on that turn accepted the exact label you named. If a node ran twice and either execution found it, the check passes.
- **Intent not found** — every addressed classifier on that turn took `not_found`. If any one of them accepted a label, the check fails.

Leave the node name empty to address every classifier that ran. Name a node to address only that node's executions. Labels compare exactly and case-sensitively — they are identifiers, not prose.

A missing or mis-typed classifier **fails** (`intent unavailable`), it does not skip. A green suite that never ran a classifier is meaningless. Seeded steps refuse intent checks before Run: a seeded turn is injected without running the graph, so there is no classification to assert.

A cell whose checks all pass is green; any failure turns it amber and is listed in the inspector. Checks never stop a run, and they are not a score: the Lab makes no quality claim either way.

Above the step list, the script also has a **Global Regex Forbid** list. It works exactly like a step's **Regex Forbid** — the same patterns, the same pass/fail — except it applies to *every* turn in the script, seeded turns included. Use it for the constraints that hold for the whole dialog rather than repeating them on each step:

```
(?i)as an (?:ai|assistant)      # the refusal boilerplate
__[A-Z_]+__                     # an unsubstituted variable marker leaking through
```

Listing the same pattern globally and on a step is harmless — it is checked once, not twice. A malformed pattern fails the turn as `invalid regex` rather than passing silently, which is the same behaviour a step-level pattern has.

Word counting is language-specific

**Max Words** splits on whitespace, so it is not meaningful for scripts that do not use whitespace-delimited words.

## Read the results

- **Summary** (default) collapses each turn to one row with a coloured dot per sample — green (clean), amber (a check failed), red (error), open outline (not run, because an earlier turn in that column errored). Click a dot to expand and select that cell.
- **Grid** shows every sample side by side per turn, full transcript style. Switch to it when you want to read several answers at once rather than scan verdicts.
- Click any cell to open the shared **[turn inspector](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/turn-inspector.html)** — route, timing, the node parameters that turn actually ran with, the rendered prompt and output, retrieval hits, the intent decision, and tool calls. Everything is attributed to the node that produced it, and clicking a node in the Route breadcrumb narrows the whole panel to that node; see the reference page for the full block list. Drag the pane's left edge to resize it (the width is remembered), or use the **Inspector** toolbar button to collapse it.
- The Lab adds one block the other hosts do not have: **Checks**, listing each authored check for that step with its pass/fail.
- **⇧-click two cells** (or the ⊙ in a column header) to pin them; the inspector's prompt section becomes a two-sided line diff — `+` green for lines only in the selected cell, `−` red for lines only in the other. The red side is usually the interesting one: it shows what a variant *dropped*. Each node is compared against its own counterpart, so a change in the generate prompt shows up there and nowhere else. If a node ran in one variant and not the other, it is called out as present on one side only — often the whole explanation for why the two answers differ.

Turns without diagnostics

Seeded turns are injected without running the graph, and turns after an **Error** never execute — neither produces diagnostics, so the inspector says which case it is rather than showing an empty panel. A **CheckFail** (including an unexpected tool call) still completes the turn and keeps diagnostics.

## Tool calls

By default an unexpected tool call — a step with no `ToolResults` entry — is a **CheckFail** on that cell (later steps still run). That assertion holds even if the variant's scene agent has a live `RegisterTool` handler. Tick **Use live tools** on the variant only when the run should exercise that handler; canned results still pin a step. See [Test tool calls in Chat and the Dialog Lab](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-tool-calls-in-editor.html).

## Export and import

**Export…** writes the completed run as **JSONL format version 3**: one header line (script, variants with workflow/model provenance, seeds, server identity, timestamps, run issues) plus **one line per cell**, including seeded and skipped turns, with structured check failures, timings, and diagnostics.

**Import…** (next to Export) opens a v3 file as **read-only results** — Summary, Grid, and inspector work as usual so you can review a past run. It does **not** recreate agents, workflows, or runnable configuration; the authoring fields above stay independent for your next local run. Re-exporting an imported run writes the same completed result back out. Older incomplete export formats are rejected with a clear message.

Write your own scoring script against the JSONL if you need automated follow-up evaluation — the Lab deliberately does not judge results itself.

Reproducibility

Same seed only reproduces the same output at `temperature = 0`, and only against the **same server executable** — the export header records server identity for exactly this reason.

## From an existing chat

In `Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Chat` (Unity) or `Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Tryll Chat` (Unreal), press **Compare in Lab…** to open the Lab with the current agent and the conversation so far captured as the script's seeded steps, plus **one blank generated step** at the end. Fill in that continuation user line (what you want to test next), then Run. An empty continuation is blocked with a clear error rather than running zero work.

______________________________________________________________________

## Current scope

- Saving a Dialog Lab experiment as a durable asset (promote variants to a project asset and reload later) is not wired yet — variants live in the window for now.
- Intent-classification charts, variable replacements, and the engine/scheduler group have no dedicated inspector block yet — they remain visible in the raw-JSON escape hatch. See [Turn Inspector](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/turn-inspector.html#raw-json).
- No in-editor judge and no simulated player, by design — see the reasoning in `docs/research/clients/dialog-lab-requirements.md`.

# Test Tool Calls in Chat and the Dialog Lab

Exercise a [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html) workflow in the Unity or Unreal editor without entering Play / PIE: talk to it in Chat, then script it in the Dialog Lab — either with canned results, or with the same live handler the game will run.

This page is about **editor testing**. To declare tools and handle them in game code, start with [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html).

Prerequisites

- A workflow with a `ToolCall` node (`disposition = AwaitResult` if the model should see the result).
- A language model whose chat template supports tool calling. See [Tool Calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html).
- A scene `TryllAgentComponent` / `UTryllAgentComponent` with that workflow assigned.

______________________________________________________________________

## Register the handler on the scene component

Both Chat and the Lab reach tools through the **scene** agent component, not through a Play-mode instance. Register the handler on that component in edit mode, or the turn pauses with nobody to answer.

Put the handler on a sibling `MonoBehaviour` with `[ExecuteAlways]`, and register in `OnEnable` — the same pattern as the demo `GetPriceTool`:

```
[ExecuteAlways]
[RequireComponent(typeof(TryllAgentComponent))]
public sealed class GetPriceTool : MonoBehaviour
{
    private void OnEnable()
    {
        GetComponent<TryllAgentComponent>()
            .RegisterTool("get_price", HandleGetPrice);
    }

    private string HandleGetPrice(TryllToolCall call)
    {
        // Parse call.ArgumentsJson, return a string the model will see.
        return "450";
    }
}
```

Register in `OnRegister` (not `BeginPlay`) so Chat and the Lab see the handler outside PIE — the same pattern as `UTryllGetPriceTool`:

```
void UMyPriceTool::OnRegister()
{
    Super::OnRegister();
    Agent = GetOwner()->FindComponentByClass<UTryllAgentComponent>();
    if (Agent != nullptr)
    {
        Agent->RegisterTool(TEXT("get_price"),
            FTryllSimpleToolHandler(
                [this](const FTryllToolCall& Call) { return LookUp(Call); }));
    }
}
```

Chat's agent is not Play's agent. Unity Chat calls `CreateAgent` on the scene component, so handlers already registered there are applied automatically. Unreal Chat builds a separate preview agent and copies the component's registered handlers onto it when the preview attaches; later `RegisterTool` / `UnregisterTool` calls are forwarded to that preview as well.

______________________________________________________________________

## Chat — one conversation, inspect the call

1. Register the handler as above.
1. Open **Window → Tryll → Chat** (Unity) or **Window → Tryll → Tryll Chat** (Unreal). Assign the scene agent and press **Start**.
1. Send a line that should trigger the tool.
1. Select the assistant answer and open the [turn inspector](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/turn-inspector.html). The **Tool calls** block shows the name, arguments, and result the handler returned.

If the turn stays paused, or ends as `PauseTimedOut` (a `ToolCall` with `pause_timeout_ms` `0` inherits the server's `workflow.tool_call_pause_timeout_ms`, 2000 ms in the shipped `server-config.json`), nothing registered that tool on the component Chat is using. Check that the handler's `OnEnable` / `OnRegister` ran (the GameObject / actor is enabled) and that the tool name matches the workflow exactly.

______________________________________________________________________

## Dialog Lab — canned results (default)

The Lab creates its **own** agent per variant. By default it does **not** call your scene handler.

Author a `ToolResults` entry on each script step that should call a tool (tool name + result string). Leave a step **without** an entry to assert that the model must not call that tool there. An unexpected call, a missing expected call, or a different tool than the one listed is a **CheckFail** on that cell — the same amber verdict as `MustContain` — and later steps still run. That assertion holds even if `GetPriceTool` is registered on the same merchant.

That is the default. No extra toggle.

See [Compare dialog variants](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-dialog-variants.html) for scripts, repeats, and checks.

______________________________________________________________________

## Dialog Lab — live tools (opt-in)

Tick **Use live tools** on the variant when the point of the run is to exercise the real handler (a stateful price ladder, a quest flag, …).

- Canned results still win. Pin a step with `ToolResults` when you want a fixed value.
- An uncanned call is answered by the scene agent's `RegisterTool` handler, if it has one for that name.
- If the variant is opted in but the scene agent has no handler, the cell still fails — same message as the default.

Without the toggle, a live `GetPriceTool` on the merchant will **not** answer Lab calls. That is deliberate: existing scripts that left a step uncanned to prove the model stayed quiet keep that meaning.

The Lab snapshots the flag with the run (JSONL `use_live_tools`). The scene object itself is not part of that snapshot.

______________________________________________________________________

## Reset stateful handlers between Lab repeats

One Lab agent serves every repeat of a variant, and that agent is not the scene component's, so `OnAgentCreated` / `OnAgentReady` never fire for the Lab. A handler that keeps per-conversation state (call counts, ladders) must reset at the start of each repeat.

When **Use live tools** is on, the Lab dispatches a parameterless `ResetToolState` once per repeat, before any turn of it:

- **Unity:** `gameObject.SendMessage("ResetToolState")` on the scene agent's GameObject. Implement a public `void ResetToolState()` on a sibling `MonoBehaviour`.
- **Unreal:** any parameterless `UFUNCTION()` named `ResetToolState` on a component of the owning actor.

The name is the contract. Renaming it silently stops Lab repeats from resetting. A stateless handler declares nothing.

In game and in Chat the handler should also subscribe to the component's own create / interactions-removed events — those *do* fire there.

# Agentic Coding With Tryll

AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot can build Tryll agents for you: author the workflow, wire it into your game, and test it. This page covers how to set them up for Tryll and how to brief them so they deliver a working result.

## Start every session with `AGENTS.md`

Both plugins ship an **`AGENTS.md`** file at their root — in the TryllClient plugin folder for Unreal, and at the package root for Unity. It gives a coding agent the essentials in one read:

- how Tryll works — an agent is a graph of nodes, not a single prompt;
- where Tryll differs from cloud LLM SDKs, which is where coding agents most often go wrong;
- links to the pages in these docs that cover each topic in depth.

Instruct the agent to read `AGENTS.md` before it writes any code or assets.

## Unreal

### Why use MCP

Much of an Unreal project lives in binary assets — levels, Blueprints and Tryll workflow assets — that a coding agent cannot edit as text. Epic's **Model Context Protocol** (MCP) plugin, available as an experimental plugin in UE 5.8, lets the agent work directly in the running editor instead.

For Tryll workflows, install the **Tryll MCP** plugin alongside it. It gives the agent dedicated tools for creating and editing workflow assets. Epic's general-purpose editing tools are not designed for Tryll's workflow format and should not be used to write workflows.

### Requirements

- Unreal Engine 5.8. Tryll MCP depends on Epic's experimental **Toolset Registry** plugin, which is not available in 5.7. The TryllClient plugin itself supports both 5.7 and 5.8.
- The TryllClient plugin, set up as described in [First inference (Unreal)](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/getting-started/first-inference-unreal.html).

### Set up

1. Copy the `TryllMCP` folder from the Tryll release into your project's `Plugins/` folder, next to `TryllClient`.

1. In **Edit > Plugins**, enable **Tryll MCP**, **Model Context Protocol** and **All Toolsets**, then restart the editor. **All Toolsets** provides Epic's tools for levels, assets and Blueprints.

1. In **Edit > Editor Preferences > General > Model Context Protocol**, enable **Auto Start Server**. The server then starts with the editor, at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp` by default.

1. Connect your coding agent to that address. For Claude Code, add a `.mcp.json` file at the project root:

   ```
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "unreal-mcp": {
         "type": "http",
         "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"
       }
     }
   }
   ```

1. Open the editor first, then start the agent session. An agent session started before the MCP server is running will not see the Unreal tools; if that happens, restart the session.

Only one editor can use port 8000 at a time. If the server fails to start, the Output Log shows `HttpListener unable to bind to 127.0.0.1:8000`. Close any other open editor, then restart this one.

### Authoring workflows

Tryll MCP provides four tools, grouped under `TryllMCP.TryllWorkflowToolset`:

| Tool                | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DescribeNodeTypes` | Lists the available node types and their parameters, including value ranges, allowed values, and which parameters are exits. Pass a single type, such as `Generate`, to describe only that one. |
| `ValidateWorkflow`  | Checks a workflow without changing the project, and reports every problem in one response.                                                                                                      |
| `WriteWorkflow`     | Creates or replaces a workflow asset and saves it. A workflow with errors is rejected and the existing asset is left unchanged.                                                                 |
| `ReadWorkflow`      | Returns an existing workflow in the same format `WriteWorkflow` accepts.                                                                                                                        |

A workflow is always written as a whole. To change part of one, the agent reads it, edits it, and writes it back. The format looks like this:

```
{
  "startNode": "guard",
  "variables": [
    { "name": "price", "type": "Int", "allowOutputSubstitution": true, "value": 120 }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "name": "guard", "type": "RegexGuardrail",
      "params": { "notTriggeredExit": "haggle" } },
    { "name": "haggle", "type": "Generate",
      "params": { "systemPrompt": "You are a merchant. The fuel cell costs __PRICE__ credits.",
                  "bSubstituteAgentVariables": true } }
  ]
}
```

- Parameter names match those listed by `DescribeNodeTypes`. An unknown parameter name is reported as an error, together with the valid names.
- Parameters you set are applied as given. Parameters you omit keep their default, or are inherited from the model catalog.
- Exits are parameters, such as `defaultExit` or `triggeredExit`, that hold the name of the next node. An empty exit ends the turn.

Recommended sequence for the agent: call `DescribeNodeTypes` for the node types it plans to use, run `ValidateWorkflow` until no errors remain, save with `WriteWorkflow`, then confirm the result with `ReadWorkflow`.

## Unity

No MCP setup is required for Tryll in Unity. Workflows are written in C# with `TryllGraphBuilder`, or stored as `TryllWorkflowAsset` files, both of which coding agents can edit directly. Provide `AGENTS.md` and follow the practices below. Unity's own MCP integration remains useful for scene work, but Tryll does not depend on it.

## Best practices for briefing the agent

These apply in both engines.

- **Scope each task to one agent and one workflow.** Broad requests — several NPCs, a UI and a scene at once — dilute the agent's effort, and most of it goes into the parts that are not Tryll. Build up in steps.
- **Write the acceptance tests into the prompt**, as exact player lines and the expected response. For example: *"Ask the price of a fuel cell: the merchant quotes 120. Offer 90: the merchant counters and does not accept 90."* Concrete tests lead the agent to play the game and check the result, which catches problems that reading the code does not, such as the model repeating an example line from its prompt verbatim.
- **Point the agent at the relevant documentation.** Name the pages for the feature you are building, for example [Keep Merchant Prices Deterministic](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/keep-merchant-prices-deterministic.html) or [Substitute Agent Variables in Output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/substitute-agent-variables-in-output.html), and ask it to consult [Workflow Nodes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/index.html) before setting node parameters.
- **Download the models in advance** with the [Model Manager](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html), so the agent spends its time on the feature itself.
- **Unreal: require the agent to save its work.** Levels and assets exist only in the open editor until they are saved. Ask the agent to save them and confirm the files exist on disk.
- **Unreal: keep asset paths consistent.** Paths are case-sensitive — `/Game/TradingPost` and `/Game/tradingpost` are different locations.

## Related

- [Edit Workflows in the Unreal Graph Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/edit-workflows-in-unreal-graph-editor.html) — review or adjust an agent-authored workflow by hand.
- [Test an Agent in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/test-agent-in-editor.html) — talk to a workflow without entering Play.

# Build a Chat Agent with a Graph

Create an agent whose graph is a simple `RegexGuardrail → Generate` chain, send a message, and get a streamed reply.

Prerequisites

- A connected session with `CreateSession` already called — see [Connect and Manage a Session](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/connect-and-manage-session.html).
- A model listed in `models.json` that is either already `Loaded` or at least `Local`. If not, see [Use Your Own Local Model](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-your-own-local-model.html).

## Steps

1. In the Project window: right-click → **Create → Tryll → Workflow Asset**. Name it `ChatWorkflow`.
1. In the Inspector, expand **Graph** and add two nodes:
   - `guard` — **Params** type `RegexGuardrail`. Leave **Triggered Exit** empty (END) to drop jailbreaks silently, and set **Not Triggered Exit** = `answer`.
   - `answer` — **Params** type `Generate`. **Default Exit** stays empty (END).

Set **Start Node** = `guard` and **Default Model Name** = your model. 3. Attach a `TryllAgentComponent` to a GameObject and assign `ChatWorkflow` to its **Workflow Asset** field. 4. Wire events and send:

```
var agentComp = GetComponent<TryllAgentComponent>();

agentComp.OnAnswerText.AddListener(
    (nodeName, text, isDelta, isFinal) => chatText.text += text);
agentComp.OnTurnComplete.AddListener(
    (status, _, _) => typingIndicator.SetActive(false));

// When the agent is created, send the first message.
agentComp.OnAgentCreated.AddListener(() => agentComp.SendMessage("Hello!"));
```

1. In the Content Browser, right-click → **Tryll → Workflow Asset**. Name it `ChatWorkflow` and open it. On the **guard** node, set **Triggered Exit** to `""` (END) and **Not Triggered Exit** to `"answer"`. The **answer** node's **Default Exit** can be left empty (END).
1. Add a `UTryllAgentComponent` to your actor and assign `ChatWorkflow` to its **Workflow Asset** slot.
1. In Blueprint:
   - Bind **On Agent Ready** to a handler that calls **Send Message**.
   - Bind **On Answer Text** to append each chunk to a UI text block.
   - Bind **On Turn Complete** to flip the "typing" indicator off.

```
#include <tryll/TryllClient.h>

namespace TC = Tryll::Client;
namespace NP = Tryll::NodeParams;

NP::RegexGuardrailParamsT guardParams;
// guardParams.triggered_exit defaults to "" (END) — drop jailbreaks silently.
guardParams.not_triggered_exit = "answer";

TC::GraphDescription graph;
graph.AddRegexGuardrail("guard", guardParams)
     .AddGenerate("answer", NP::GenerateParamsT{})
     .SetStartNode("guard")
     .SetDefaultModelName("My Local Model");

auto agent = client.CreateAgent(graph);

// Register persistent callbacks, then send — fire-and-forget.
agent.SetOnAnswerText(
    [](std::string_view /*nodeName*/, std::string_view text, bool, bool)
    { std::cout << text << std::flush; });
agent.SetOnTurnComplete([](::Tryll::TurnStatus, std::string_view, std::int32_t)
    { std::cout << "\n"; });
agent.SendText("Hello!");
```

```
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription, RegexGuardrailParams, GenerateParams

# 1. Build the graph.
guard_params = RegexGuardrailParams(
    # triggered_exit defaults to "" (END) — drop jailbreaks silently.
    not_triggered_exit = "answer",
)

graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("guard",  guard_params)
    .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
    .set_start_node("guard")
    .set_default_model_name("My Local Model")
)

# 2. Create the agent.
agent = client.create_agent(graph)

# 3. Send a message. send_message blocks and returns the full reply.
reply = agent.send_message("Hello!")
print(reply)
```

## Verify it worked

Server-side, with `log_level` set to `"trace"` in [`server-config.json`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/server-configuration.html), each node logs a start and an end line that names the exit it took. One turn through this graph includes:

```
[trace] [WORKFLOW] start  entry=ExecuteOnMessage
[trace] [NODE]     start  node=guard
[trace] [NODE]     end    node=guard  exit=not_triggered  duration_ms=0.2
[trace] [NODE]     start  node=answer
[trace] [NODE]     end    node=answer  exit=default  duration_ms=812.4
[trace] [WORKFLOW] end    status=success  total_ms=813.0
```

Client-side, Python returns the full reply string from `send_message`, while Unity, C++, and Unreal see each streamed chunk arrive in the `OnAnswerText` event / `SetOnAnswerText` callback / `OnAnswerText` delegate, followed by a `TurnComplete` with status `Success`.

## Common pitfalls

- **Unknown or unacquired model.** A graph whose model name is wrong, missing from `models.json`, or not yet on disk fails `CreateAgent` with error [3003 `GraphCompilationFailed`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent). Calling `LoadModel` with a name that is not in the catalog fails with [6005 `ModelResolutionFailed`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#6xxx-model-download). Double-check the name with `client.list_models()`.
- **"Graph validation failed"** (error [3003](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent)) — check for a bad start node name or duplicate node names in the graph. The same code covers an exit field that names a node not in the graph — fix the string, or leave it empty to route to END.
- **Silent nothing after sending.** Check that the start node is not an always-`END` branch (e.g., guardrail that matches everything). The server log will show which route was taken.
