# Clone a Voice from an Audio Sample

Give an NPC a custom voice from a short recording. Voice-cloning TTS models condition synthesis on a *reference clip*: a recording of the target voice. There is no training or preprocessing step. You put a WAV file in your project's storage folder and point the agent's [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html) at it with **Reference Voice**.

| Model                               | Languages                                             | Clip length               | Status |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------ |
| `Pocket TTS (int8)`                 | English                                               | 10–20 s (first 30 s used) | Public |
| `Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M)` | zh, en, de, it, pt, es, ja, ko, fr, ru (via **Lang**) | 3–10 s                    | Public |

The same mechanism also powers plain **voice selection**: ship several reference clips and give each NPC a voice profile that names one. One loaded cloning model serves many distinct voices concurrently.

Prerequisites

- Voice output already working — see [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html).
- A TTS model with voice cloning in the catalog (see the table above).
- A process storage root (the server's storage folder) — see [Ship Storage Folders for Builds](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/ship-storage-folders-for-builds.html).

## One voice per character

Cloning is how a character keeps **the same voice in every sentence and every turn**. The clip fixes the speaker; the model only adds the words. That makes cloning the right tool for named characters, and a better fit than models that invent a voice from a text description. Those models (for example Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign) sample a new voice on each synthesis call, and Tryll synthesizes a reply sentence by sentence, so the voice would change mid-reply. Use them to *create* clips, not to speak at runtime.

**The clip's mood carries over.** Cloning copies the register and energy of the clip along with the timbre: an angry clip gives an angry-sounding voice. Record the base clip in the character's usual mood. To switch moods at runtime, give the profile one clip per mood — see [Add Emotions to a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-emotions-to-a-voice.html).

## Where clips come from

- **Record an actor.** This gives the best quality and one true identity across every mood. Follow [What to record](#what-to-record) below.
- **Design a voice with a text prompt, outside Tryll.** Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign turns a description such as "Man in his thirties, Eastern European accent, irritated" into speech. Render a few takes, keep the one you like, and save it as the character's clip. See [Design a Voice Clip with Qwen3-TTS](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-voice-with-qwen3-tts.html).
- **Use stock or synthetic voice libraries,** as long as the licence covers use in your product.

## 1. Record (or choose) a reference clip

- **Pocket TTS: 10–20 seconds** of the target voice is the sweet spot. **Qwen3-TTS Base** reduces the clip to a single speaker fingerprint, so **3–10 seconds** is enough. A longer clip does not help it.
- For Pocket TTS, only the **first 30 seconds** of the file condition the voice — anything after that is ignored, so **put the best, continuous speech at the very start** and cut leading silence, breaths, or intros. A clip whose opening seconds carry little speech produces weak conditioning, audible as the voice drifting between sentences.
- **One speaker, clean audio.** The clip's recording quality is reproduced in the synthesized speech — background noise, reverb, and compression artifacts all carry over. Record in a quiet room.
- **Mono 16-bit PCM WAV**, ideally at 24 kHz (other sample rates are resampled automatically).

### What to record

There is **no required script**: the voice encoder only looks at the audio — no transcript is involved — so any text works. What you say matters far less than *how* you say it:

- **Record in character — style transfers.** The clip's tone, pace, energy, and emotion carry over into everything the NPC says. A weary old wizard should be read slowly and gravelly; an energetic merchant bright and fast. A flat, monotone read produces a flat, monotone NPC.
- **Speak naturally and continuously**, with a bit of pitch movement — mix a statement, a question, some emphasis. Short natural pauses are fine; long gaps, throat-clearing, and "umm, okay, so…" intros waste the 30-second window.
- **Vary the wording.** A few different sentences beat repeating one phrase. If you want a standard script, phonetically balanced passages like the *Rainbow Passage* or a handful of Harvard sentences fill 20–30 s nicely — but ordinary conversational text with varied vocabulary is nearly as good.
- **Record in the language you'll synthesize** (English for Pocket TTS). A speaker's accent carries over, which can be exactly what you want for a character. Qwen3-TTS Base speaks any of its 10 languages from one clip; set **Lang** on the voice profile.

Iteration is free and fast, so treat it as a loop: record ~40 s in character → trim so strong speech starts at 0:00 → generate a line → listen → re-record if the delivery isn't right.

Convert with whichever tool you already use:

1. Open the recording (any format).
1. **Tracks → Mix → Mix Stereo Down to Mono** (if stereo).
1. Cut everything before the speech starts; keep the best ≤ 30 s.
1. **File → Export Audio…** → format **WAV**, encoding **Signed 16-bit PCM**.

```
ffmpeg -i recording.mp3 -ac 1 -ar 24000 -sample_fmt s16 ^
    -af "silenceremove=start_periods=1:start_threshold=-40dB" -t 30 voice.wav
```

(`-af silenceremove…` strips leading silence; `-t 30` keeps the first 30 seconds.)

The server log prints each clip's duration when it loads and warns when only part of it is used — check it if cloning sounds off.

Consent and rights

A reference clip captures a real person's voice. Make sure you have the speaker's consent and the rights to use the recording in your product. Tryll does not verify or restrict clips — this is your content responsibility, exactly like any other licensed asset.

Model attribution

The Pocket TTS weights are [Kyutai's](https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-01-13-pocket-tts/), licensed **CC-BY-4.0**: shipping them inside your game requires crediting Kyutai (e.g. in your credits screen or license notices).

## 2. Put the clip in the storage folder

**Reference Voice** is a path **relative to the process storage root**, set when the server starts — the same root used by string storages and knowledge bases:

```
<storage root>/
  └─ voices/
      └─ wizard_eldrin.wav
```

The clip lives with the game on the machine running the Tryll server. It never crosses the network — the client only sends the path.

## 3. Point the agent at the clip

### Unity

1. Set the storage root once, if you haven't already: **Edit → Project Settings → Tryll Client → Storage Data Folder**. Create a `voices/` subfolder there and drop your WAV in.
1. Create a voice profile: right-click in the Project window → **Create → Tryll → Voice Profile**.
1. Set **Tts Model Name** to `Pocket TTS (int8)` from the model dropdown. If it isn't listed, register it first in the [Model Manager](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html) window.
1. In **Reference Voice**, click the **…** browse button and pick the WAV. In the file dialog, switch the extension filter to **All files** to see `.wav` files. The field stores the storage-relative path (e.g. `voices/wizard_eldrin.wav`) — you can also type it directly.
1. Assign the profile to the **Voice** field of the character's `TryllAgentComponent`.
1. Enter Play mode and send a message — the agent speaks in the cloned voice through its `TryllSpeaker`.

### Unreal

1. Set the storage root once in **Project Settings → Plugins → Tryll Client → Storage → Storage Data Folder**, create `voices/` there and drop your WAV in.
1. Create a **Tryll Voice Profile** data asset and pick `Pocket TTS (int8)` from the model dropdown (register it in the [Model Manager](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html) panel if missing).
1. In **Reference Voice**, click the **...** button and select the WAV — switch the file dialog's filter to **All files (\*.\*)** to see `.wav` files. The stored value is the storage-relative path.
1. Assign the profile to the **Voice Profile** property of the character's **Tryll Agent** component.
1. Make sure the actor has a **Tryll Speaker** component, then PIE and send a message.

### Python

```
from tryll_client import VoiceProfile

wizard = VoiceProfile(
    tts_model_name="Pocket TTS (int8)",
    reference_voice="voices/wizard_eldrin.wav",  # relative to storage root
)
agent = client.create_agent(graph, voice=wizard)
```

Leave Speaker Id at 0

Cloning models are single-speaker: the voice comes entirely from the reference clip. Setting **Speaker Id** to anything other than `0` fails agent creation with an out-of-range error (`3023`).

Qwen3-TTS Base needs a clip

Pocket TTS falls back to a bundled default voice when **Reference Voice** is empty. Qwen3-TTS Base has no default voice. Without a clip, synthesis fails with an error telling you to set the voice profile's `reference_voice`.

### Switching moods at runtime

A profile can hold one clip per mood as named **delivery modes**, and game code switches between them with `SetAgentDeliveryMode("angry")`, from the next sentence. The full recipe, from making the clips to switching at runtime, is in [Add Emotions to a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-emotions-to-a-voice.html).

To give the character a **different voice** rather than a different mood, for example another actor, replace the whole profile with `SetAgentVoice` while the agent is idle.

Leaving **Reference Voice** empty uses the model's default voice (Pocket TTS only).

### A different clip per language

Put a per-language clip in a `loc/<locale>/` folder next to the one you linked, for example `voices/loc/de/mack.wav` beside `voices/mack.wav`. With the session locale set to `de`, the voice uses it automatically; without one, it falls back to the linked clip. See [Ship in Another Language](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/ship-in-another-language.html).

## 4. Verify

Send a message and listen: the agent speaks new text in the reference clip's voice, consistently across sentences and turns. Two agents with different **Reference Voice** clips speak in different voices at the same time on the same loaded model.

If the voice drifts between sentences, the reference clip is conditioning too weakly — almost always because its first seconds are silence or sparse speech. Re-trim so continuous speech starts at 0:00 (the server log's per-clip warning tells you when only part of a long clip is used).

## Limitations

- **Pocket TTS is English only.** The sherpa-onnx Pocket TTS conversion covers Kyutai's English model. Qwen3-TTS Base clones in 10 languages. Supertonic 3 covers 31 languages with fixed voices — see [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html).
- **Mood comes from the clip, not from a parameter.** Cloning models do not take a **Voice Description** or a delivery-mode **Instruction**; setting either fails with `3023`. Use one delivery mode per mood, each with its own clip (see [Add Emotions to a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-emotions-to-a-voice.html)). Maya1 is the voice that takes delivery as text.
- A bad or missing clip path, in the profile or in any delivery mode, fails agent creation (or `SetAgentVoice`) with `3023`, and the message names the field.
- Cloning quality tracks clip quality. If the voice sounds muffled or noisy, re-record the reference clip.

# Design a Voice Clip with Qwen3-TTS

Make a reference clip for a character without recording an actor. Qwen3-TTS **VoiceDesign** creates a voice from a text description, such as "a gruff man in his fifties with a low, gravelly voice". You render a short line in that voice, save it as a WAV, and the agent's voice profile [clones](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html) it at runtime.

VoiceDesign runs **outside Tryll**, while you author content. Tryll does not use it to speak at runtime: a description-based model samples a new voice on every call, and Tryll synthesizes a reply sentence by sentence, so the voice would change in the middle of a reply. A clip fixes the voice once, and the cloning model then keeps it the same in every sentence.

Prerequisites

- A cloning TTS model for runtime: `Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M)` or `Pocket TTS (int8)`. See [Clone a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html).
- A web browser for the hosted demo, or Python if you run VoiceDesign on your own machine.

## 1. Open VoiceDesign

- **Hosted demo.** Open the [Qwen3-TTS demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS) on Hugging Face and stay on the **Voice Design** tab. It has three inputs: **Text to Synthesize** (the words of the clip), **Language**, and **Voice Description** (who is speaking and how).
- **On your own machine.** Install Qwen's `qwen-tts` Python package and run `qwen-tts-demo Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign`. It opens the same interface locally. See the [Qwen3-TTS repository](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-TTS) for setup.

The other two tabs are not needed here. **Voice Clone (Base)** is the same cloning that Tryll runs. **TTS (CustomVoice)** speaks with Qwen's preset speakers.

## 2. Write the voice description

The description decides the voice. Vague words give a generic voice, and a different one each time. These rules come from Alibaba Cloud's [Voice Design guide](https://help.aliyun.com/en/model-studio/voice-design-user-guide):

- **Be specific.** Use words for qualities you can hear, such as *deep*, *husky*, *crisp*, *nasal*, *fast-paced*. Avoid *nice*, *normal*, *good*.

- **Combine several dimensions.** "Female voice" alone says almost nothing. Cover most of these:

  | Dimension            | Examples                                                                               |
  | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Gender               | male, female                                                                           |
  | Age                  | child, teenager, young adult, middle-aged, elderly, or an age such as "in her sixties" |
  | Pitch                | high, medium, low; "slightly low"                                                      |
  | Speed                | fast, medium, slow                                                                     |
  | Timbre               | resonant, husky, gravelly, breathy, crisp, mellow                                      |
  | Accent               | Scottish accent, light Eastern European accent                                         |
  | Emotion and delivery | calm, cheerful, irritated, fearful, whispering                                         |
  | Role                 | tavern keeper, army sergeant, news anchor, storyteller                                 |

- **Describe the sound, not your taste.** "Warm, slow, slightly breathy" works. "A voice players will love" does not.

- **Do not ask for a real person.** Describe the qualities instead of naming an actor or a celebrity.

- **Keep it short.** One or two sentences. Drop repeated synonyms and filler.

- **Write it in English or Chinese.** The text to synthesize can be in any of the model's languages.

Some examples:

| Too vague                     | Better                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "Old man."                    | "A man in his seventies with a low, gravelly voice, speaking slowly and kindly, like a village storyteller."                 |
| "Female warrior, cool voice." | "A woman in her thirties with a firm, slightly low voice and a light Scottish accent, speaking briskly with calm authority." |
| "A merchant."                 | "A cheerful middle-aged man with a bright, slightly nasal voice, speaking fast and eagerly, like a market trader."           |

For a character who will need **several moods**, write the description in two parts: the **identity** (gender, age, pitch, timbre, accent) and the **delivery** (the emotion). Keep the identity part word for word, and change only the delivery for each mood. See [Add Emotions to a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-emotions-to-a-voice.html).

## 3. Write the text to synthesize

- **The model speaks the text word for word.** Put stage directions in the description, never in the text.
- **Write a line the character would say, in the mood you want.** The words help the delivery: an angry clip is easier to get from an angry line.
- **Use the language the character speaks in the game.** Set **Language** to match, or leave it on **Auto**. Pocket TTS speaks English only.
- **Match the clip length to the runtime model.** Qwen3-TTS Base needs **3–10 seconds**. Pocket TTS works best with **10–20 seconds**, so write two or three sentences. Render the whole clip in one go: takes joined from separate renders can sound like different people.

## 4. Render several takes, keep the best

The same description gives a slightly different voice on every render. Render a few takes, and keep the one that fits the character best. Listen for:

- a voice that stays the same from the first word to the last;
- clean audio with no clicks, warbling or cut-off words;
- speech that starts right away, without a long silence.

If no take fits, change the description, not just the seed. Add the dimension that is off: the age, the pitch, or the speed.

## 5. Save the clip and use it

1. Download the take with the download button on the **Generated Audio** player.
1. Convert it to **mono 16-bit PCM WAV** (24 kHz is ideal) and trim any silence at the start. The Audacity and ffmpeg steps are in [Clone a Voice → Record a reference clip](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html#1-record-or-choose-a-reference-clip).
1. Put it in the storage folder, for example `<storage root>/voices/innkeeper/neutral.wav`.
1. Point the voice profile's **Reference Voice** at it, as in [Clone a Voice → Point the agent at the clip](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html#3-point-the-agent-at-the-clip).

Licence and rights

Check the licence of the Qwen3-TTS model and the terms of the service you render with before you ship a generated clip in a product. Do not describe a real person's voice.

## Related

- [Clone a Voice from an Audio Sample](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html) — how the clip is used at runtime
- [Add Emotions to a Voice](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-emotions-to-a-voice.html) — one clip per mood, switched with delivery modes
- [Reference: TTS Models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/tts-models.html) — Qwen3-TTS Base and Pocket TTS
- [Alibaba Cloud: Voice Design guide](https://help.aliyun.com/en/model-studio/voice-design-user-guide) — how to write a voice description
- [Qwen3-TTS on GitHub](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-TTS) — the models, local setup, and example descriptions

# Add Emotions to a Voice with Delivery Modes

Make a character sound angry, afraid or joyful, and switch between moods while the game runs. A voice profile holds one voice and a list of **delivery modes**: named ways of speaking, such as `angry` or `whisper`. Game code switches the mode with `SetAgentDeliveryMode`, and the next sentence is spoken in the new mood.

With a **cloning** model (Qwen3-TTS Base or Pocket TTS), each mood is a **reference clip of the same character speaking in that mood**. This page shows how to make those clips, put them in a profile, and switch between them.

Prerequisites

- Voice output working — see [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html).
- A cloning model, `Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M)` or `Pocket TTS (int8)`, and a neutral reference clip for the character — see [Clone a Voice from an Audio Sample](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html).

## Why one clip per mood

Cloning copies the **register and energy** of the reference clip along with the voice. In our measurements, neutral text cloned from a shouted, angry clip came out raised and loud on both models. Cloned from a sad clip, it came out low and flat. Cloning models have no emotion parameter: setting a delivery mode's **Instruction** on them fails with `3023`. So the clip *is* the mood:

1. One clip per character per mood, for example `voices/guard/neutral.wav`, `voices/guard/angry.wav`, `voices/guard/afraid.wav`.
1. The neutral clip in the profile's **Reference Voice**. That is the built-in `neutral` mode.
1. One delivery mode per mood in the same profile, each with its own **Reference Voice**.
1. `SetAgentDeliveryMode("angry")` at runtime. It needs no agent rebuild.

**Every mood must sound like the same person.** A clip from another speaker changes who is talking, not just how.

## 1. Plan the moods

- **Pick the few moods your game uses.** Each one is a clip to make and to check. Three to five per character is plenty for most NPCs.
- **Use the same mode names on every character.** Then one call, such as `SetAgentDeliveryMode("angry")`, works on everyone. A mode with no fields set sounds like `neutral`, so a character without an angry clip can still define an empty `angry` mode.
- **Keep names short and lowercase**, such as `angry`, `afraid`, `joyful`. Game code and the editor's dropdown use them as written.

## 2. Make one clip per mood

There are two ways to get a set of clips that sound like one person.

### Record one actor

This gives the best result. Record every mood with the same actor, in the same session, with the same microphone and room. Follow the clip rules in [Clone a Voice → Record a reference clip](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/clone-a-voice.html#1-record-or-choose-a-reference-clip). Ask for each mood in character, and keep the same distance to the microphone, even when the actor shouts or whispers.

### Design the moods with Qwen3-TTS

Without an actor, render each mood with Qwen3-TTS **VoiceDesign**. The steps for one clip are in [Design a Voice Clip with Qwen3-TTS](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-voice-with-qwen3-tts.html). For a set of moods:

1. **Split the description into identity and delivery.** The identity (gender, age, pitch, timbre, accent) stays **word for word** in every mood. Only the delivery changes.
1. **Write a line in each mood.** An angry line for the angry clip, a frightened line for the afraid one.
1. **Render several takes per mood** and keep the ones that sound most like the neutral clip. Listen to them side by side. Drop a take that sounds like someone else, even if its mood is right.

For example, a palace guard:

| Mood      | Voice description                                                                                                                                                      |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `neutral` | A man in his forties with a deep, slightly hoarse voice and a light Northern English accent. **He speaks calmly, at an even pace.**                                    |
| `angry`   | A man in his forties with a deep, slightly hoarse voice and a light Northern English accent. **He is furious and shouts, fast and sharp.**                             |
| `afraid`  | A man in his forties with a deep, slightly hoarse voice and a light Northern English accent. **He is frightened; his voice shakes and he speaks quickly and quietly.** |

Each render is a new sample, so designed moods can drift slightly away from each other. Picking takes by ear keeps the drift small.

Put the clips together in one folder per character:

```
<storage root>/
  └─ voices/
      └─ guard/
          ├─ neutral.wav
          ├─ angry.wav
          └─ afraid.wav
```

## 3. Add the modes to the voice profile

1. Select the character's **Voice Profile** asset (**Create → Tryll → Voice Profile** if it has none).

1. Set **Tts Model Name** to the cloning model and **Reference Voice** to the neutral clip.

1. Under **Delivery Modes**, add one element per mood. Set its **Name** (`angry`) and its **Reference Voice** (`voices/guard/angry.wav`, with the **…** button or typed). Leave **Instruction** empty.

1. Open the character's **Tryll Voice Profile** data asset.

1. Set the TTS model to the cloning model and **Reference Voice** to the neutral clip.

1. Under **Delivery Modes**, add one element per mood with its **Name** and **Reference Voice**. Leave **Instruction** empty.

```
from tryll_client import DeliveryMode, VoiceProfile

guard = VoiceProfile(
    tts_model_name="Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M)",
    reference_voice="voices/guard/neutral.wav",
    delivery_modes=[
        DeliveryMode(name="angry",  reference_voice="voices/guard/angry.wav"),
        DeliveryMode(name="afraid", reference_voice="voices/guard/afraid.wav"),
    ])
agent = client.create_agent(graph, voice=guard)
```

A mode can also set **Speed Scale**, for example `1.15` to make `afraid` a little faster.

By default, the server prepares every clip in the profile when the agent is created, so the first sentence in a new mood has no extra delay. Set **Prepare** to `Lazy` to prepare each clip on its first use instead. A bad or missing clip path, in the profile or in any mode, fails agent creation with `3023`, and the message names the field.

## 4. Switch the mood at runtime

```
await agentComp.SetDeliveryModeAsync("angry");    // the guard loses his temper
await agentComp.SetDeliveryModeAsync("neutral");  // and calms down again
```

Call **Set Delivery Mode** on the **Tryll Agent** component with the mode name. It reports completion through its delegate.

```
agent.set_delivery_mode("angry")
agent.set_delivery_mode("neutral")
```

```
agent.SetDeliveryMode("angry", 1.0f);
```

- **It applies from the next sentence.** The call is accepted at any time, even mid-turn. A sentence already sent to the TTS model keeps its mood.
- **`neutral` is built in.** It always exists and means the profile's own **Reference Voice**.
- **Intensity does not blend clips.** A clip is all or nothing. On Pocket TTS, `intensity` only scales the mode's **Speed Scale**; on Qwen3-TTS Base it does nothing.
- **An unknown name** fails with `3024 UnknownDeliveryMode`, and the current mode stays.

To try a mood without code, use the agent component's **Voice Delivery** override in the Inspector (Unity) or Details panel (Unreal). Its dropdown lists `neutral` and the profile's modes, and changing it on a live agent switches the mood at once.

### Decide when to switch

Tryll does not detect the mood for you: only the API switches the mode, and the language model cannot. Your game owns the character's emotional state, the same way it owns health or quest progress, and calls `SetAgentDeliveryMode` when it changes. Pass the same mood into the prompt too, so that *what* the character says matches *how* it sounds. See [Talking NPC → An NPC who shows emotion](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/use-cases/talking-npc.html#step-4-an-npc-who-shows-emotion).

## Example: the Unity demo

The Unity demo's **EmotionalVoiceCharacter** is a complete example. Kira, a K-pop singer giving a magazine interview, speaks with one Qwen3-TTS voice and eight moods:

- **Voice profile:** `Assets/Voices/VoiceCharacterWithEmotions`, on `Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M)`.
- **Neutral clip:** `voice/young_female/female_young_calm.wav`.
- **Delivery modes:** `angry`, `very_angry`, `fear`, `hysteria`, `joy`, `sad`, `flirty` and `terror`, each with its own clip in `TryllStorage/voice/young_female/`.
- **Workflow:** `Assets/Workflows/EmotionalVoiceCharacter`.

The clips were made with Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign, with one description per mood. To hear it, open `DemoScene`, select the **EmotionalVoiceCharacter** object, pick a mood in the agent component's **Voice Delivery** dropdown, then enter Play mode and talk to Kira. Change the mood while she speaks to hear the switch at the next sentence.

## Other TTS models

How a mode expresses a mood depends on the model:

| Model                      | What a mood is                                                       |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Qwen3-TTS Base, Pocket TTS | A reference clip per mood (this page)                                |
| Maya1                      | A text **Instruction**, such as `angry` or `whisper`, with intensity |
| Supertonic 3, Orpheus      | No emotion control: a mode can only change speed, or stay empty      |

The details for each model are in [Voice Profile → Delivery modes](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html#delivery-modes).

- [Design a Voice Clip with Qwen3-TTS](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-voice-with-qwen3-tts.html)

# Use Voice Input

Voice Input is the Tryll subsystem that streams raw PCM audio to the server, runs it through a speech-to-text (STT) model, and delivers transcripts back to your application. This page covers the full lifecycle: creating a `VoiceInput` handle, starting and finishing utterances, streaming audio, and cleaning up. It ends with links to hotwords biasing and model selection.

For the mental model behind this — the utterance lifecycle, push-to-talk vs. hands-free, offline vs. streaming recognisers, and the transcript-update kinds — see [Concept: STT and Voice Input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/stt-and-voice-input.html).

## Prerequisites

- A connected session. No STT engine setting is needed: the STT model's catalog entry names its engine (Sherpa-ONNX).
- An STT model on disk — download one in the editor Model Manager, or from code (`DownloadModel` in C++, `download_model` in Python, `RequestDownloadModel` in Unity and Unreal).

Optionally, warm the STT engine up at session creation so the first utterance does not pay its start-up cost:

```
// C++ — `engines` is an optional warm-up hint, not a requirement.
client.CreateSession({
    .engines = {{::Tryll::ModelRole_Stt, ::Tryll::InferenceEngine_SherpaOnnx}},
});
```

```
# Python
client.create_session(engines=[(ModelRole.Stt, InferenceEngine.SherpaOnnx)])
```

The Unity and Unreal plugins build this hint from the Model Manager's manifest when they create the session, so there is nothing to add there.

## 1. Create a VoiceInput handle

A `VoiceInput` is a stateful server-side object that holds the loaded STT model and the current utterance state. Create one per microphone source; most games need only one.

**C++**

```
#include <tryll/VoiceInput.h>

Tryll::Client::VoiceInputConfig cfg;
cfg.modelName        = "Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)";
cfg.inputFormat      = { .sampleRate = 48000, .channels = 1, .bitsPerSample = 16 };
cfg.vadThreshold     = 0.5f;   // Silero VAD speech-probability threshold
cfg.vadMinSilenceMs  = 1000;   // silence that ends a segment (ms)
cfg.vadSpeechPadMs   = 250;    // padding around detected speech (ms)

auto vi = client.CreateVoiceInput(cfg);
```

**Python**

```
voice = client.create_voice_input(
    model_name="Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)",
    sample_rate=48000, channels=1, bits_per_sample=16,
)
```

**Unity (C#)**

```
var cfg = new VoiceInputConfig
{
    ModelName       = "Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)",
    InputFormat     = new AudioFormat { SampleRate = 48000, Channels = 1, BitsPerSample = 16 },
    VadThreshold    = 0.5f,
    VadMinSilenceMs = 1000,
    VadSpeechPadMs  = 250,
};
var (voice, err) = await client.CreateVoiceInputAsync(cfg);
if (!err.IsOk) { /* handle */ }
```

**Unreal (C++)**

```
FTryllVoiceInputConfig Config;
Config.ModelName              = TEXT("Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)");
Config.InputFormat.SampleRate = 48000;

Subsystem->CreateVoiceInput(Config,
    [](TSharedPtr<FTryllVoiceInput> Voice, FTryllError Err)
    {
        if (!Err.IsOk()) { /* handle */ return; }
        // Store Voice — it is now ready for BeginUtterance.
    });
```

The server loads the model (or reuses a cached copy) and returns a `voice_input_id`. Every client wraps that id in a `VoiceInput` handle (`VoiceInput` in C++ and Python, `TryllVoiceInput` in Unity, `FTryllVoiceInput` in Unreal); you call the utterance methods on the handle.

### A note on `vadSpeechPadMs`

The voice-activity detector hands the recognizer only the part of the audio it judged to be speech, cropped tight. Recognizers are trained on recordings, which always begin with a little room tone, so a crop with no silence around it costs you the opening word — and for a very short utterance, everything. A one-word "Fireball" cropped to 0.9 seconds transcribes as nothing at all; with 100 ms of silence added to each end it transcribes correctly.

`vadSpeechPadMs` is that silence. The server adds it around each segment before decoding, so leave it at the default unless you have a reason not to. Raising it above 500 ms has no effect.

## 2. Set up transcript callbacks

Register a callback before starting utterances so you receive transcripts as they arrive. Tryll delivers four update kinds:

| Kind             | When                                               |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `SpeechStart`    | VAD detects rising edge; no text yet               |
| `Partial`        | In-progress hypothesis from online (streaming) STT |
| `SegmentFinal`   | Engine committed a chunk; utterance still open     |
| `UtteranceFinal` | Last update for this Begin/End cycle               |

**C++**

```
vi.SetOnTranscriptUpdate([](const Tryll::Client::TranscriptUpdate& u) {
    if (u.kind == ::Tryll::TranscriptUpdateKind_UtteranceFinal)
        ProcessFinalTranscript(u.text);
});
```

**Python**

```
from tryll_client.voice_input import TranscriptUpdateKind

def on_transcript(kind: int, text: str, audio_ms_consumed: int) -> None:
    if kind == TranscriptUpdateKind.UtteranceFinal:
        process_final_transcript(text)

voice.set_on_transcript_update(on_transcript)
```

**Unity (C#)**

```
voice.OnTranscriptUpdate += update =>
{
    if (update.Kind == TranscriptUpdateKind.UtteranceFinal)
        ProcessFinalTranscript(update.Text);
};
```

**Unreal (C++)**

```
Voice->OnTranscriptUpdate.AddLambda([](const FTryllTranscriptUpdate& U)
{
    if (U.Kind == ETryllTranscriptUpdateKind::UtteranceFinal)
        ProcessFinalTranscript(U.Text);
});
```

## 3. Begin an utterance

`BeginUtterance` opens a recording window and arms the VAD.

**C++**

```
Tryll::Client::UtteranceOptions opts;
opts.autoFinishOnSilence = true;
opts.maxUtteranceMs      = 30000;
vi.BeginUtterance(opts);
```

**Python** — `VoiceInput.begin_utterance(auto_finish_on_silence=..., max_utterance_ms=...)`. The transcript callback runs on the reader thread: start a turn from it with `send_message_async`. The blocking `send_message` deadlocks on that thread.

**Unity (C#)**

```
var opts = new UtteranceOptions
{
    AutoFinishOnSilence = true,
    MaxUtteranceMs      = 30000,
};
voice.BeginUtterance(opts);
```

**Unreal (C++)**

```
FTryllUtteranceOptions Opts;
Opts.bAutoFinishOnSilence = true;
Opts.MaxUtteranceMs       = 30000;
Voice->BeginUtterance(Opts);
```

The server only transcribes. On a non-empty `UtteranceFinal`, start the turn yourself: `SendText` (C++), `send_message_async` (Python, from the transcript callback), or `SendMessage` on the agent component (Unity / Unreal). The engine voice components do that when a target agent is set, and drop the final with a warning if that agent already has a turn in flight. Leave the target unset when you want to filter or rewrite the text before sending.

## 4. Stream audio

Send PCM chunks as fast as they arrive. The buffer is fire-and-forget: no acknowledgement, no backpressure from the server.

**C++**

```
// Called from your audio capture code at ~20 ms intervals.
// pcmChunk is a std::vector<std::int16_t> of mono samples.
vi.SendAudioBuffer(pcmChunk);   // binds to std::span<const std::int16_t>
```

**Python**

```
voice.send_audio_buffer(pcm_bytes)   # int16 little-endian PCM bytes
```

**Unity (C#)**

```
// Called on the main thread, e.g. from a coroutine that polls
// Microphone.GetPosition and reads new samples with AudioClip.GetData.
// SendAudioBuffer takes mono 16-bit samples (ReadOnlySpan<short>).
var pcm = new short[floatSamples.Length];
for (int i = 0; i < pcm.Length; i++)
    pcm[i] = (short)(Mathf.Clamp(floatSamples[i], -1f, 1f) * short.MaxValue);
voice.SendAudioBuffer(pcm);
```

**Unreal (C++)**

```
// Called from the audio capture thread.
Voice->SendAudioBuffer(PcmChunk);
```

Audio must be raw signed-16-bit PCM at the sample rate declared in `inputFormat`. The server resamples to the model's expected rate as needed. No encoding (opus, mp3, etc.) is supported on the voice path.

## 5. End or cancel an utterance

If `autoFinishOnSilence` is true the server closes the segment automatically. You can also close it explicitly:

```
vi.EndUtterance();    // C++ — commit; produces UtteranceFinal
vi.CancelUtterance(); // C++ — discard; no UtteranceFinal fired
```

```
voice.end_utterance()     # Python
voice.cancel_utterance()  # Python
```

```
voice.EndUtterance();    // Unity (C#)
voice.CancelUtterance(); // Unity (C#)
```

```
Voice->EndUtterance();    // Unreal (C++)
Voice->CancelUtterance(); // Unreal (C++)
```

## 6. Input modes

### Push-to-talk

Call `BeginUtterance` when the player presses a button and `EndUtterance` when they release it. Disable `autoFinishOnSilence` so VAD does not cut short a deliberate pause mid-sentence.

### Hands-free (VAD-driven)

Keep `autoFinishOnSilence = true`. The server commits each phrase on silence and fires `UtteranceFinal`. A non-empty final is the text you send (see §3). The engine voice components drop that final when the target agent already has a turn in flight. Empty finals close the utterance and do not start a turn; during silence the server emits empty `SegmentFinal` heartbeats you can surface as a "listening…" hint. Open a fresh `BeginUtterance` for the next turn — typically after the agent's reply and any TTS playback finish, which keeps the mic from transcribing its own output.

## 7. Destroy the handle

Always destroy the `VoiceInput` when you are done with it. This frees the model slot on the server.

In C++ the handle is move-only and has no `Destroy()` method: its destructor cancels any active utterance and destroys the server-side object. Let it go out of scope (or reset the object that owns it); move it to keep it alive longer.

```
voice.destroy()  # Python — or use `with client.create_voice_input(...) as voice:`
```

```
voice.Dispose();  // Unity (C#)
```

```
Subsystem->RequestDestroyVoiceInput(Voice);  // Unreal (C++)
```

## Next steps

- [Bias Voice Input with Hotwords](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input-hotwords.html) — nudge the STT decoder toward game-specific proper nouns and spell names without retraining.
- [Pin and Unpin Models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/pin-and-unpin-models.html) — keep the STT model warm between sessions to avoid reload latency.

## Related reference

- `CreateVoiceInputRequest` — wire message sent to start a VoiceInput session.
- `BeginUtteranceRequest` — wire message sent to open an audio capture window.
- `WireTranscriptUpdate` — server push carrying incremental and final transcript text.

# Bias Voice Input with Hotwords

Open-vocabulary speech-to-text engines guess every word from acoustic evidence alone, which means they often mangle game-specific proper nouns — the NPC name "Aeltharion" becomes "Al Therion", the spell "frostbolt" becomes "frost bolt". Sherpa-ONNX exposes a *hotwords* list that nudges the decoder toward a designer-authored set of phrases without retraining the model.

This recipe shows how to ship a phrase list with your game and apply it to a `VoiceInput`.

## Prerequisites

- A working `VoiceInput` session — see [Use Voice Input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html) for the full setup walkthrough.
- An STT model that supports hotwords. Most transducer / CTC families do; encoder-decoder families (Whisper, SenseVoice, Moonshine, Canary) log a warning and ignore the list when the voice input is created. The matrix and the warning are in [Which models support hotwords](#which-models-support-hotwords) below.

## 1. Author a phrase list

Hotwords live in a `StringStorage` of kind `List`, shipped as a UTF-8 text file in your game's storage data folder — one phrase per line. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored:

```
# data/voice-hotwords.txt
# fantasy NPC names
Aeltharion
Cor'than
Bjornthor

# spells / abilities
fireball
frostbolt
magic missile
```

The file path is **relative to the process storage root** (Project Settings **Storage Data Folder**, default `TryllStorage/`). The server loads it on demand the first time a `VoiceInput` references it — no `CreateStringStorage` call is needed.

## 2. Reference the file when creating `VoiceInput`

**C++**

```
#include <tryll/TryllClient.h>
#include <tryll/VoiceInput.h>

Tryll::Client::VoiceInputConfig viCfg;
viCfg.modelName            = "Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)";
viCfg.inputFormat          = micFormat;
viCfg.hotwordsStoragePath  = "data/voice-hotwords.txt";
viCfg.hotwordsScore        = 1.8f;   // bonus per matched phrase; default 1.5

auto vi = client.CreateVoiceInput(viCfg);
```

**Python**

```
voice = client.create_voice_input(
    model_name="Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)",
    sample_rate=16000, channels=1, bits_per_sample=16,
    hotwords_storage_path="data/voice-hotwords.txt",
    hotwords_score=1.8,
)
```

**Unity (C#)**

```
var cfg = new VoiceInputConfig
{
    ModelName            = "Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)",
    InputFormat          = AudioFormat.Default,
    VadThreshold         = 0.5f,
    VadMinSilenceMs      = 1000,
    VadSpeechPadMs       = 250,
    HotwordsStoragePath  = "data/voice-hotwords.txt",
    HotwordsScore        = 1.8f,
};
var (voice, err) = await client.CreateVoiceInputAsync(cfg);
```

On `TryllVoiceInputComponent`, set the same values in the inspector: `Hotwords Storage Path` (relative to Storage Data Folder; empty disables) and `Hotwords Score` (default 1.5).

**Unreal (C++)**

```
FTryllVoiceInputConfig Config;
Config.ModelName             = TEXT("Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)");
Config.InputFormat.SampleRate = 16000;
Config.HotwordsStoragePath   = TEXT("data/voice-hotwords.txt");
Config.HotwordsScore         = 1.8f;

Subsystem->CreateVoiceInput(Config,
    [](TSharedPtr<FTryllVoiceInput> Voice, FTryllError Err)
    {
        if (!Err.IsOk()) { /* handle error */ return; }
        // Voice is ready — call BeginUtterance to start capturing.
        // BeginUtterance options include auto_finish_on_silence and
        // max_utterance_ms.
    });
```

The referenced file must exist under the process storage root; a missing file fails `CreateVoiceInput` with `StorageFileNotFound`.

## Picking a score

The score is the bonus added to a matched phrase during beam search (default 1.5). No score value turns biasing off: an empty `hotwordsStoragePath` is what disables it.

| Score     | Bias             | Use when…                                                                                         |
| --------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1.0       | light            | a smaller bonus than the default; still biases                                                    |
| 1.5       | gentle (default) | the lexicon is broad and you do not want false positives                                          |
| 1.8 – 2.5 | moderate         | proper nouns + spell names — typical game lexicon                                                 |
| 3.0 – 4.0 | aggressive       | the recognizer keeps picking a phonetically-similar real word and you accept some false positives |

The score applies to every phrase in the list — unless a line sets its own. Append `:<number>` to a lexicon line to bias that phrase alone:

```
Kaelthorne :3.0
Veyra
frostbolt
```

Here `Kaelthorne` is biased at 3.0 and the rest at whatever the session's `hotwordsScore` is. Use it for the one name a recognizer keeps mangling, instead of raising the score for the whole list and paying for it everywhere.

### The score you set is one of two

The server applies hotword bias in two places, and only one of them is yours to set per session:

|                     | What it does                                                | Where it is set                                              |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Candidate boost** | makes a hotword's tokens reachable by the recognizer at all | the server's model catalog (`stt_hotwords_score`), per model |
| **Phrase weight**   | weights matched phrases against one another                 | `hotwordsScore` on the VoiceInput — the one in this guide    |

The catalog value is what lets the recognizer consider `Kaelthorne` in the first place; `hotwordsScore` then decides how strongly `Kaelthorne` competes with the other phrases in your lexicon. You normally only touch the second.

### Turning biasing on for a model

Biasing needs beam-search decoding, which the server chooses when it loads the model — so it is a per-model decision, not something a single voice input can switch on. The shipped catalog enables it for **Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3** and no other model.

To change that for your project, use the **Hotword biasing** control in the Model Manager (beside Memory placement) — it is available on STT models:

|             |                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Default** | follow the server's setting for this model                                                                                                                                              |
| **Off**     | never bias. Supplying a lexicon then fails with `HotwordBiasDisabled` (4106) instead of quietly doing nothing                                                                           |
| **On**      | always bias. Beam-search decoding is then in force for every voice input on this model, costing a few percent of decode time and changing its transcripts — *on but unused is not free* |

From code, the same choice is a per-model hint on the session: `hotword_hints` on `create_session` in Python; in C++, a `TryllClient::ModelPlacementHint` with `hotwords` set, passed in `SessionConfig::placementHints`:

```
using Tryll::Client::TryllClient;

TryllClient::SessionConfig cfg;
cfg.placementHints.push_back({
    .modelName = "Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)",
    .hotwords  = ::Tryll::HotwordBias_On,
});
client.CreateSession(cfg);
```

```
from tryll_client import HotwordBias

client.create_session(hotword_hints={"Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)": HotwordBias.On})
```

If hotwords seem to do nothing at all on a model — no value of `hotwordsScore` changes anything — that model is not enabled for biasing. Check the control above, and the server log, which says `hotwords=unavailable` on the model's load line.

**Raising the score is not free, and past a point it is actively destructive.** Bias nudges the beam toward your phrases everywhere, including in speech that contains none of them, and short utterances have the least context to resist it. Measured on Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 with a nine-phrase fantasy lexicon, at score 6.0:

| Spoken                  | Transcribed                             |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| "Fireball"              | "Mord"                                  |
| "Hello, how are you?"   | "Mords soul. Mordrian souls souls soul" |
| a four-sentence passage | unaffected                              |

So tune against two sets, not one: utterances that contain your terms, and utterances that do not. The second set is what tells you when to stop. Start at 1.5, raise until the terms land, then check the second set before keeping the value.

## Which models support hotwords

Two things have to be true: the decoder must have a beam for the bias to act on, and the model bundle must carry a sub-word vocabulary the server can encode your phrases with.

| Family                                                           | Hotwords             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Zipformer transducer / Parakeet TDT (Transducer, NemoTransducer) | yes                  |
| Streaming Zipformer (online transducer)                          | yes                  |
| Zipformer-CTC, NeMo CTC, Paraformer, Dolphin, WeNet CTC          | no — no beam to bias |
| Whisper                                                          | **no**               |
| SenseVoice                                                       | **no**               |
| Moonshine, Canary, FireRedASR, CohereTranscribe                  | **no**               |

When you pass a hotwords list to a model that cannot use it, the server logs a warning when the voice input is created and ignores the phrases, rather than accepting the list silently:

```
[Sherpa-ONNX] Hotword biasing unavailable for STT family 'whisper'
              (this decoder has no token-level bias hook); ignoring
              9 supplied phrase(s) on this session.
```

The model's load banner also states it up front:

```
[Sherpa-ONNX] STT model loaded: … | family=nemo_transducer | … |
              decoding=modified_beam_search | hotwords=available
```

The session is otherwise unaffected. Hotword-capable models load with beam-search decoding, which costs a few percent of decode time.

## Caveats

- **Write plain words.** The server hands your phrases to the recognizer's own tokenizer, so `Aeltharion` is what you want in the file — not a pre-tokenized `▁Ael th ar ion`. Lexicons written in the older `▁`-piece form still work; the server folds them back to graphemes. There is no longer any reason to run `text2token.py` over a lexicon by hand.
- **A whole utterance biases better than a fragment.** The recognizer decodes one speech segment at a time, and a phrase near a segment boundary has less context to be recognised from. If a term is being missed, check whether the pause structure of the speech is splitting the sentence before blaming the score.
- **The score is the default for the whole voice input.** A lexicon line that ends with `:<number>` overrides it for that phrase only.
- **The lexicon is loaded from the process storage root.** The server reads the file on demand and caches it. Ship the file with your game data and every session on that server can use it.
- **Out-of-vocabulary characters are dropped.** If your lexicon contains characters the model's tokenizer cannot represent (e.g. CJK characters against a pure-English Zipformer), they are silently dropped from the bias.

## Related

- [Use Voice Input](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-voice-input.html)
- [`StringStorage` reference](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/string-storage.html)

# Add Lip Sync to a MetaHuman (Unreal)

Make a MetaHuman's mouth move in time with an agent's Tryll TTS voice. This uses the **Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync** plugin (`UnrealPlugin/TryllMetaHumanLipSync`), a separate plugin installed alongside [TryllClient](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/client-api/unreal/cpp/index.html). It has two solvers, and both feed the face through Live Link:

- **Neural** (default) runs Epic's realtime speech-to-animation model on the CPU over the TTS audio. It drives the whole face.
- **Viseme** plays the server's viseme track through Epic's ARKit mapping. It drives the mouth and jaw, and runs no model.

See [Choose a solver](#choose-a-solver).

## Requirements

- Unreal Engine 5.7, Windows 64-bit.
- The TryllClient plugin with voice output working — see [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html).
- A MetaHuman in your project. Both kinds work: characters assembled in the in-engine MetaHuman Creator and characters downloaded from Quixel Bridge.

## Enable and set up

1. Install the plugin into your project's `Plugins/` folder and enable **Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync** in **Edit > Plugins**. It is off by default.
1. Open **Project Settings > Plugins > Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync** and click **Set Up**. The status line changes to *Set up.*

Set Up copies Epic's speech-to-animation model from your engine installation into your project as `Content/TryllMetaHumanLipSync/solar-1-2700_blend-0v65.uasset` and configures it for CPU inference. Nothing is redistributed by Tryll. The asset is generated, so add it to `.gitignore` and run Set Up on each fresh clone.

Until Set Up has run, **Play** is blocked with a notification naming the step, and packaging a Win64 game target fails at build time with the same message. This applies with either solver. Dedicated server targets are not affected.

### Fresh clones and build machines

Run Set Up from the command line instead of the editor:

```
UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe <Project>.uproject -run=TryllMetaHumanLipSyncSetup
UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe <Project>.uproject -run=TryllMetaHumanLipSyncSetup -verify
```

Both exit with `0` when the project is set up and `1` otherwise. `-verify` checks without changing anything.

## Add lip sync to a character

Open the MetaHuman's Blueprint and add two components:

1. **Tryll Speaker**, next to an agent component whose **Voice Profile** is set, as in [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html).
1. **Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync**.

That's all. When the character starts, the component finds the speaker and the skeletal mesh named `Face` on the same actor, and the mouth follows the voice.

### Other layouts

If the components are not on the MetaHuman itself, set **Target MetaHuman** to the character. If the owning actor has several Tryll Speakers, set **Speaker** to the one to follow. With nothing set, the component also looks in the owner's child actors for the face.

## Choose a solver

Set **Solver** on the component. It is read once when the character starts.

|                            | Neural                                                 | Viseme                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Drives                     | The whole face                                         | Mouth and jaw                                                                                                           |
| Input                      | The TTS audio                                          | The server's viseme track                                                                                               |
| Voice change               | None                                                   | Turn on **Emit Visemes** in the agent's [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html) |
| CPU per speaking character | About 4 to 5 ms per 20 ms of audio                     | No model runs                                                                                                           |
| Face timing                | Trails the audio by the lookahead plus one 20 ms block | Follows the audio as it plays                                                                                           |

### Use the Viseme solver

1. In the agent's **Voice Profile** asset, tick **Emit Visemes**. Without it no track arrives and the mouth stays still; the component logs a warning when the character starts. Every speaking node of the agent (Speak and Generate And Speak) then sends a track.
1. Set **Solver** to **Viseme**.
1. Check **ARKit Mapping** points at Epic's `PA_MetaHuman_ARKit_Mapping` pose asset. The default is `/Game/MetaHumans/Common/Face/ARKit/PA_MetaHuman_ARKit_Mapping`, where exported MetaHumans keep it. The MetaHuman Character plugin also ships one in its `Face/ARKit` folder.

For what the viseme track is and how to tune it, see [Add Lip Sync to a Character](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-lip-sync-to-a-character.html). Its Unreal **Tryll Lip Sync** component uses the same viseme settings on faces with ARKit morph targets.

## Settings

| Setting          | Default | Notes                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Target MetaHuman | unset   | The character to animate. Unset means the owner, then its child actors.                                                    |
| Speaker          | unset   | The Tryll Speaker to follow. Unset means the only one on the owner.                                                        |
| Solver           | Neural  | **Neural** or **Viseme**. Read once when the character starts.                                                             |
| Subject Name     | empty   | Live Link subject name. Empty derives `TryllMetaHumanLipSync_<actor label>`, suffixed only if that name is already in use. |

Neural solver only:

| Setting        | Default | Notes                                                                                                   |
| -------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mood           | Neutral | Emotional tone applied by the model.                                                                    |
| Mood Intensity | 1.0     | 0 to 1.                                                                                                 |
| Lookahead      | 80 ms   | 80 to 240. Higher is smoother and adds the same amount of latency. Read once when the character starts. |

Change mood while the game runs with **Set Mood** (`SetMood(Mood, Intensity)`).

Viseme solver only:

| Setting                                        | Default   | Notes                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Viseme Settings > Intensity                    | 1.0       | Scales every mouth pose. `0` keeps the mouth at rest.                                                                  |
| Viseme Settings > Smoothing Per Second         | 16        | How quickly the mouth moves toward each new shape. Lower is softer, higher is snappier.                                |
| Viseme Settings > Closure Smoothing Per Second | 60        | Faster rate for lip closures (p, b, m, f, v), so the lips meet on short sounds.                                        |
| Viseme Settings > Attack Decay Ms              | 50        | Cross-fade between consecutive shapes.                                                                                 |
| Viseme Settings > Max Hold Ms                  | 400       | Returns the mouth to rest if a turn is cancelled mid-sentence.                                                         |
| Viseme Settings > Sync Offset Ms               | 0         | Shifts the mouth against the audio. Positive moves it earlier.                                                         |
| Viseme Settings > Compensate Output Latency    | on        | Holds the mouth back by the audio engine's output buffer, so it lines up with the sound as heard.                      |
| Viseme Settings > Compensate Smoothing Lag     | on        | Looks ahead by the delay the smoothing adds, so changing smoothing does not shift sync.                                |
| Viseme Poses                                   | empty     | The pose for each viseme as ARKit channel weights. Empty uses the built-in table. Read once when the character starts. |
| ARKit Mapping                                  | see above | Epic's ARKit to MetaHuman pose asset.                                                                                  |

Viseme Settings can be changed while the game runs.

## Troubleshooting

Every message is logged under `LogTryllMetaHumanLipSync` with the owning actor's name. **Get Lip Sync Status** returns the same state from Blueprint, and **On Lip Sync Status Changed** fires when it changes.

| Status                 | Cause                                                                              | Fix                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SpeakerNotFound`      | No Tryll Speaker on the owner.                                                     | Add one, or set **Speaker**.                             |
| `SpeakerAmbiguous`     | More than one Tryll Speaker on the owner.                                          | Set **Speaker**.                                         |
| `FaceNotFound`         | No skeletal mesh named `Face` on the owner, its child actors, or Target MetaHuman. | Set **Target MetaHuman** to the character.               |
| `LiveLinkUnavailable`  | The Live Link plugin is disabled.                                                  | Enable it.                                               |
| `AnimBlueprintMissing` | The plugin's face AnimBP is missing from its content.                              | Reinstall the plugin.                                    |
| `ModelMissing`         | Set Up has not run in this project.                                                | Run Set Up.                                              |
| `ModelLoadFailed`      | The model asset exists but ONNX Runtime rejected it.                               | See the NNE log lines just above the message.            |
| `InferenceFailed`      | ONNX Runtime failed while the character was speaking.                              | See the NNE log lines just above the message.            |
| `ArkitMappingMissing`  | Viseme solver: the **ARKit Mapping** asset could not be loaded.                    | Point **ARKit Mapping** at `PA_MetaHuman_ARKit_Mapping`. |

With the Viseme solver, a status of `Bound` and a mouth that never moves means no viseme track is arriving: turn on **Emit Visemes** in the agent's voice profile. The component warns about this at start when it can find the agent component on the same actor.

## Performance

With the Neural solver, each speaking character costs about 4 to 5 ms of CPU per 20 ms of audio, measured on a Ryzen 9 7900X. Characters that are not speaking cost nothing. The face trails the audio by the lookahead plus one 20 ms block.

The Viseme solver runs no model.

## What it does to the character

The component sets the anim class on the `Face` mesh to the plugin's own face AnimBP, `ABP_TryllMetaHumanLipSyncFace`. It copies the neck and spine pose from the Body mesh, reads the Live Link subject, and provides a montage slot. With the Viseme solver, the AnimBP passes the Live Link ARKit curves through the **ARKit Mapping** pose asset, the same way Epic's `ABP_MH_LiveLink` handles ARKit input. Whatever face AnimBP the character had is not used while the component is on it. The MetaHuman's rig logic runs as normal in the mesh's post-process AnimBP, so no MetaHuman assets are referenced by the plugin, other than the ARKit Mapping you point it at.

- [Add Voice Output to an Agent](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/add-voice-to-an-agent.html)
- [Concept: TTS and Voice Output](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tts-and-voice-output.html)

# Use Your Own Local Model

Register a GGUF file already on disk so Tryll can load it without a Hugging Face download.

Prerequisites

- A `.gguf` file inside the server's **process storage root**, e.g. `<Project>/TryllStorage/LocalModels/my-model-q4_k_m.gguf`. Unity and Unreal default the root to `<Project>/TryllStorage/`; a server you run yourself uses `--storage-root`, `storage_root`, or the folder of `tryll_server.exe`. See [Server Configuration → Storage root](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/server-configuration.html#storage-root).
- A JSON file inside your game project, if you use the Unity or Unreal plugin. Any file name. Do **not** edit the shipped `data/models.json` — updates overwrite it.
- No engine setup. The catalog entry's `engine` decides which engine runs the model.

## Steps

1. **Put the catalog JSON somewhere inside the project.** Any file name, any folder. Same schema as `models.json`. The key fields are `name` plus one `variants` entry with `engine = "llama-cpp"`, a `local_path` **directory**, and the `files` inside it:

   ```
   {
     "models": [
       {
         "name": "My Local Model",
         "variants": [
           {
             "engine": "llama-cpp",
             "local_path": "LocalModels",
             "files": ["my-model-q4_k_m.gguf"],
             "kv_cache_type": "q8_0",
             "tool_call_support": "unsupported"
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   A relative `local_path` resolves against the process storage root, so `"LocalModels"` above means `<storage root>/LocalModels/`. An absolute path also works when it points inside that root. A path outside the root (for example `C:/models`) is ignored with a warning, and the model never resolves. A Client Prod server ignores `local_path` entirely.

   Leave the shipped `models.json` unchanged. A relative `chat_template_file` is resolved against the directory that contains your catalog file, so keep those template files inside the project. The catalog is optional — leave the setting empty if you are not adding models.

   **Unity:** Project Settings → Tryll Client → Custom Models → Catalog, or Browse.

   Auto-launch runs at `BeforeSceneLoad`, before any scene `Awake`. Subscribe before that so the first process sees the file:

   ```
   [RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(RuntimeInitializeLoadType.AfterAssembliesLoaded)]
   static void PointAtCatalog()
   {
       TryllRuntimeSettings.BeforeAutoLaunch += () =>
       {
           var settings = TryllRuntimeSettings.Load();
           if (!settings.TrySetUserModelsCatalogPath("Assets/Tryll/my-models.json", out string error))
               Debug.LogError(error);
       };
   }
   ```

   Calling `TrySetUserModelsCatalogPath` after the server is already running restarts it. The open client session is dropped.

   A player build copies the catalog saved in Project Settings to `Server/data/user-catalog/` next to the game, including relative chat templates. To pick a different file at runtime in a build, put it under `Assets/StreamingAssets/` and set that project-relative path from code.

   **Unreal:** Project Settings → Plugins → Tryll Client → Models → Catalog, or Browse. From code or Blueprint, `Set User Models Catalog Path`.

   The first auto-launch runs in the Tryll subsystem's `Initialize`, before BeginPlay. Set the path from your GameInstance `Init` (or from Project Settings) so the first process sees it. Calling the setter while a server is already running restarts it when Auto Launch Server is on, and the open session is dropped.

   A packaged build copies the catalog saved in Project Settings to `Server/data/user-catalog/` next to the game, including relative chat templates. A different file selected from code in a packaged game is used only when that file is already a loose file inside the project directory.

   The stored path is relative to the project and must stay inside it. If you launch `tryll_server` yourself, pass the same file as `--user-models-path`. There is no shipped user catalog. An omitted path still names a sibling `user_models.json`, and a missing file is silent. An optional `models.d` directory is loaded when it exists; the install does not create it.

1. **Validate (optional).** From the server directory, point at the file you linked:

   ```
   tryll_server --check-catalogs --user-models-path "C:/YourProject/Assets/Tryll/my-models.json"
   ```

1. **Restart the server** (or let the editor relaunch it). Your model appears in `ListModels` / the Model Manager alongside the shipped catalog.

1. **If something goes wrong:** a malformed user file is skipped and the server still starts on the shipped catalog. The startup log names the file and the fix. Duplicate names against a shipped model are ignored for that entry only (rename yours).

## Unity / Unreal

The Catalog field above is the place to link the file. Auto-launch passes it as `--user-models-path`. In a packaged game that path is the staged copy under `Server/data/user-catalog/`. A folder named `<ProjectRoot>/Tryll/models.d` is still passed as `--user-models-dir` when it exists, for extra drop-in files.

## See also

- [Model management](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html) — merge rules and catalog schema
- [Server configuration](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/server-configuration.html) — `user_models_catalog_path`

# Use a LoRA Adapter

Run an LLM node with a **LoRA adapter**: a small GGUF file, fine-tuned for one base model, that changes how that model behaves for one job. A small adapter can teach a small model a narrow task, such as a fixed rewrite style or one character's way of speaking, without shipping a second model.

Any node that runs a language model takes adapters: [Generate](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate.html), [Generate and Speak](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/generate-and-speak.html), [Tool Call](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html), [Classify Intent (LLM)](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-intent-llm.html), [Classify Attributes (LLM)](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-attributes-llm.html) and [Summarize](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/summarize.html). The base model is loaded once. Each node that names an adapter runs it on its own context, so one agent can run a fine-tuned node next to nodes that use the plain base model.

Getting an adapter

Tryll does not train adapters, and this page does not cover fine-tuning. If you need an adapter for your game, [contact the Tryll developers](https://tryllengine.com/).

Prerequisites

- A LoRA adapter in **GGUF** format, trained for the **same base model** that the node runs. An adapter made for another model fails agent creation.
- That base model in the catalog and downloaded — see [Manage Models in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html).
- The server's **process storage root**. Unity and Unreal default it to `<Project>/TryllStorage/`. See [Server Configuration → Storage root](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/server-configuration.html#storage-root).

## 1. Put the adapter in the storage folder

The adapter's path is **relative to the storage root**, like voice clips and string storages:

```
<storage root>/
  └─ lora/
      └─ merchant_style.gguf
```

The file stays on the machine that runs the Tryll server. The client only sends the path. For a packaged build, ship the folder with the game, as described in [Ship Storage Folders for Builds](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/ship-storage-folders-for-builds.html).

## 2. Add the adapter to the node

Each LLM node has an **Adaptation** table with a **Loras** list. Every entry has a **Path** and a **Scale**.

1. Open the workflow in the [graph editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/edit-workflows-in-graph-editor.html) (or select the workflow asset) and select the LLM node.
1. Expand **Adaptation → Loras** and add an element.
1. In **Path**, click the **…** button and pick the `.gguf` file. The field stores the storage-relative path, such as `lora/merchant_style.gguf`. You can also type it.
1. Leave **Scale** at `1` for now.

The workflow validator flags an absolute path or a `..` path as an error before Play, and a missing or non-`.gguf` file as a warning.

In code:

```
using Tryll.Client;

var gen = new TryllGenerateParams { SystemPrompt = "You are a merchant." };
gen.Adaptation.Loras = new[]
{
    new TryllLoraAdapter { Path = "lora/merchant_style.gguf", Scale = 1f },
};
```

1. Open the workflow asset in the [graph editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/edit-workflows-in-unreal-graph-editor.html) and select the LLM node.
1. In the Details panel, expand **Adaptation → Loras** and add an element.
1. In **Path**, click the browse button and pick the `.gguf` file. The stored value is the storage-relative path.
1. Leave **Scale** at `1` for now.

In C++:

```
UTryllGenerateParams* P = UTryllNodeParamsFactory::MakeGenerateParams(this);

FTryllLoraAdapter Lora;
Lora.Path.Path = TEXT("lora/merchant_style.gguf");
Lora.Scale = 1.0f;
P->Adaptation.Loras.Add(Lora);
```

```
from tryll_client.graph import GenerateParams, LoraAdapter, ModelAdaptation

gen = GenerateParams(
    system_prompt="You are a merchant.",
    adaptation=ModelAdaptation(loras=[
        LoraAdapter(path="lora/merchant_style.gguf", scale=1.0),
    ]),
)
```

```
using namespace Tryll::NodeParams;

GenerateParamsT gp;
gp.system_prompt = "You are a merchant.";

auto lora = std::make_unique<LoraAdapterT>();
lora->path  = "lora/merchant_style.gguf";
lora->scale = 1.0f;
gp.adaptation = std::make_unique<ModelAdaptationT>();
gp.adaptation->loras.push_back(std::move(lora));
```

The other LLM nodes take the same `adaptation` field.

## 3. Create the agent and check it

Create the agent as usual. The server loads the adapter when it creates the node's context, and logs each load with its size. If the path or the file is wrong, agent creation fails, and the error names the file:

| Error                         | Cause                                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `3009 StorageOutsideRoot`     | The path is absolute or leaves the storage root with `..`.                                                                                                       |
| `3010 StorageFileNotFound`    | No file at that path under the storage root.                                                                                                                     |
| `3003 GraphCompilationFailed` | The file is not a LoRA GGUF, or it was trained for a different base model. Also: an empty path, the same file listed twice, or more than 8 adapters on one node. |

Then talk to the agent and compare its replies with the base model's. Setting **Scale** to `0` turns the adapter off without changing the graph, which gives you a quick before-and-after.

## 4. Tune the scale

**Scale** sets how strongly the adapter changes the model. The range is `0` to `4`:

- `1` applies the adapter **as trained**. Start here.
- `0` turns it **off**. The node runs the plain base model.
- Between `0` and `1` the effect is **weaker**. Lower the scale when the adapter takes over too much: replies all sound alike, or the node starts ignoring its system prompt or the character's details.
- Above `1` the effect is **stronger**. Raise it carefully, in small steps, when the adapter's effect is too faint. High values tend to make the output repetitive or broken.

Change the scale in steps of about `0.25` and compare the same dialog each time. The [Dialog Lab](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-dialog-variants.html) does this well: give each variant its own agent with a different scale, run the same script with several seeds, and compare the replies side by side.

The adapter is fixed when the agent is created

`adaptation` is **structural**. Changing the path or the scale on a live agent with [Change Agent Parameters](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/change-agent-parameters.html) fails with `3006 ParamNotMutable`. To try another scale, recreate the agent.

## Several adapters on one node

A node takes **up to 8 adapters**. Each one adds its change, multiplied by its scale, to the base model. The changes add up, so the order of the list does not matter. Each file may appear only once per node.

Stacking adapters that were trained separately can weaken each one or make them conflict. If you stack adapters, retune their scales together.

## Memory

An adapter's weights are loaded next to the base model's weights, on the GPU when the model runs there. The cost is roughly the adapter's file size. A rank-16 adapter for a 3–4B model is about 50–100 MiB. Each file is loaded once and shared by every node and agent that names it, and it is freed when the last of them is gone. The [Memory window](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/inspect-server-memory.html) counts adapters with their model.
