# Pin and Unpin Models

Keep a model warm in memory or explicitly release it. Useful when you want the first turn to be fast, or when memory pressure forces you to pick which model lives.

Prerequisites

- A connected session, with `CreateSession` already called.
- A model listed in `models.json` with status `Local` or `Downloaded` — see [Use Your Own Local Model](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-your-own-local-model.html).

## When to pin

| Situation                                                  | Pin?                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Single chat model used all session long                    | **Yes** — avoids the first-turn load delay.                      |
| Many agents with different models, short-lived             | **No** — let `OnDemand` eviction recycle memory as agents close. |
| Embedding model for RAG                                    | **Yes** — embeddings run every turn; you do not want it evicted. |
| Model used only once during startup (e.g. a warm-up probe) | **No** — let it fall out when you destroy the probing agent.     |

The two [retention policies](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/model-management.html) apply to **language, embedding, STT, and TTS** (not VAD — VAD is download-only and rejected by `LoadModel`):

- **`Pinned`** — set by `LoadModelRequest` / Blueprint **Request Load Model**. Only unloaded when you send `UnloadModelRequest` **and** no active contexts still reference the model.
- **`OnDemand`** — the default. Set implicitly when you create an agent (or voice input / TTS / embedding use) and the model is not already loaded. The server frees unused OnDemand models after `DestroyAgent`, and again immediately before the next validated model load (across all four caches).

## Steps — pin a model

```
TryllClient.Instance.LoadModelComplete += (modelName, success) => {
    if (success) Debug.Log($"{modelName} pinned");
    else         Debug.LogError($"Failed to pin {modelName}");
};
TryllClient.Instance.RequestLoadModel("My Local Model");
```

Call **Request Load Model** on `UTryllSubsystem` with the model name. Bind **On Load Model Complete** to wait for `bSuccess = true`.

```
try {
    client.LoadModel("My Local Model");
} catch (const Tryll::Client::TryllError& ex) {
    std::cerr << "load failed: " << ex.what() << "\n";
}
```

```
client.load_model("My Local Model")   # returns when load completes
```

After a successful pin, the model stays in memory across agent create / destroy cycles until you explicitly unload it.

## Steps — unpin a model

```
TryllClient.Instance.UnloadModelComplete += (modelName, success) =>
    Debug.Log($"{modelName} unloaded: {success}");
TryllClient.Instance.RequestUnloadModel("My Local Model");
```

Call **Request Unload Model** on `UTryllSubsystem` with the model name. Bind **On Unload Model Complete**.

```
client.UnloadModel("My Local Model");
```

```
client.unload_model("My Local Model")
```

`UnloadModelRequest` is safe even if the model is currently in use by an active agent. The server drops the pin and sends `Ack` immediately. A model that no context holds is freed at once. A model that agents still hold stays resident until those agents' contexts are destroyed (for example by `DestroyAgent`); finishing a turn does not free it.

## Verify it worked

Check status with `ListModels`:

- `Status = Loaded` → model is in memory (pinned or on-demand with active users).
- `Status = Local` or `Downloaded` → model is on disk but not in memory.

Server-side log lines:

```
[Session 1] LoadModel requested: 'My Local Model'
[ModelManager] Pinned 'My Local Model'
[Session 1] UnloadModel requested: 'My Local Model'
[ModelManager] Unloaded 'My Local Model'
[Session 1] Model 'My Local Model' unloaded immediately
```

If the last line reads `unload deferred (active contexts)` instead, agents still hold the model. It stays resident until their contexts are destroyed.

## Common pitfalls

- **Pinning and never unpinning.** Pinned models survive session tear-downs (they are global). A long-lived server can accumulate pins if clients forget to unload. Pair every `LoadModelRequest` with a matching `UnloadModelRequest` on shutdown.
- **Expecting pin to change load cost of subsequent sessions.** Correct — pinning is global. A second client connecting will find the model already `Loaded`.
- **Trying to pin an `Absent` model.** Pin requires the model to be at least `Local` / `Downloaded`. If it is `Absent`, call `DownloadModel` first.
- **Trying to pin a VAD model.** VAD entries are catalog/download metadata only. `LoadModel` returns `ModelResolutionFailed`. Download the VAD bundle explicitly first — offline STT only resolves and loads VAD files that are already on disk (otherwise it falls back to flush-only mode).

- [Concept: Lifetime and Ownership](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/lifetime-and-ownership.html)

# Verify Required Models Before Play

Both editor plugins register models per-project as **Production** or **Experimental** in the [Model Manager](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html), then download them there. If a teammate pulls a repo change that adds or replaces a registered model, that download step is easy to miss — the next time you press Play (or open the Tryll Chat window) with a stale local model cache, `CreateAgent` used to fail with a `GraphCompilationFailed` error that gave no hint a download was the fix.

The editor guard closes that gap. It runs automatically at every point an agent is about to be created in the editor. The automatic **Play / PIE** check is on by default and can be turned off per project if you prefer to manage model provisioning yourself — see [Turning off the Play/PIE check](#turning-off-the-playpie-check).

## What it checks

On each guarded entry point, the guard loads your project's model manifest (the same Production/Experimental registrations you set in the [Model Manager](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html)), compares every registered model of every kind (language, embedding, STT, TTS, VAD) against the live `ListModels` status, and treats anything `Absent` as needing attention.

## Where it runs

| Entry point                         | Behaviour                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Play** (Unity) / **PIE** (Unreal) | Blocks automatically: downloads every missing registered model behind a cancelable progress dialog, then continues into Play/PIE once ready. Cancelling, or a model that fails to download, keeps you in the editor instead. |
| **Tryll Chat window/panel**         | Same automatic, blocking treatment as Play — the guard runs right after the session is created and before the chat agent is built.                                                                                           |
| **Model Manager window/panel**      | Lighter-touch: after the model list loads, if anything registered is missing you get a Yes/No prompt instead of an automatic download — this is also where you'd go to fix it manually.                                      |

Unity: what a cancelled Play looks like

Unity has no way to pause entering Play mid-transition, so the guard cancels the transition, runs the check with a progress dialog, and — once every model is confirmed downloaded — automatically re-enters Play for you. You don't need to press Play twice.

## Turning off the Play/PIE check

The automatic **Play (Unity) / PIE (Unreal)** check is on by default but can be disabled per project:

- **Unreal:** Project Settings → Plugins → **Tryll Client** → *Editor* → **Enable Play Mode Model Guard** (the `bEnablePlayModeModelGuard` field on `UTryllRuntimeSettings`, saved to `DefaultGame.ini`). Uncheck it to enter PIE immediately with no pre-flight model check.
- **Unity:** Project Settings → **Tryll Client** → *Play Mode (Editor)* → **Enable Play Mode Model Guard** (the `EnablePlayModeModelGuard` field on `TryllRuntimeSettings`). Uncheck it to enter Play immediately with no pre-flight model check.

The toggle affects **only** the automatic Play/PIE check — the Tryll Chat window/panel still verifies models before creating its agent, and the Model Manager still prompts for missing ones. With the check off, a required model that isn't on disk surfaces as a `CreateAgent` failure at runtime instead of being caught (and offered for download) before Play.

## A model that can't be downloaded

Some registered models are supplied as a local file path rather than a HuggingFace repo (see [Use Your Own Local Model](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-your-own-local-model.html)). If one of those is registered but missing on disk, the guard cannot fetch it — it surfaces a clear error naming the model instead of attempting a download. Provide the file or remove the registration in the [Model Manager](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html).

## Relationship to auto model downloading

Earlier releases had a server-side `allow_auto_model_downloading` session flag that made the *server* silently fetch a model mid-`CreateAgent`. That flag has been removed — model registration is now the only way to acquire models deliberately. This guard is the editor-side replacement: it catches the same "model referenced but never downloaded" case, earlier, and with a clear prompt instead of a silent multi-gigabyte download hidden inside a normal request.

Editor-only in both engines — packaged/Standalone builds never run this code, since they bundle Production models at build time and never download at runtime.

## Related

- [How-to: Manage Models in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html) — where registrations live and how to fix a missing model manually.
- [How-to: Use Your Own Local Model](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-your-own-local-model.html) — non-downloadable models.

# Estimate the RAM and VRAM Your Setup Needs

Work out, before you ship, roughly how much **system RAM** and **GPU VRAM** a given model line-up will use — so you can pick models that fit your target hardware and avoid out-of-memory surprises on a player's machine. After you load the line-up, [Inspect Server Memory](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/inspect-server-memory.html) is the live check against this recipe.

Prerequisites

- The models you plan to use, listed in `models.json` (each has a download size you can read — see [Use Your Own Local Model](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/use-your-own-local-model.html)).
- A rough idea of your context length (how long conversations get).

## What uses RAM vs. VRAM

With GPU offload on (the default), the four things that cost memory split cleanly:

| What                                | RAM (system)                     | VRAM (GPU)                          | Scales with                     |
| ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| **Language model weights**          | ≈ download size                  | ≈ download size                     | model file size                 |
| **KV cache** (conversation context) | negligible                       | **large — hundreds of MB to ~2 GB** | context length × model          |
| **Embedding model** (for RAG)       | tens of MB                       | tens of MB                          | model file size (small)         |
| **STT / Sherpa TTS** (voice in/out) | ≈ 1–2× download size             | **none**                            | model file size                 |
| **SNAC TTS** (Orpheus, Maya1)       | ≈ download size + ~50 MB decoder | ≈ download size if offloaded        | GGUF size (llama.cpp placement) |

Two facts do most of the work:

- **Weights cost the same in both RAM and VRAM.** A GGUF model is memory-mapped (counts as RAM) *and* offloaded to the GPU (counts as VRAM), so a 4 GB model occupies ~4 GB of *each*. See [Models and Inference Engines](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/models-and-inference-engines.html).
- **Sherpa voice models live in RAM only** in the shipped plugin payload, which has no CUDA ONNX Runtime. Speech-to-text and Sherpa text-to-speech (Supertonic, Pocket TTS) then run on the CPU, so they add **zero VRAM** — only system RAM. (A source build with `TRYLL_ONNX_RUNTIME_CUDA=ON` can put STT, or TTS with an explicit `vram` placement hint, on the GPU.) llama.cpp SNAC voices (Orpheus, Maya1) are GGUF backbones: they follow the same RAM/VRAM placement as a language model, plus a ~50 MB CPU decoder.

## The recipe

**VRAM** ≈ (sum of language + embedding model download sizes) + a **KV-cache allowance**.

- KV allowance is the part that grows with conversation length. As a rough guide on a Q4 model: budget **~0.7 GB** for short/RAG-style turns and up to **~1.5–2 GB** for long multi-turn dialogs. Each language-model node pays for its own window: `Generate` / `GenerateAndSpeak` default to the variant or server `default_n_ctx` (commonly 8192); `ClassifyIntentLLM` and `ToolCall` default to
- Count those per-node windows separately — a classifier at 2048 is a small slice of an 8192 generator.

**RAM** ≈ (language model download size) + (STT size + TTS size, each ×~1.5 if you use Sherpa voice) + a few hundred MB of runtime overhead. For Orpheus or Maya1, add the GGUF download size the same way you would a language model, plus ~50 MB for the shared SNAC decoder.

- The language model's weights show up in *both* budgets (mmap); that is expected, not double-counting a leak.

Look up each model's **download size** — the table in [Built-in model sizes](#built-in-model-sizes) below lists the measured sizes. (The raw numbers come from the `downloads.json` manifest. The editor **Model Manager** window also surfaces each model's size once it is downloaded — see [Manage Models in the Editor](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/manage-models-in-editor.html); the catalog file `models.json` lists *which* models exist but not their size.) That download size is the number you plug in.

## Built-in model sizes

Measured on-disk sizes of the downloaded models, taken from the `downloads.json` manifest (exact bytes, rounded here). Use these as the per-model number in the recipe above. Language and embedding sizes count toward **both** RAM and VRAM; STT, VAD, and Sherpa TTS (Supertonic, Pocket TTS) sizes count toward **RAM only**. Orpheus and Maya1 count like a language model.

| Orpheus 3B FT (Q4_K_M)       | ≈ 2.0 GB      |
| Maya1 3B (i1-Q4_K_M)         | 2.1 GB        |

RAM/VRAM reminder

For STT and Sherpa TTS, the *runtime* RAM is roughly 1–2× the download size (the speech runtime allocates working buffers on top of the model file). For language and embedding models — and the Orpheus/Maya1 GGUF voices — the weights occupy ≈ the download size in **each** of RAM and VRAM (mmap + GPU offload).

## Worked example

A voice NPC: **Llama 3.1 8B** (≈4.9 GB) for chat, **All-MiniLM-L6-v2** (≈21 MB) for RAG retrieval, and **Supertonic 3 (int8)** (≈145 MB) for speech output, with moderately long conversations.

| Budget   | Calculation                                                  | Total        |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------ |
| **VRAM** | 4.9 GB (weights) + 0.02 GB (embedding) + ~1.0 GB (KV)        | **≈ 5.9 GB** |
| **RAM**  | 4.9 GB (weights, mmap) + ~0.3 GB (Supertonic TTS) + overhead | **≈ 5.5 GB** |

So this NPC wants a **6 GB+ GPU** and comfortably runs in **8 GB system RAM**. Swapping to a 3B model (≈2.0 GB) drops the VRAM need to **~3 GB**.

## Verify on your hardware

Estimates get you in the ballpark; the real number depends on your GPU, driver, and context length. To confirm, run your agent and watch the process:

- **Windows:** Task Manager → *Details* tab → add the **GPU Memory (dedicated)** and **Memory (working set)** columns for `tryll_server.exe`. Or use Performance Monitor's `GPU Process Memory \ Dedicated Usage`.
- Drive a few realistic, long conversations — the **peak** during the longest dialog is what you must fit, since the KV cache is largest then.

## Common pitfalls

- **Forgetting the KV cache.** Weights are only part of the VRAM bill; a long conversation can add ~1–2 GB on top. Size for your *longest* expected dialog.
- **Assuming every voice is VRAM-free.** In the shipped payload, speech-to-text and the Sherpa voices (Supertonic 3, Pocket TTS) run on the CPU and use **no VRAM** — a bigger one costs RAM, not GPU. Orpheus and Maya1 are different: they are 3B llama.cpp GGUF models and follow the same RAM/VRAM/Auto placement as a language model, so budget them like one (only their ~50 MB SNAC decoder stays on the CPU). See [Choose Where Models Run](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/choose-where-models-run.html).
- **Pinned models never freeing.** A [pinned](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/pin-and-unpin-models.html) model stays resident for the whole server lifetime. If you pin several, their footprints add up — budget for all pinned models at once, not one at a time.
- **CPU-only builds.** Without GPU offload, weights *and* KV cache live in **RAM** instead of VRAM — shift those numbers from the VRAM column to the RAM column.
- **Multiple `Generate` nodes / agents.** Each model context carries its own KV cache; two agents on the same model still pay two KV caches.

# Ship Storage Folders for Builds

Tryll nodes that use relative `string_storage` or `embedded_string_storage` paths need those files readable by the **server process** at runtime. The storage root is **process-wide**: the launcher sets it at startup (`--storage-root`). Sessions no longer send `storage_data_folder`.

Default for Unity and Unreal projects: **`<Project>/TryllStorage/`**, outside `Assets/` and `Content/`. See the deployment-modes contract in the contributor docs if you need every mode rule.

## File layout conventions

```
your_game/
  TryllStorage/
    responses/
      refusal_lines.txt          # CannedResponse — List kind
      polite_reject.txt
    intent/
      npc_instructions.json      # IntentToInstruction — Map kind
    rag/
      adventure_quests.json      # EmbeddedStringStorage config (Path A)
      adventure_quests.kb.json   # records file
      adventure_quests.usearch   # optional pre-built HNSW index
    models/                      # Client Dev downloads land here (created if missing)
    hotwords/
      wake_words.txt             # voice hotwords — List kind
```

Node params reference files **relative to the storage root**:

```
string_storage          = "responses/refusal_lines.txt"
embedded_string_storage = "rag/adventure_quests.json"
hotwords_storage_path   = "hotwords/wake_words.txt"
```

### File formats

| Extension             | Kind                          | Format                                                                                |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.txt`                | List                          | UTF-8 text, one value per line. Lines starting with `#` and blank lines are skipped.  |
| `.json`               | Map                           | JSON array of `{"id": "key", "text": "value"}` objects.                               |
| `.mm.json`            | Multimap                      | Same format as Map; duplicate keys allowed.                                           |
| `.json` *(KB config)* | EmbeddedStringStorage config  | JSON object with `embedding_model`, `records_file`, and optional `index_file` fields. |
| `.kb.json`            | EmbeddedStringStorage records | JSON array of `{"id": "…", "text": "…", "metadata": {…}}` objects.                    |
| `.usearch`            | HNSW index                    | Binary file produced by the server on first load; ship it to avoid rebuild overhead.  |

Translations ship with the folder

Localized content lives in `loc/<language>/` folders beside the files they translate, so anything that copies the storage folder already carries them. If you filter what gets staged, make sure the filter keeps `**/loc/**` — a missing translation folder degrades silently to the default language rather than failing the build. See [Ship an Agent in Another Language](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/ship-in-another-language.html).

## Setting the storage root

The **server** owns the root. Clients configure the launcher; they do not send a per-session path on `CreateSession`.

Set **Project Settings → Tryll Client → Storage Data Folder**. Default `TryllStorage` (project-relative, outside `Assets/`). A path under `Assets/` is rejected. The editor launches the server with `--storage-root` pointing at that folder.

Set **Project Settings → Plugins → Tryll Client → Storage Data Folder**. Default `TryllStorage` (outside `Content/`). A path under `Content/` is rejected. The plugin passes `--storage-root` on auto-launch.

Pass `--storage-root` when you start the server, or set `storage_root` in `server-config.json`. Managed launchers expose project name, project directory, and storage root options.

## Platform-specific packaging

### Unity

Keep authored content in `<Project>/TryllStorage/` — **not** under `Assets/StreamingAssets/`. Unity would copy StreamingAssets with no model filter and would create `.meta` files for every download and derived index.

At build time `TryllServerBuildPostprocessor` copies the storage tree into `<Game>_Data/StreamingAssets/Tryll/` in the **build output**, filtering models by the Production manifest. It never writes into your project's `Assets/`.

Player storage root: `Application.streamingAssetsPath/Tryll`.

Players are unreleasable for now

Packaged players still launch the Client Dev server until a Client Prod binary ships. Do not ship those builds to end users yet.

Android / WebGL

`streamingAssetsPath` on Android is inside a `.jar` and on WebGL it requires HTTP access — neither is readable as a filesystem path by an external server process. For those targets you will need a custom extraction step or a bundled server.

### Unreal

Keep authored content in `<Project>/TryllStorage/` — **not** under `Content/`. The server cannot read Unreal `.pak` archives, and staging whole `Content/` folders has no per-model filter.

`TryllClient.Build.cs` walks the storage directory and stages each file as **NonUFS** under `$(ProjectDir)/TryllStorage/`, filtering models by the Production manifest. You do not need *Additional Non-Asset Directories to Copy* for Tryll content.

Packaged storage root: `<packaged project dir>/TryllStorage/` (project dir, not the exe folder).

Players are unreleasable for now

Same Client Dev temporary launch as Unity. Do not ship those builds to end users yet.

### C++ / Python (desktop)

Ship the storage folder beside your server config:

```
your_app/
  tryll_server.exe
  data/
    server-config.json     # optional storage_root; or pass --storage-root
  TryllStorage/
    responses/…
    rag/…
    models/…
```

```
{
    "storage_root": "../TryllStorage"
}
```

Or pass `--storage-root` on the command line (CLI wins over config).

## Verification

1. Check that `CreateAgentRequest` succeeds without `3010 StorageFileNotFound`.
1. Enable `log_level: "debug"` in `server-config.json` to see path-resolution log lines at node-create time.
1. If you receive `3009 StorageOutsideRoot`, the path escapes the configured root — check that the path is relative and contains no `..` components.

# Compare Tool-Call Models

Pick a catalog model for a `ToolCall` node using measured exact accuracy, not parameter count. Two models with the same overall score can be strong and weak in opposite places — the tables below are for choosing by *job*, not for crowning a winner.

Everything here is greedy decoding (temperature 0, seed 42) on the shipped tool-call catalog. Temperature 0.3 and 0.7 move the field by about a point; use greedy numbers unless you already know you will sample hotter in game.

How a case is scored

Exact accuracy: the call matches the expected tool name and every argument, or the model correctly calls nothing. No partial credit, no judge model. Constrained decoding holds the syntax; these numbers are about *which* tool and *which* arguments.

## Which table to read

| Your tools look like…                                      | Read                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Game commands, NPC actuation, log queries, trading         | [Tryll-authored suites](#tryll-authored-suites) |
| Generic APIs, several tools at once, "don't call anything" | [BFCL slice](#bfcl-slice)                       |

The two corpora do **not** rank models the same way. NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B leads the authored suites and sits in a pack on BFCL. Llama 3.1 8B is usable on authored command parsing and collapses on BFCL parallel cases. Read the corpus that matches the shape of *your* tools.

Catalog models whose `tool_call_support` is `unsupported` are not in these tables. That catalog label is advisory, not the check: `CreateAgent` inspects the model's chat template and rejects a `ToolCall` node with [3003 `GraphCompilationFailed`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/error-codes.html#3xxx-agent) when the template does not render tool definitions. See [Not every model can call tools](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html#not-every-model-can-call-tools).

### Shape matters more than the average

Pass rate per suite, pooled across three temperatures, for four models chosen because their *profiles* differ. Outer ring is 100%.

Bonsai 8B (Q1_0) is the argument for not shipping on the headline number alone. It is near-perfect on both command-parsing suites and near the floor on `servant_room` and `merchant_bargain`. Given a radio command it is a top-tier model; given a conversation to read it is not.

### Pick a job, then a model

If you already know the kind of tool you are shipping, read that column, not the average. Figures are greedy, cases passed / cases in the suite.

| Model                  | Commands (20) | Game log (20) | NPC reaction (20) |
| ---------------------- | ------------- | ------------- | ----------------- |
| NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B | 20 / 20       | 19 / 20       | 20 / 20           |
| Ministral 3 14B        | 20 / 20       | 19 / 20       | 19 / 20           |
| Qwen 3.5 4B            | 18 / 20       | 19 / 20       | 16 / 20           |
| Qwen2.5 7B             | 19 / 20       | 18 / 20       | 16 / 20           |
| Bonsai 8B (Q1_0)       | 20 / 20       | 18 / 20       | 9 / 20            |
| Llama 3.1 8B           | 17 / 20       | 12 / 20       | 14 / 20           |
| Llama 3.2 1B           | 14 / 20       | 7 / 20        | 2 / 20            |

- **Commands** is `heist_command_per_action` — several tools with different parameter shapes, player speech mapped onto a fixed vocabulary.
- **Game log** is `game_log_query` — two tools, four filters, the player never names every slot. The hardest authored suite, and the closest to a companion that looks things up.
- **NPC reaction** is `npc_reaction` — zero-argument tools. Nothing is scored except the decision (attack, trade, follow, leave, or stay quiet). This is the floor of the authored corpus.

A worked example: you want a companion that answers "where did I last see the orc?" by calling a query tool. Read **Game log**, not the overall column. Orchestrator, Ministral 14B, and Qwen 3.5 4B are 19 / 20 there; Llama 3.1 8B is 12 / 20 even though it is an 8B model.

For the schema and prompt shape that suite uses, see [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html).

| Qwen2.5 7B Instruct (Q4_K_M)          | 79.3%          |
| Qwen2.5 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)          | 77.3%          |
| Qwen 3.5 2B (Q4_K_M)                  | 72.7%          |
| Bonsai 27B (Q1_0 1-bit)               | 69.0%          |
| Mistral 7B Instruct (Q4_K_M)          | 62.0%          |
| Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct (Q4_K_M)        | 53.7%          |
| Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (Q4_K_M)        | 46.3%          |
| Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)        | 29.3%          |
| Llama 3.2 1B Instruct (Q4_K_M)        | 10.0%          |

Eleven models sit between 82% and 85%. Below that the field drops off, and **parallel** is what does it: one utterance that should produce several calls. Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.2 3B, and Llama 3.2 1B score **0 / 54** parallel cases. Bonsai 27B is 10 / 54 there, which is why a 27B model ranks sixteenth on this corpus and near the top of the authored one.

If your game issues one tool per player line, BFCL parallel is the wrong number to optimise for. If a single line must open every door, it is the right one — and you need `parallel_tool_calls = true` on the node as well.

______________________________________________________________________

## What these numbers do not tell you

- **VRAM and RAM.** An 8B Q4 and a 27B 1-bit are different machines. See [Estimate memory footprint](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html).
- **Whether the template can render tools at all.** That is a fail-fast at `CreateAgent`, not a score.
- **Multi-turn tool use.** Both corpora are single-turn.
- **Your prompt and your schema.** A model that scores 19 / 20 on the game-log suite still fails if your own tool has five required filters and no name for "unfiltered". Shape the schema first — [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html).

## Related

- [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html)
- [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html)
- [Concept: Tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html)
- [Estimate memory footprint](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/estimate-memory-footprint.html)

# Design a Tool-Call Prompt

How to write the tool schema and the `ToolCall` node's `system_prompt` so a small on-device model fills the right slots — and leaves the others alone.

The recipes come from iterating the Tryll-authored tool-call suites against the catalog (twenty models, greedy decoding). The finding that paid off was not cleverer prose. It was changing what the model is *asked to say*.

Tryll does not let you pick a tool-call format. The model's chat template renders the schema you declare. Your levers are the tool list, the parameter names and types, the descriptions, and the system prompt. A tool on the `ToolCall` node has a `name`, a `description`, and `parameters`; each parameter has only a `name`, a `type`, and a `description`. There is no `enum` field and no optional flag: the node marks every declared parameter as required in the schema it renders, so allowed values go in the parameter's `description`. See [Tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html).

How claims are marked

- **Tested** — measured on the authored suites; the effect repeated across the catalog.
- **Hint** — real, but narrower: one suite, or a design rule rather than a score delta.
- **No effect / made it worse** — we tried it; do not spend time here.

______________________________________________________________________

## The failure that looks like a knowledge gap

Small models extract a filter the player *did* name very reliably. They fail at restraint. Asked "where did I see the orc?" with optional `region` / `event_type` / `time_window`, they invent a region rather than omit the argument — and they invent the **first allowed value listed**.

On the game-log suite that pattern was the bulk of the error: specified filters were right about 97% of the time; an unspecified `region` was wrong 63% of the time, and `Ironwood` (then the first region listed) beat the other three regions 51 to 7. That is slot-filling pressure, not geography.

The same pressure shows up as a guessed door (`left`, the first door listed) when the player said "lock the door" without saying which.

______________________________________________________________________

## Recipe 1 — name "unfiltered", put it first, require the slot

**Tested.** This is the change that moved the field.

Do not ask the model to *omit* a parameter. Give "the player did not narrow this down" a real value, list it first among the allowed values, and keep the parameter required — which the `ToolCall` node does for every declared parameter. The thing a pressured model reaches for becomes the right answer.

Across the catalog, adding `any` this way took the game-log suite from 46% to 77% exact accuracy. The three fields that gained `any` dropped from 44–63% wrong (when they should have been unfiltered) to roughly the error rate the models already had on filters they were told to set.

```
from tryll_client.graph import ToolDefinition, ToolParamDefinition

search_events = ToolDefinition(
    name="search_events",
    description="Find matching events in the activity log.",
    parameters=[
        ToolParamDefinition(name="entity", type="string",
            description='Who or what the question is about. '
                        'Pass "any" when the player did not name one.'),
        ToolParamDefinition(name="event_type", type="string",
            description='Kind of logged event: one of "any", "kill", "sighting", '
                        '"dialogue", "loot", "quest". '
                        'Pass "any" when the player did not imply one.'),
        ToolParamDefinition(name="region", type="string",
            description='Where it happened: one of "any", "Ironwood", "Riverwood", '
                        '"Karhold", "Gutter Ward". '
                        'Pass "any" when the player did not name a place.'),
        ToolParamDefinition(name="time_window", type="string",
            description='When it happened: one of "any", "today", "last_session", '
                        '"last_week". Pass "any" when the player did not give a time.'),
    ],
)
```

The node renders each tool for the chat template as a JSON schema with `type` and `description` per property and all four names in `required`.

The system prompt has to say the same thing the schema does:

```
Every call sets all four filters. When the player did not narrow one down,
pass `any`. That is the correct value, not a fallback — `any` means "do not
filter on this". Never guess a region, a time window, or a subject the player
did not mention.
```

The same pattern applies to actuation: lead the door and window value lists with `unspecified` (both parameters are required, like every declared parameter), and tell the servant that "unspecified" is the right answer when the master did not say which.

Your client then treats `any` / `unspecified` as "no filter / ask which one", instead of hoping the model leaves a JSON key out.

______________________________________________________________________

## Recipe 2 — do not add a parameter you can live without

**Tested. Made it worse.**

"Where did I *last* see the orc?" is not expressible if the tool has no "most recent" knob. Adding a required `sort` argument so that line could be answered made every model we re-ran *worse* — not only on the new slot, but on the four existing filters. Counts on four models: 19→18, 19→15, 18→12, 15→9 out of 20.

Each extra required parameter adds to the pressure to fill every slot. Four filters was the ceiling on that suite, not an arbitrary choice. Rename tricks did not help either: swapping `last_session` so the word "last" would stop pulling a time window changed nothing. A query with no "last" in it still drew a time filter.

If a distinction cannot be said without a fifth argument, prefer a slightly wrong query over a schema the model cannot fill. Keep the tool list short for the same reason — see [What makes tool calls reliable](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html#what-makes-tool-calls-reliable-or-unreliable).

______________________________________________________________________

## Recipe 3 — do not forbid the call you want

**Tested.**

A prompt that says "never call a tool with every parameter unspecified" will be obeyed — including on the line whose correct call is exactly `operate_window(unspecified, unspecified)` ("Do something about that window"). Half the field answered in character instead of calling, which is what we asked for and then scored as a miss.

Write the exception where you mean it: greetings and questions get no call; a vague *order* still gets a call, with `unspecified` filled in. Put that in the system prompt next to the rule for `unspecified`, not as a blanket ban.

______________________________________________________________________

## Recipe 4 — split tools on intent, not on wording

**Hint.**

Three tools that sound alike need a rule the model can apply in one step:

- `propose_price` — they named a figure.
- `request_discount` — they want a lower price and named no figure.
- `refuse_deal` — they are walking away ("No deal.", "Forget it.").

"Not at that price, no." is not a refusal in that scheme — it is a discount request with no number. If you cannot say in one sentence why a line maps to exactly one tool, do not score it, and do not ship it as a distinct tool. Ambiguous splits train you to argue with the eval; they do not make the runtime call more reliable.

Parameterless classifier tools (`attack_player`, `start_trading`, `end_dialogue`) are a different job again. Models that extract arguments well still decline to fire a zero-argument tool and answer in character instead. That is capability, not missing instructions — every suite already tells the model when *not* to call. See [Compare tool-call models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html#pick-a-job-then-a-model) for which catalog models hold up on that flavour.

______________________________________________________________________

## Recipe 5 — descriptions are the prompt the model actually sees

**Hint** — this is also the concept-page advice; the eval did not contradict it.

The chat template inlines your `description` strings next to the JSON schema. "Pass `any` when the player did not name a place" on the `region` field does more than a long character biography in `system_prompt`. Keep the system prompt for routing (which tool, when to stay quiet) and put slot-filling rules on the slots.

Use `temperature = 0` on the `ToolCall` node. Sampling is not a meaningful lever here; both corpora move about a point from greedy to 0.7.

______________________________________________________________________

## What not to do

| Temptation                                                              | What happened                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Declare a parameter with no sentinel and hope the model "just omits it" | Every declared parameter is required, and models fill the first listed value. |
| Put the sentinel last in the value list (`…, "unspecified"`)            | The guessed value is still the first one listed.                              |
| Add `sort` / extra filters so every English distinction is expressible  | Accuracy fell on the new slot *and* the old ones.                             |
| Rename values to dodge a word in the utterance                          | No change.                                                                    |
| Ban "all unspecified" in the prompt to stop chit-chat from calling      | It also stops the vague order you wanted.                                     |

Abstention ("Hello", "Nice weather") is mostly model quality. A clear do-not-call line in the prompt is necessary and not sufficient; weaker models still grab a tool whose argument matches a noun in the sentence.

______________________________________________________________________

- [Compare tool-call models](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/compare-tool-call-models.html)
- [Define and handle tool calls](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/define-and-handle-tool-calls.html)
- [Design an NPC prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-npc-prompt.html) — the same "measure, then write" approach for spoken dialogue
- [Concept: Tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html)

# Fix Tool-Call Text in Answers

What to check when the player sees a tool call instead of dialogue. A chat bubble reads like this:

```
<|tool_call>call:get_price{items:<|"|>Sushi<|"|>,player_offer:<|"|><|"|>}<tool_call|>
```

That is the model's own tool-call syntax — Gemma 4 in this example; on Mistral-family models the reply starts with `[TOOL_CALLS]`. It usually comes with this server warning:

```
[warning] [answer] stripped unknown native TTS tag '<|tool_call>' from audio input; original text is unchanged
```

The name in brackets (`answer`) is the node that produced the text. The warning means the voice skipped the markup. The chat text still contains it, so the bubble shows it.

The text can come from three places, and each has a different fix. The diagnostics for the turn tell you which one you have.

Prerequisites

- The agent was created with `enable_diagnostics = true`. In the editor, open the turn in the [turn inspector](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/turn-inspector.html); elsewhere, read `TurnComplete.debug_info` ([Turn Diagnostics JSON](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/turn-diagnostics-json.html)).
- The graph has a [`ToolCall`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/tool-call.html) node, or a prompt that mentions a tool.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Find the node that wrote the text

In `debug_info.nodes[]`, find the entry whose `diagnostics.output.text` is the bubble. Its `_type` and a few fields beside it tell you which case this is:

| The text is on                             | And you also see                                                                                                                       | Case                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A `GenerateNode` or `GenerateAndSpeakNode` | `engine.chat_turn.tool_count: 0`                                                                                                       | [A speech node wrote a call](#2-a-speech-node-wrote-a-call)                   |
| A `ToolCallNode`                           | `output.parse_fallback: true`, `output.parse_failure: malformed_call`, `parameters.mode: call_or_answer`, `exit_route: no_tool_called` | [The tool node sent an unparsed call](#3-the-tool-node-sent-an-unparsed-call) |
| Either, on this turn and earlier ones      | An `assistant` message in `input.prompt[]` whose `content` is the markup                                                               | [The markup is in history](#4-the-markup-is-in-history) — fix A or B first    |

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. A speech node wrote a call

This is the common case. A `Generate` or `GenerateAndSpeak` node has no tools and no grammar (`tool_count: 0`, `has_grammar: false`), so it cannot call anything. It wrote the call as dialogue because its prompt asked it to.

Two things are usually true together:

- **The speech prompt tells the model to call the tool.** A line such as "Call get_price with the requested items" belongs on the `ToolCall` node. The speech node also sees earlier turns' real calls in its history, rendered in the model's tool syntax, so it has a template to copy.
- **The turn skipped the tool node.** Look at the nodes before the speech node. Often a classifier exited `not_found`, or the graph took a branch that does not pass through the `ToolCall` node. The speech node then gets the full trade procedure and no tool result.

For a [`ClassifyIntentLLM`](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/nodes/classify-intent-llm.html) gate, `output.classification` says why it missed:

| `not_found_reason` | Meaning                                           | Usual fix                                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `below_threshold`  | The top label's `top_prob` was under `threshold`. | Two labels claim the same line — make the descriptions disagree. Then set `threshold` from real `top_prob` values. |
| `below_margin`     | Top and second label were closer than `margin`.   | The same overlap. Add "— not …" clauses rather than lowering `margin`.                                             |

A short "yes" is the usual culprit: "yes, show me prices" and "yes, I agree to that price" split the probability, so neither label clears the gate.

**Fix:**

1. **Take tool instructions out of the speech prompt.** Tell the speech node how to use a result that is already in the conversation, and what to say when there is none:

   ```
   If the conversation contains a price returned for the item, quote it exactly.
   If it does not, do not state a price — name the goods, or ask which item the
   player means.
   ```

1. **Give `not_found` its own speech node.** Wire the classifier's `not_found_exit` to a `Generate` / `GenerateAndSpeak` node whose prompt has no trade procedure and no tool name. A missed classification then produces a clarifying line instead of a call.

1. **Fix the labels** as in the table above. See [Design an intent-classifier prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-an-intent-classifier-prompt.html).

A classifier has only `found` and `not_found` exits. It does not route by label. If only some intents need the tool (a price question does, "what do you have?" does not), put a classifier whose only job is "does this line need the tool?" directly in front of the `ToolCall` node. Set its `not_found_intent` to the "no" label, so those lines exit `not_found` and skip the tool.

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. The tool node sent an unparsed call

The `ToolCall` node ran, and the model tried to call the tool, but the output could not be parsed as a call. `output.parse_fallback: true` means exactly that: the parse failed, **no call was recorded**, and `output.text` holds the raw output. The node exits `no_tool_called`.

What happens to that raw text depends on `mode`:

| `mode`                     | Raw text                                                                        |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `call_or_answer` (default) | Sent to the client as the answer and stored in history. **This is the bubble.** |
| `detect_only`              | Not sent. The node exits `no_tool_called` silently.                             |
| `require_call`             | Not sent. The turn continues with no tool result.                               |

Two fields next to `parse_fallback` say why the parse failed:

- **`output.parse_failure`** — `malformed_call` when the output contains the model's tool-call marker but the call does not parse. That is this case. `no_call` means the model answered in prose instead, which is not a leak.
- **`output.parse_error`** — where the parser gave up: a byte offset into `output.text` and the text from there on. The offset is usually the start of the call that failed, so `unparsed from byte 0` means the first call is already broken.

Read the call that starts at that offset. Common signs:

- Two calls glued together while `parallel_tool_calls` is `false`.
- A string closed with ordinary quotes (`"""`) instead of the model's quote token (Gemma 4's `<|"|>`).
- A required argument missing, or values the prompt never mentioned.

**Fix:**

1. If a separate speech node answers after `no_tool_called`, set `mode = detect_only`, so a failed parse is never shown to the player.
1. Set `temperature = 0` in the `ToolCall` node's `sampling`, the recommended setting for tool calls. A node left at `temperature = 1` samples freely inside the call as well as around it.
1. Make the schema easier to fill: fewer arguments, enums for known values, and a real sentinel (`none`, `any`) instead of an empty string. See [Design a tool-call prompt](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/design-a-tool-call-prompt.html).

Without diagnostics, the server log carries the same reason after `[LlamaCppChatTurn] tool-call parse failed, returning raw content:`.

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. The markup is in history

Each leaked bubble is stored as an assistant message (unless the node's `history_role` is `None`). On later turns it appears in `input.prompt[]` as an `assistant` entry whose `content` is the markup and which has **no** `tool_calls` array:

```
{ "role": "assistant", "content": "<|tool_call>call:get_price{items:[<|\"|>Sushi<|\"|>]}<tool_call|>" }
```

A real historical call looks different — empty `content` and a `tool_calls` array:

```
{ "role": "assistant", "content": "",
  "tool_calls": [ { "id": "c00000002", "name": "get_price", "arguments_json": "{\"items\":\"Sushi\"}" } ] }
```

Every saved bubble shows the model again that tool syntax is an acceptable reply, so leaks get more frequent as the conversation goes on. After fixing the cause, remove the leaked turns — see [Seed and edit dialog history](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/seed-and-edit-dialog-history.html) — or start a fresh conversation to test.

______________________________________________________________________

## Do not filter the markup out

The [output filter](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/filter-llm-output-artifacts.html) has no rule for tool-call markup, and deleting the tags in your client only hides the symptom:

- The turn still has no tool result, so the player still gets no price.
- The server has already stored the reply with the markup, so the next turn's prompt still contains it.

Fix the prompt, the routing, or the tool node.

______________________________________________________________________

- [Concept: Tool calling](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/concepts/tool-calling.html) — `mode`, `require_call` and history projection

# Localize Prompts with Your Localization System

Store a prompt as a Text ID in the localization system you already ship, and have Unity or Unreal resolve it to plain text before the agent is created. The server still receives a string. There is no Tryll string table.

## 1. Tick Localized and set the table

On a workflow asset, set **Text Table** to the table that holds your prompts. On each prompt field (system prompt, template, instruction, acknowledge text, TTS delivery instruction, and a ClassifyIntent entry's prompt), tick **Localize text**. The box is then a Text ID, for example `tobin.system`. The inline text stays in the asset; only the resolved string is sent.

Leave the box unticked when that field should stay inline. A Summarize template that already says `Write in {{language}}` is a good candidate to leave inline: the session language fills the key, and the template itself does not need a translation.

Give prompt authors their own table, and keep it out of machine translation. A prompt is instructions to a model, not UI copy. Tryll does not enforce that split.

## 2. Point the project at a text provider

The provider answers `GetText(table, id)` and reports the game's current language. When one is set, that language is the session language unless you pass a locale into `CreateSession`. An empty string passed in still means no session language.

### Unity

Assign a `TryllTextProviderAsset` under **Project Settings → Tryll Client → Text Provider**. The same asset is used in the editor preview and in Play.

- **Unity Localization** (`com.unity.localization`), when that package is installed: create a **Unity Localization Text Provider**. Tryll reads the raw table entry. Turn Smart String formatting off for prompt entries. `{}` placeholders and Mustache `{{ }}` must not be nested in the same string; a Smart String would format the braces before the server sees the Mustache tags.
- **JSON Text Provider**, for a demo or a prototype: one JSON `TextAsset` per language, each a flat object `{ "id": "text" }`. Lookup tries the current locale, then the language subtag (`de-DE` then `de`), then the first other file that has the key. That last step uses another language, so it logs a warning once per key. A file that is not valid JSON logs an error with the line and column, and the inspector shows the same reason. Call `SetLocale("de")` to switch at runtime; the asset's **Locale** field is the start language and does not change in Play mode.
- **Your own class**: implement `ITryllTextProvider`. A code-only provider works in Play. The inspector preview also needs `ITryllTextProviderEditor` (`ListLocales`, `ListIds`, `GetTextForPreview`, `OpenInEditor`). Without that, the field says it has no editor support.

A provider set on `TryllClient.TextProvider` from code wins over the settings asset. Setting that property to null turns resolution off even when the settings asset has a provider.

Raise `LocaleChanged` on the main thread. Tryll sends requests from that event.

I2 Localization, in about ten lines:

```
public sealed class I2TryllTextProvider : TryllTextProviderAsset
{
    public override string CurrentLocale => I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.CurrentLanguageCode;

    public override Task<string> GetTextAsync(string table, string id)
    {
        string text = I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.GetTranslation(id);
        return Task.FromResult(string.IsNullOrEmpty(text) ? null : text);
    }

    void OnEnable() => I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.OnLocalizeEvent += RaiseLocaleChanged;
    void OnDisable() => I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.OnLocalizeEvent -= RaiseLocaleChanged;
}
```

Shared snippets (`{{text.some_id}}` inside a prompt) are the provider's job in this version. Resolve them before you return the string.

### Unreal

**Project Settings → Tryll Client → Text Provider** is **None** by default, so the Tryll **Locale** field sets the session language, as before. Pick `UTryllStringTableTextProvider` to resolve Text IDs from Unreal String Tables. It reads `FText::FromStringTable` and follows the game culture. While it is set, that culture is the session language and wins over the **Locale** field.

Pick the workflow's **Text Table** with the String Table asset picker. The asset reference makes the cooker package the table, and Tryll loads it before the first lookup, so a table that nothing else uses still works in a packaged game. A custom `UTryllTextProvider` subclass may ignore the table and use only the key. Implement `GetText` and `GetCurrentLocale`, and call `UTryllSubsystem::NotifyTextLocaleChanged` when the language changes. Override `SupportsEditorPreview` when the details panel should show a preview.

Test a runtime language switch with **Play → Standalone Game**, not in the viewport. Play in Editor shares one culture with the editor, so `SetCurrentCulture` switches the editor's own language too, and the editor loads no game translations unless `Localization.ForceLoadGameLocalizationInEditor` is set.

### C++, Python, and Java

Those clients have no provider seam. Resolve the string in your game and assign it:

```
params->SystemPrompt = Loc.Get(TEXT("bartender.system"));
```

```
p.system_prompt = loc.get("bartender.system")
```

## 3. Check the texts before you play

Under a ticked field the inspector shows a key list (typing a new key is allowed), **Open**, and a language switcher.

- **Found** — the first lines of the entry, with `{{ }}` marked.
- **Missing in this language** — red. A fallback from another language is shown and marked as fallback. Language fallback is the provider's job; Tryll does not invent one at send time.
- **Missing in some languages** — yellow. **Check texts** is the full matrix across every language the provider lists.
- **Empty ID** — red, "Enter a Text ID".
- **No editor provider** — grey. The runtime provider has no preview API.

**Check texts** on the workflow runs every Text ID against every language the provider lists. A missing cell is red.

Creation fails on the client before anything is sent when a ticked field has an empty ID, no provider is set, the provider returns no text, or the provider throws. The error names the asset, node, field, table, and ID (`InvalidParamValue`, 3007). There is no silent fallback to the inline string.

`ChangeParams` follows the same rules. Params with a ticked field are resolved first, so you can change a Text ID at runtime. With an asynchronous provider, the change can reach the server a frame later.

A Dialog Lab override on a ticked field is the text under test: it wins, and the field is unticked for that run.

Resolved text is plain text. The server's existing checks still apply: Mustache, `{{intents_block}}`, and the rest.

## 4. Change language on a live agent

When the provider raises its language-changed event, Tryll sets the session locale and re-resolves ticked fields that are not structural, then sends `ChangeAgentParam` for each live agent. A turn that is still running returns `AgentBusy` (3004); the update is sent when the turn ends, before your turn-complete handler runs. `AgentBusy` here is expected and is not reported as an error.

- **Your runtime changes stay.** The update starts from the agent's current params, so values you set with `ChangeParams` are kept. Only nodes whose text changed are sent.
- **One agent is all or nothing.** If any Text ID of an agent is missing in the new language, nothing is sent to that agent, and it keeps its previous prompts in full. Unity raises `TryllClient.LocalizedTextFailed`; Unreal broadcasts `OnLocalizedTextFailed` on the Tryll subsystem. The session language has already changed, so recreate the agent or switch back. In Unreal, a server that rejects an update raises the same event.
- **Wait for the update before work that must see it (Unreal).** The Tryll subsystem broadcasts `OnLocalizedTextApplied`. It fires once per agent, when the server has acknowledged every prompt that changed, or right away when none changed. A busy agent gets it after its turn ends. If the language changes again before the acknowledgements arrive, only the latest change fires it. Start a KV prefill, a conversation reset, or your own `ChangeParams` from this event, not from the language change itself: those run against the old prompts if they reach the server first.
- **An agent created during the switch** is updated as soon as its creation completes.
- **An explicit session language wins.** If you passed a locale to `CreateSession`, a later provider change does not touch the session language. Prompts still follow the provider.

| Reaches a live agent                                               | Needs the agent recreated                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Voice language and the `{{language}}` keys, via the session locale | A ticked ClassifyIntent entry prompt (the `intents` list is structural) |
| Ticked non-structural prompt fields, from the next turn            | Files already bound (a knowledge base, canned lines)                    |
|                                                                    | A voice input that is already open — close it and open it again         |

There is no restart API. Recreating an agent to pick up structural text or files that are already bound is the same save-and-restore you already use for dialog state: export the dialog, destroy the agent, create it again, and import. See [Save and Load Agent State](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/save-and-load-agent-state.html).

# Ship an Agent in Another Language

Everything Tryll offers for localization, in the order you will need it: choose languages your models can serve, set one language for the session, ship translated content files, and make the model actually write in that language.

The language setting does not translate anything

Setting a language makes an NPC **speak** German. It does not make the model **write** German — that comes from your prompts, your content files, and the model you chose. Sections 4 and 5 are the load-bearing ones; skip them and you get a German voice reading English words.

## 1. Choose languages your models can serve

Open *Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Model Manager* (Unity) or the Model Manager panel (Unreal), connect, and register the models you ship. Each model's detail pane lists the languages it declares and whether it covers your project language.

Registering caches those languages into the project's model manifest — which is why the language picker and the inspector warnings keep working with no server running.

Three facts the catalog will tell you, which decide your shippable locale set:

- **Supertonic 3** speaks 31 languages from one loaded model. Switching costs nothing at runtime.
- **Pocket TTS** — the voice-*cloning* family — is **English-only**. Cloned character voices cannot go multilingual.
- The shipped **streaming** STT choices cover English, bilingual zh-en, and Russian. Other languages use an offline recognizer.

**The voice stack caps your locale set, not the language model.** A 1–4B model reads almost anything; your microphone and speaker decide what you can ship.

From code

`ListModels` reports a `languages` list per model. A language is offerable only if *every* model in your pipeline covers it, so the answer is an intersection — `TryllLanguages` (Unity) and `UTryllLanguages` (Unreal, Blueprint-callable) do that for you:

```
var (models, err) = await TryllClient.Instance.RequestListModelsAsync();
var codes = TryllLanguages.Offerable(models,
    "Supertonic 3 (int8)", "Whisper Base Multilingual (int8)");

foreach (var code in codes)
    dropdown.options.Add(new Dropdown.OptionData(
        TryllLanguages.DisplayName(code)));   // "de" → "German"
```

A model that declares nothing is skipped rather than treated as restrictive — undeclared means "the catalog didn't say", not "supports nothing". Use `HasLanguageInfo` to tell "no overlap" apart from "no data" before showing a player an empty menu.

## 2. Set the language

Pick it in *Project Settings ▸ Tryll Client ▸ Language*. The list comes from your registered models, annotated with how many catalog models can serve each one — `German (de) — 7 models` — so you can spot a language that hangs off a single model before committing to it. New projects start on English.

Every agent created afterwards uses it automatically, including agents created later in the session.

From code, you can override per session:

```
// Omit locale (pass null) and the project setting is used.
// Storage is not a session argument — the launcher sets --storage-root.
TryllClient.Instance.CreateSession(
    engines, settings.GameName, locale: "de-DE");
```

```
Subsystem->CreateSession(TEXT("my-game"), TEXT("de-DE"));

// Omit Locale to use the project setting. To explicitly opt out:
Subsystem->CreateSession(
    TEXT("my-game"), TEXT(""), /*bUseProjectLocaleWhenEmpty=*/false);
```

```
TryllClient::SessionConfig cfg;
cfg.locale = "de-DE";
client.CreateSession(cfg);
```

```
client.create_session(locale='de-DE')
```

Tags are BCP-47: `de`, `de-DE`, `pt-BR`, `zh-Hans-CN`. A malformed tag is rejected with `InvalidLocale` (2004) rather than silently ignored.

### Changing it mid-session

```
TryllClient.Instance.RequestSetSessionLocale("pt-BR");   // "" clears it
```

```
Subsystem->SetSessionLocale(TEXT("pt-BR"));              // "" clears it
```

```
client.SetSessionLocale("pt-BR");                        // "" clears it
```

```
client.set_session_locale("pt-BR")                       # "" clears it
```

| Follows the change, from each agent's next turn                                              | Does not                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Speech-output language on every agent                                                        | A knowledge base already bound to a node                                              |
| The `{{language}}` template keys                                                             | Canned lines already bound to a node                                                  |
| Ticked non-structural prompt fields (system prompt, template, instruction, acknowledge text) | A ticked ClassifyIntent entry prompt — that list is structural, so recreate the agent |
| File resolution for the *next* load                                                          | A voice input already open                                                            |

Ticked prompts are resolved by your localization system. See [Localize prompts with your localization system](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/localize-prompts.html).

The right-hand column is structural — those parameters are fixed at agent creation. So a live switch is the right tool for the **voice and prompt** half; changing *authored content* still means recreating agents. Most games treat a language change as "set it, then reload the scene", which gets both halves.

It is also not turn-atomic: switch mid-sentence and that one line may be written in the old language and spoken in the new one. Send it between turns.

A live switch does not re-check existing agents. If their TTS model does not declare the new language, no `3017` is raised — the voice just speaks with the model's own handling of that tag. Check coverage before switching live (for example with `TryllLanguages.Offerable`).

## 3. Ship translated content files

Translations live in a **`loc/<language>/` folder beside the file you link**.

```
StorageData/
  deathonset/
    lore.json                 ← you link this; it is the default content
    canned.txt
    loc/
      de/lore.json            ← used when the session runs in German
      pt-BR/lore.json
  shared/
    intent_ids.json           ← no loc/ folder = language-neutral, on purpose
```

Resolution, most specific first:

```
deathonset/loc/pt-BR/lore.json      ← used if it exists
deathonset/loc/pt/lore.json         ← else if it exists
deathonset/lore.json                ← else: the file you linked
```

Three consequences worth internalising:

- **You always link the default file.** Never a path inside `loc/`. The graph names one path and the shipped folder decides which language answers. If you browse to a translation by mistake, the editor offers to link the default instead.
- **A folder with no `loc/` is language-neutral.** That is the whole declaration — no flag, no metadata. Intent IDs, guardrail patterns and other config just sit there and are shared by every language.
- **Fallback is per file.** Ship `loc/de/lore.json` before `loc/de/canned.txt` exists and only the knowledge base switches. A partially translated game works.

This covers every file-backed parameter: knowledge bases and their `.usearch`/`.bm25` sidecars, canned responses, guardrail patterns, intent maps, voice-input hotwords, and the voice profile's reference clips (including each delivery mode's clip).

`loc` is a reserved folder name

Do not use `loc/` for your own content inside a storage folder. A project that wants symmetry may also ship `loc/en/`, but nothing requires it — the linked file *is* the default.

You may not need to translate knowledge bases at all

With a multilingual embedding model, `Retrieve` and `ClassifyIntent` match a German question against an English knowledge base, so the model only has to *read* English and *write* German. That removes most of the translation cost. It only helps the dense leg — BM25 cannot match across languages, so `Hybrid` retrieval degrades to dense-only.

## 4. Make the model write the language

The generated half has no string to translate, so it needs a prompt strategy. Three options, in increasing order of quality:

**a. Ask, from the template.** Three keys are available wherever Mustache rendering is supported — on `Generate`, `GenerateAndSpeak`, `ToolCall` and `Transform`:

| Key                 | Renders                                                        |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `{{language}}`      | `German` — the English language name, which models follow best |
| `{{locale}}`        | `de-DE` — the full tag                                         |
| `{{language_code}}` | `de` — the bare code                                           |

```
{{#language}}Always reply in {{language}}.{{/language}}
{{user_message}}
```

The section collapses to nothing when no language is set, so the same template works unlocalized.

**b. Author the prompt in the target language.** Writing the system prompt *in* German reduces mid-response drift far more reliably than an English prompt asking for German. Tick **Localized** on that field and store the text in your localization system — see [Localize prompts with your localization system](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/how-to/localize-prompts.html). The `loc/` lookup in §3 applies to file-backed storage params. Inline prompt text on the workflow is sent as authored until you tick Localized.

**c. Use a different model per language.** A node's `model_name` can differ per locale. A model genuinely strong in the target language beats prompt engineering on a weak one.

**The criticality gradient.** Critical narrative lines → `CannedResponse` + `Speak` with fully translated text (zero model risk). Constrained barks → a per-language `grammar`. Ambient chatter → free generation. This lets you ship a locale where the model is mediocre without shipping mediocre *important* lines.

## 5. Voice in and out

**TTS.** Every agent's [voice profile](https://docs.tryllengine.com/v0.9/reference/voice-profile.html) uses the session language as its `lang` default. A profile that sets its own **Lang** still wins — use that only to override one character (a French witness in a German playthrough), never to set the game's language. Fixed-language voices (Pocket TTS, Orpheus, Maya1) reject a non-empty **Lang**; leave it empty.

**STT.** A multilingual recognizer (Whisper, Canary) receives the language as a hint. A recognizer whose weights fix its language ignores it: with STT the model choice *is* the language choice.

Speaking a language the recognizer was not told about

A wrong language hint does not fail loudly — Whisper returns confident nonsense. This is why Tryll only passes the hint to models whose catalog declares that language, and refuses the combination outright rather than guessing.

## 6. Errors you will see

| Error                             | Means                                                                                       | Fix                                                                                       |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `InvalidLocale` (2004)            | The tag is not `language[-script][-region]`                                                 | Use `de`, `de-DE`, `pt-BR`                                                                |
| `ModelLanguageUnsupported` (3017) | A voice or voice input would rely on the session language but its model does not declare it | Pick a covering model, set the voice profile's own `lang`, or change the session language |

`3017` is raised when a speaking agent's voice is set (at **agent creation** or `SetAgentVoice`) and at **CreateVoiceInput** for STT — the same mismatch the inspector warned about, at the point it starts to matter. Three deliberate exemptions: a voice with its own `lang` is never checked (you opted out of the session language), a model that declares *no* languages is never checked (undeclared means unknown, not unsupported), and an agent whose graph never speaks is never checked.

## 7. Never translate these

Translating identifiers breaks routing **silently** rather than loudly:

`intents_ids` · slot names (`output_name`, `input`) · node names · exit names (`*_exit`) · variable names and `__MARKER__` names · storage names · model catalog names · tool names and parameter names.

Related: branch on variables or intent IDs, never on literal model output — `BranchParams.values` matched against text is a localization trap.

## What to expect

- **Token cost rises.** Non-English text runs roughly 2–4× the tokens for the same content, which changes `context_size` sizing, when history starts being trimmed, and per-turn latency. A graph tuned in English can degrade in Japanese with no visible cause.
- **Writing quality drops before reading quality does.** Small on-device models understand a language long before they write it well. If prose is poor, the fix is §4b or §4c — not more instructions.
- **Most studios ship the AI feature in fewer locales than the game.** That is a legitimate answer, and usually the right one.
